context.Background() returns an empty, non-cancellable root context, used at the top of a program or request as the starting point. You build real contexts from it with WithCancel, WithTimeout, or WithValue. context.TODO() is similar but signals 'I have not decided which context to use yet'.

errgroup from golang.org/x/sync runs a group of goroutines and collects the first error any of them returns. You call g.Go(func) for each task and g.Wait() to block until all finish, getting back the first non-nil error. errgroup.WithContext also cancels the shared context as soon as one goroutine fails, stopping the others.

golang.org/x/sync/semaphore provides a weighted semaphore to limit how many goroutines do something at once. You Acquire(ctx, n) before the work and Release(n) after, blocking when the total weight would exceed the limit. It is a clean way to throttle concurrency, like allowing only 10 simultaneous downloads.

singleflight collapses duplicate concurrent calls for the same key into one actual execution, sharing the result among all callers. If ten goroutines ask for the same cache key at once, only one runs the expensive fetch and the others receive its result. This prevents a 'thundering herd' of identical requests, common in caching layers.

runtime.NumGoroutine() returns the number of goroutines currently alive in the program. It is handy in debugging and tests to detect goroutine leaks—if the count keeps climbing, goroutines are not exiting. In production you usually expose this via metrics rather than calling it directly.

GOMAXPROCS sets how many OS threads can execute Go code simultaneously, effectively the number of P's in the scheduler. By default it equals the number of CPU cores available. In containers with CPU limits you may want to set it manually, and libraries like automaxprocs do this based on cgroup limits.

runtime.Gosched() voluntarily yields the processor, letting other goroutines run before resuming. Since Go's scheduler is preemptive (especially after Go 1.14), you rarely need it. It is mostly useful in tight loops without function calls in very old code, or in tests that want to nudge scheduling.

Since Go 1.14, the scheduler is asynchronously preemptive, meaning it can interrupt a goroutine even if it never makes a function call. Before that, a tight CPU-bound loop could hog a thread and starve other goroutines. Now the runtime sends a signal to pause long-running goroutines so others get a fair turn.

Channel types can be restricted to one direction: chan<- int is send-only and <-chan int is receive-only. Functions often declare parameters this way to document and enforce who sends and who receives. A bidirectional channel converts automatically to a directional one when passed to such a function.

Sending to or receiving from a nil channel blocks forever. This sounds like a bug but is useful in select statements: setting a channel variable to nil disables its case, letting you dynamically turn channel operations on and off. It is an advanced trick for building flexible pipelines.

The done-channel pattern uses a dedicated channel that is closed to signal goroutines to stop. Goroutines select on '<-done' and return when it closes, because a closed channel immediately yields. Today context.Context with its Done() channel has largely replaced hand-rolled done channels for cancellation.

A defer statement schedules a function call to run when the surrounding function returns, no matter how it exits. It is commonly used to close files, unlock mutexes, or call cancel() so cleanup is not forgotten. Deferred calls run in last-in-first-out order, and their arguments are evaluated when defer is reached, not when it runs.

panic stops normal execution and unwinds the stack running deferred functions; recover, called inside a deferred function, stops the unwinding and returns the panic value. Together they let a server catch a crash in one request handler without taking down the whole process. Idiomatic Go reserves panic for truly unexpected situations and uses error values for normal failures.

You can add a timeout to a channel operation by selecting on it and on time.After: 'case <-time.After(2*time.Second): handle timeout'. If the real channel does not deliver within the duration, the timeout case fires instead. For repeated or cancellable timeouts, a context with a deadline is usually cleaner than time.After.

time.After(d) returns a channel that delivers the current time after duration d, commonly used in select for timeouts. Each call creates a new timer that fires once. In tight loops it can leak timers until they fire, so for repeated use prefer a reusable time.Timer or time.NewTicker.

time.NewTicker delivers the time on its channel at a regular interval, used for periodic tasks like polling or heartbeats. You must call ticker.Stop() when done to release its resources, otherwise the underlying timer keeps running. Reading from ticker.C inside a for-select loop is the usual pattern.

time.NewTimer fires once after a duration, sending the time on its channel. Unlike Ticker it does not repeat, and you can call timer.Stop() to cancel it before it fires or timer.Reset() to restart it. Timers are the building block for one-shot delays and timeouts that you might cancel.

You must never copy a sync.Mutex (or a struct containing one) after it has been used, because the copy carries a stale lock state and breaks mutual exclusion. This is why you pass such structs by pointer, not by value. go vet's copylocks check catches accidental copies of locks.

The Go memory model defines 'happens-before' rules that say when one goroutine is guaranteed to see another's writes. For example, a channel send happens before the corresponding receive completes, and unlocking a mutex happens before the next lock. If no such relationship exists between two goroutines, you have a data race and the behavior is undefined.

Go uses composition through embedding: you put a type inside a struct without a field name, and its methods and fields are promoted to the outer struct. It is how Go reuses behavior instead of class inheritance. Embedding a sync.Mutex, for instance, lets you call Lock() directly on the outer struct.

A Go interface defines a set of method signatures, and any type that implements those methods satisfies the interface automatically—there is no 'implements' keyword. This implicit satisfaction keeps packages decoupled, since a type does not need to know about the interfaces it fulfills. Small interfaces like io.Reader and io.Writer are everywhere in the standard library.

The empty interface interface{} can hold a value of any type because every type implements zero methods. Since Go 1.18 the alias 'any' is the preferred spelling for it. You extract the concrete value with a type assertion or a type switch, and overusing it loses the safety of static typing.

A type assertion extracts the concrete value from an interface, written v, ok := x.(int). The ok form is safe: ok is false if the assertion fails. Without the ok variable, a failed assertion panics, so the two-value form is preferred when the type is uncertain.

A type switch chooses a branch based on the dynamic type held in an interface, written 'switch v := x.(type)'. Each case names a type, and inside that case v has that concrete type. It is the clean way to handle a value that could be one of several types.

Go added generics in version 1.18, letting you write functions and types parameterized by type, like func Max[T constraints.Ordered](a, b T) T. Type parameters use constraints (themselves interfaces) to limit which types are allowed. Generics reduce code duplication for containers and algorithms that previously needed interface{} or copy-paste.

A constraint in Go generics is an interface that specifies which types a type parameter accepts. The built-in 'comparable' constraint allows types usable with == and !=, needed for map keys. The golang.org/x/exp/constraints package and the standard 'cmp.Ordered' provide reusable constraints like Ordered for sortable types.

Go handles errors as ordinary values: functions return an error as their last result, and callers check 'if err != nil'. There are no exceptions for normal failures, which makes error paths explicit and visible in the code. This verbosity is intentional, forcing you to decide what to do at each failure point.

Since Go 1.13 you wrap an error with context using fmt.Errorf with the %w verb: fmt.Errorf("loading config: %w", err). The wrapping preserves the original error so callers can inspect it. This builds an error chain that shows where a failure happened and what the underlying cause was.

errors.Is reports whether an error, or anything it wraps, matches a target sentinel error like io.EOF. It walks the wrapped error chain so you can check for a specific cause even when the error has been annotated. Use it instead of == to compare wrapped errors.

errors.As searches an error chain for one of a specific type and, if found, assigns it to a variable so you can read its fields. For example, you can pull a *os.PathError out of a wrapped error to learn which file caused the problem. It is the typed counterpart to errors.Is.

A sentinel error is a predefined error value, like var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found"), that callers compare against to detect a known condition. Combined with error wrapping and errors.Is, sentinels let code react to specific failures. The standard library uses sentinels such as io.EOF and sql.ErrNoRows.

Build tags (build constraints) control which files are compiled for a given platform or condition, written as '//go:build linux' at the top of a file. They let you provide platform-specific implementations, like one file for Windows and another for Unix. The filename suffix style, like file_linux.go, achieves the same for OS and architecture.

Calling t.Parallel() inside a test signals that it can run concurrently with other parallel tests in the same package. Go pauses the test until all non-parallel tests finish, then runs the parallel ones together, speeding up suites with slow I/O. Each parallel test must avoid shared mutable state to stay correct.

Table-driven tests define a slice of test cases as structs, then loop over them running the same assertions. This pattern keeps tests compact and makes adding a new case as easy as adding a struct literal. Wrapping each case in t.Run(name, ...) gives every case its own named subtest in the output.

t.Run(name, func) creates a named subtest, which shows up separately in test output and can be selected individually with -run. Subtests make table-driven tests readable and let you target one failing case. Each subtest can call t.Parallel() to run alongside its siblings.

A benchmark function named BenchmarkXxx takes a *testing.B and loops b.N times over the code you want to measure, run via 'go test -bench'. The framework chooses b.N automatically to get a stable timing. You use b.ReportAllocs() to also report memory allocations per operation.

In a benchmark, b.ResetTimer() discards any setup time before the measured loop so expensive preparation does not skew results. You call it after building test data but before the 'for i := 0; i < b.N; i++' loop. There are also b.StopTimer and b.StartTimer for pausing measurement mid-loop.

Go added native fuzzing in version 1.18 with FuzzXxx functions that take a *testing.F. You seed inputs with f.Add and provide a fuzz target with f.Fuzz; running 'go test -fuzz' then generates random inputs to find crashes and edge cases. Any failing input is saved as a regression seed so the bug stays tested.

pprof is Go's built-in profiler for CPU, memory, goroutines, and blocking. You collect a profile with 'go test -cpuprofile' or by importing net/http/pprof in a server, then analyze it with 'go tool pprof'. It produces flame graphs and call lists that show exactly where time or memory is spent.

Importing net/http/pprof for its side effects registers profiling handlers under /debug/pprof on the default HTTP mux. You can then grab a live CPU or heap profile from a running server with 'go tool pprof http://host/debug/pprof/profile'. It is the standard way to profile production Go services.

The Go execution tracer records detailed runtime events—goroutine scheduling, GC, syscalls, channel blocking—into a trace file. You collect it with runtime/trace or 'go test -trace' and view it in a browser with 'go tool trace'. It is the best tool for understanding concurrency problems like why goroutines stall.

Escape analysis is the compiler's process of deciding whether a value can live on the stack or must 'escape' to the heap. Stack allocations are free to clean up, while heap allocations create garbage-collector work. You can see the decisions with 'go build -gcflags=-m', which helps you spot unexpected heap allocations in hot code.

Go uses a concurrent, tri-color mark-and-sweep garbage collector designed for low pause times, usually well under a millisecond. It runs alongside your program rather than stopping it for long, trading a bit of CPU for short, predictable pauses. GOGC and the soft memory limit (GOMEMLIMIT) let you tune how aggressively it collects.

GOGC controls the garbage collector's aggressiveness; the default 100 means GC runs when the heap doubles since the last collection. Raising it (e.g., 200) collects less often, using more memory but less CPU; lowering it does the opposite. Since Go 1.19 you can also set GOMEMLIMIT to cap total memory as a complementary control.

GOMEMLIMIT, added in Go 1.19, sets a soft limit on the total memory the Go runtime targets, like GOMEMLIMIT=512MiB. The garbage collector works harder to stay under it, which helps avoid out-of-memory kills in containers. It is 'soft' because the runtime will exceed it rather than stall the program completely.

By convention, when a Go function takes a context, it is the first parameter and named ctx. This consistency means callers always know where to pass cancellation and deadlines. You should not store a Context in a struct field; instead pass it explicitly down each call.

A channel of struct{} carries no data and is used purely for signalling, since the empty struct occupies zero bytes. Patterns like done := make(chan struct{}) and 'close(done)' broadcast an event to many waiters efficiently. It clearly communicates 'this channel is a signal, not a data pipe'.

Use a mutex when goroutines share and mutate a single piece of state, like a counter or cache, where guarding access is simplest. Use a channel when you want to transfer ownership of data or coordinate sequencing between goroutines. The Go team's guidance is to pick whichever makes the code clearer, not to force channels everywhere.

Goroutines are much lighter than operating-system threads: they start with a tiny growable stack and are scheduled in user space by the Go runtime, not the OS. Creating a million goroutines is feasible, while a million OS threads would exhaust memory. The runtime multiplexes many goroutines onto a small pool of real threads.

Adding a default case to a select makes channel operations non-blocking: if no case is ready, the default runs immediately. This lets you 'try' to send or receive without waiting, useful for polling or dropping work when a buffer is full. Without a default, select blocks until some case becomes ready.

Closing a channel is a one-time broadcast: every goroutine receiving from it wakes up at once because receives on a closed channel return immediately. This is why closing—not sending—is how you tell many goroutines to stop. You cannot reopen a closed channel, so it models a permanent event like shutdown.

To safely increment a shared counter across goroutines, use atomic.Int64 with its Add method, or guard a plain int with a mutex. A bare 'count++' from multiple goroutines is a data race because the read-modify-write is not atomic. The atomic approach is fastest for a simple counter, while a mutex is clearer when several fields change together.

keywords: go context not for optional params
facts.answer: It is bad practice to use context.WithValue for ordinary function parameters or configuration. Context values are meant only for request-scoped data that must cross API boundaries, like a trace ID or authenticated user. Hiding required inputs in the context makes functions harder to understand and test.

Choosing a channel's buffer size is a tuning decision: a buffer absorbs bursts so a fast producer does not stall on a slow consumer. Too small a buffer causes blocking; too large hides backpressure and wastes memory. Unbuffered (size zero) is the safe default because it forces a synchronization handshake and reveals slow consumers.

go test -cover reports the percentage of statements executed by your tests, and -coverprofile writes a file you can inspect. 'go tool cover -html=cover.out' opens a browser view highlighting covered and uncovered lines. Coverage is a guide, not a goal—100 percent does not mean bug-free, but low coverage flags untested code.

Calling t.Helper() inside a test helper function tells the testing framework to report failures at the caller's line, not inside the helper. This makes failure messages point to the actual test case rather than the shared assertion code. It is a small touch that makes table-driven tests much easier to debug.

t.Cleanup registers a function to run when the test (and its subtests) finish, similar to defer but tied to the test's lifecycle. It is great for tearing down resources like temp files or test servers, and cleanups run in last-registered-first order. Unlike defer, it works correctly across subtests and parallel tests.

The net/http/httptest package helps test HTTP code without a real network. httptest.NewServer starts a real local server for integration-style tests, while httptest.NewRecorder captures a handler's response for unit tests. It is the standard tool for testing Go web servers and clients.

Cancelling a parent context automatically cancels all of its child contexts. This cascade lets a single cancel() at the top of a request abort every downstream operation—database queries, HTTP calls, and goroutines—built from that context. It is the core mechanism behind clean, fast shutdown in Go services.

time.Sleep pauses the current goroutine for a duration without blocking others, since the scheduler runs other goroutines meanwhile. While fine for backoff or demos, relying on Sleep for coordination is fragile; channels or sync primitives are more reliable. For cancellable delays, select on time.After and ctx.Done() instead.

golang.org/x/time/rate provides a token-bucket rate limiter, the standard way to cap how fast operations occur in Go. You create a limiter with rate.NewLimiter(eventsPerSecond, burst) and call Wait(ctx) or Allow() before each action. It smoothly throttles API calls or background work while respecting context cancellation.

Since Go 1.20, context.WithCancelCause lets you attach a specific error explaining why a context was cancelled, retrieved with context.Cause(ctx). This is more informative than the generic context.Canceled error. It helps debugging by recording which goroutine or condition triggered the cancellation.

errgroup.Group has a SetLimit method that caps how many goroutines run concurrently within the group. Calls to g.Go beyond the limit block until a slot frees up, turning errgroup into a bounded worker pool with error collection built in. It combines concurrency limiting and first-error handling in one tool.

When multiple cases in a select are ready at the same time, Go chooses one uniformly at random. This randomness prevents starvation, so a busy channel cannot permanently block a quieter one. You cannot rely on case order for priority; if you need priority, use nested selects with a default.

Contexts form a tree: each WithCancel, WithTimeout, or WithValue creates a child rooted at a parent. Cancellation flows downward (cancelling a parent cancels children) but never upward. Understanding this tree explains why you build a fresh context per request from Background rather than reusing one globally.

A sync.Mutex is ready to use in its zero value, so 'var mu sync.Mutex' needs no initialization before Lock(). The same is true for WaitGroup, Once, and RWMutex. This zero-value-usable design means you can embed them in structs without a constructor.

Slices and maps are not safe for concurrent writes; appending to a slice from multiple goroutines races on its length and backing array. You must guard shared slices with a mutex, send results over a channel, or give each goroutine its own slice and merge later. The race detector reliably catches these mistakes.

Writing to a built-in map from multiple goroutines at once triggers a runtime panic: 'fatal error: concurrent map writes'. The runtime added this check specifically to surface a common bug instead of silently corrupting the map. Protect shared maps with a sync.Mutex or use sync.Map for concurrent access.

The for-select loop is the workhorse of long-running goroutines: an infinite for loop containing a select that handles incoming work, ticks, and a ctx.Done() case for shutdown. It keeps the goroutine responsive to multiple events. Putting ctx.Done() in the select gives the goroutine a clean exit when the context is cancelled.

In a pipeline, each stage should watch a done channel or ctx.Done() so it can stop sending when downstream stages quit early. Otherwise an abandoned downstream stage leaves upstream goroutines blocked on a full channel, leaking them. Wiring cancellation through every stage is essential for a leak-free pipeline.

Bounded parallelism means running at most N tasks at once instead of spawning one goroutine per item. You achieve it with a buffered channel used as a counting semaphore, a worker pool reading a jobs channel, or errgroup.SetLimit. Bounding prevents resource exhaustion when processing huge numbers of items.

A buffered channel can act as a counting semaphore: fill a slot before work (sem <- struct{}{}) and drain one after (<-sem), with the buffer size as the concurrency limit. Sends block when the buffer is full, so only that many goroutines proceed at once. It is a simple, dependency-free way to throttle goroutines.

Storing a context.Context inside a struct is discouraged because a context describes a single operation's lifetime, while a struct usually outlives one operation. Doing so leads to using a stale or wrong context. The recommended approach is to pass ctx explicitly as a method parameter each time.

A TestMain function lets you control setup and teardown for an entire test package, useful for spinning up a database or shared server once. It receives a *testing.M, does setup, calls m.Run() to execute the tests, then does teardown before os.Exit. Without TestMain, Go runs tests directly with no package-level hook.

Staticcheck is a popular third-party static analysis tool that catches bugs, performance issues, and style problems beyond what go vet finds. It flags things like unused code, inefficient string building, and misuse of APIs. Many teams run it in CI as a stronger gate than vet alone.

golangci-lint is an aggregator that runs many Go linters (including staticcheck, govet, and errcheck) in parallel with shared caching. A single config file controls which linters run and their settings, making it the de facto standard for linting Go projects in CI. Its speed comes from running analyzers over a shared parse of the code.

errcheck is a linter that finds places where your code ignores a returned error. In Go it is easy to drop an error by not assigning it, which can hide failures like a file that did not actually close. errcheck flags those spots so you decide deliberately to handle or ignore each error.

goimports does everything gofmt does and also adds missing import statements and removes unused ones, sorting them into groups. Many editors run goimports on save so imports stay correct automatically. It is a small superset of gofmt that saves you from manually managing the import block.

The GOPROXY setting points Go at a module proxy that caches and serves dependency downloads, defaulting to proxy.golang.org. The proxy speeds up builds, provides reliable availability even if an original repo disappears, and works with the checksum database for integrity. You can set GOPROXY to a private proxy like Athens for company-internal modules.

The checksum database (sum.golang.org, set via GOSUMDB) is a public, tamper-evident log of module hashes. When you download a module for the first time, Go verifies its hash against this database to ensure no one swapped the code. Together with go.sum it protects the supply chain from compromised dependencies.

GOPRIVATE lists module path patterns, like company.com/*, that should bypass the public proxy and checksum database. This keeps internal code from being requested over the public internet and avoids checksum failures for private repos. It is the standard setting for using Go modules inside a company.

go mod vendor copies all your dependencies into a local 'vendor' directory so builds do not need network access. When a vendor directory is present, Go builds from it by default, which some teams use for hermetic or air-gapped builds. The trade-off is a larger repository and the need to re-vendor when dependencies change.

A replace directive in go.mod redirects a module path to a different version or a local directory, useful for testing a fork or local fix. For example, 'replace example.com/lib => ../lib' points to a sibling folder during development. For multi-module local development, go workspaces (go.work) are now the cleaner alternative.

Go uses semantic import versioning: a module's major version v2 or higher must appear in its import path, like example.com/lib/v2. This lets v1 and v2 of a library coexist in one build without conflict. It is why upgrading a Go dependency across a major version means changing your import statements.

Go's dependency resolution uses Minimal Version Selection: it picks the lowest version of each module that still satisfies all requirements. This is deliberately conservative, producing reproducible builds without surprise upgrades. It contrasts with package managers that grab the newest matching version, which can change unexpectedly.

The //go:embed directive, added in Go 1.16, bakes files into the compiled binary at build time. You declare a variable of type string, []byte, or embed.FS and tag it with a comment naming the files. It is perfect for shipping templates, static web assets, or migrations inside a single self-contained executable.

ctx.Err() returns nil while a context is active, context.Canceled if it was cancelled, or context.DeadlineExceeded if its deadline passed. After noticing ctx.Done() fires, goroutines often return ctx.Err() so callers learn why the operation stopped. Checking it lets you distinguish a timeout from an explicit cancellation.

To send with a timeout, select between the send case and a time.After case: if the receiver is too slow, the timeout fires and you drop or retry the value. This prevents a goroutine from blocking forever on a full or unread channel. Pairing it with ctx.Done() makes the send both time-limited and cancellable.

A heartbeat is a periodic signal a worker goroutine sends to prove it is alive and making progress. A monitor watches the heartbeat channel and, if it stops arriving within an interval, assumes the worker is stuck and restarts or cancels it. Heartbeats make long-running concurrent systems observable and self-healing.

The or-channel pattern merges several done channels into one that closes as soon as any of them closes. It is built recursively with select and is handy when an operation should stop if any of multiple cancellation signals fire. Today, combining contexts often replaces hand-written or-channels.

A tee-channel takes one input channel and duplicates every value onto two output channels, like a 'tee' in plumbing. It lets two downstream consumers each see the full stream independently. Care is needed so a slow consumer on one branch does not block the other, often handled with buffering or select.

A bridge consumes a channel of channels and flattens it into a single stream of values. It is useful when one stage produces a sequence of channels (for example one per batch) and a downstream stage wants to read them all as one continuous flow. The bridge reads each inner channel to completion before moving to the next.

Confinement is a concurrency technique where data is only ever accessed by one goroutine, removing the need for synchronization entirely. Lexical confinement enforces this through scope—for example, a goroutine owns a slice no other goroutine can reach. Confined data is race-free by construction, which is simpler and faster than locking.

To make any channel operation cancellable, put both the operation and ctx.Done() in a select: 'select { case v := <-ch: ...; case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err() }'. When the context is cancelled, the goroutine stops waiting and returns instead of blocking forever. This single pattern is the backbone of cancellable concurrent Go.

runtime.GC() forces an immediate garbage collection and blocks until it finishes. It is occasionally useful in tests or benchmarks to get a clean baseline, but you should not call it routinely in production, since the automatic collector tunes itself better. Forcing GC can hurt performance by collecting when it is not needed.

The GODEBUG environment variable toggles runtime debugging features without recompiling, such as GODEBUG=gctrace=1 to print a line on every garbage collection. Other options trace the scheduler or memory allocator. It is a quick way to observe runtime behavior in a running program for diagnosis.

Setting GODEBUG=gctrace=1 makes the runtime print a summary after each garbage collection, including pause times, heap sizes, and how many CPUs the GC used. Reading these lines helps you understand GC frequency and pause behavior under load. It is a lightweight diagnostic before reaching for full profiling.

GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000 prints a scheduler summary every 1000 milliseconds, showing how many goroutines, threads, and idle processors exist. Adding scheddetail=1 gives a per-P breakdown. These traces help diagnose why goroutines are not getting CPU time, such as one P being overloaded.

Go's scheduler uses work-stealing: each P has its own local run queue, and an idle P steals goroutines from a busy P's queue to keep all processors busy. This balances load without a single global lock on the run queue. Work-stealing is a key reason Go scales well across many cores.

The Go runtime includes an integrated network poller built on epoll, kqueue, or IOCP. When a goroutine does a blocking network read, the runtime parks it and lets the thread run other goroutines, waking the parked one when data arrives. This is how Go handles tens of thousands of network connections with few threads while code looks synchronous.

When a goroutine makes a blocking system call (like a file read), the runtime detaches the goroutine's P from its thread so the P can run other goroutines on a different thread. After the syscall returns, the goroutine reacquires a P to continue. This handoff prevents one slow syscall from stalling unrelated goroutines.

The Go memory model guarantees that a send on a channel happens before the corresponding receive completes, and the close of a channel happens before a receive that returns the zero value. These rules mean a value sent over a channel, plus everything written before the send, is safely visible to the receiver. That is why channels can transfer data without extra locks.

A plain break inside a select only exits the select, not an enclosing for loop, which surprises newcomers. To break out of a for-select loop you use a labeled break (break Loop) or set a flag and return. Knowing this avoids the bug where a goroutine never leaves its loop after a shutdown signal.

Even when using WithTimeout, you should still call the returned cancel function, usually via defer cancel(). If the work finishes before the timeout, cancel() releases the timer immediately instead of letting it fire later. Skipping it causes go vet's lostcancel check to complain and leaks a timer until the deadline.

Classic double-checked locking is error-prone in Go's memory model and unnecessary because sync.Once does the same job safely. Once.Do guarantees exactly-once initialization with the correct memory ordering across goroutines. Reaching for sync.Once instead of hand-rolled locking is the idiomatic choice.

A sync.RWMutex read lock cannot be upgraded to a write lock; you must RUnlock and then Lock, accepting that the data may change in between. Attempting to call Lock while holding RLock deadlocks. This limitation pushes you to design code that decides up front whether it needs to write.

When using context.WithValue, the key should be an unexported custom type, like 'type ctxKey int', not a plain string. This prevents key collisions between different packages storing values in the same context. Returning a typed getter function alongside it keeps the value access type-safe.

Because select picks randomly among ready cases, you cannot directly express priority. A common workaround is a nested select: first try the high-priority channel with a default, and only if it is empty fall through to a normal select. This lets urgent work jump ahead of routine work.

To fan in several channels, start one goroutine per input that forwards values to a shared output channel, and use a WaitGroup to close the output once all inputs are drained. The merge goroutine pattern lets multiple producers feed a single consumer cleanly. Closing the output only after wg.Wait() avoids closing it while a producer is still sending.

runtime.LockOSThread() pins the current goroutine to its current OS thread until you call UnlockOSThread. It is needed when calling C libraries or OS APIs that rely on thread-local state, like some graphics or signal handling. It is rare in everyday Go but essential for certain cgo and OS-level interactions.

Calling C code via cgo can block an OS thread for the duration of the C call, so heavy cgo use can starve the goroutine scheduler of threads. The runtime spins up extra threads to compensate, but this adds overhead. Designs that minimize cgo calls or batch them keep Go's lightweight concurrency advantages.

To drain a channel without blocking, loop with a select that receives in one case and breaks on default when nothing remains. Draining is sometimes needed before reusing a buffered channel or after stopping producers so no values are lost. For closed channels, a simple 'for range ch' drains all buffered values.

Well-behaved Go libraries accept a context and stop their work promptly when ctx.Done() fires, returning ctx.Err(). Standard library calls like database queries, HTTP requests, and net dials already honor context cancellation. Ignoring the passed context is a common bug that makes callers' timeouts and cancellations useless.

Use a plain sync.WaitGroup when goroutines cannot fail or you collect errors yourself, and errgroup when you want the first error and shared cancellation handled for you. errgroup wraps a WaitGroup plus error and context plumbing in a tidy API. For most request-scoped parallel work, errgroup is the more ergonomic choice.

A select with no cases, written 'select {}', blocks the goroutine forever. It is occasionally used in a main function to keep a program running while background goroutines do the work. Be aware it consumes no CPU but the goroutine can never exit, so it suits servers that run until killed.

A buffered channel naturally acts as a thread-safe FIFO queue between producers and consumers, with the buffer size as the maximum backlog. Producers block when it is full, providing built-in backpressure. For more than simple producer-consumer queuing, a worker pool reading the channel spreads the load across goroutines.

In Go HTTP servers, each incoming request carries its own context, accessed via r.Context(), that is cancelled automatically if the client disconnects or the handler returns. Passing this context into downstream calls means abandoned requests stop wasting resources. Building per-request contexts is fundamental to writing efficient Go services.

http.Server.Shutdown(ctx) stops accepting new connections and waits for in-flight requests to finish before returning, giving a graceful shutdown. You pass a context with a deadline so it does not wait forever for stuck requests. Triggering Shutdown on an OS interrupt signal lets a service drain cleanly during a deploy.

signal.NotifyContext, added in Go 1.16, returns a context that is cancelled when the program receives a given OS signal like SIGINT or SIGTERM. It cleanly ties Ctrl+C or a container stop to context cancellation, so all goroutines watching that context shut down together. It replaced the older pattern of a signal channel plus manual plumbing.

A panic in any goroutine that is not recovered crashes the entire program, not just that goroutine. There is no way to recover a panic from a different goroutine, so each goroutine that might panic should defer its own recover if you want it to survive. This is why you cannot wrap go statements in a single recover.

keywords: go context timeout vs server timeout
facts.answer: Robust Go services layer timeouts: the HTTP server has read and write timeouts, each handler derives a context timeout, and downstream calls inherit that context. The shortest deadline wins, ensuring no single request can hang resources indefinitely. Coordinating these layers prevents both leaks and premature cutoffs.

A single select can wait on receives from several channels at once, processing whichever delivers first. This multiplexing lets one goroutine coordinate inputs from many sources—work, ticks, and cancellation—without spawning extra goroutines. Adding new channels to the select extends what the goroutine reacts to.

A channel variable declared without make is nil, and operations on it block forever. Forgetting to call make before sending is a classic deadlock bug. The nil-blocks-forever behavior is intentional and even useful for disabling select cases, but unintentional nil channels cause hard-to-spot hangs.

Running 'go test -race ./...' in continuous integration catches data races before they reach production. Because the detector only finds races exercised by the tests, broad concurrency tests increase its effectiveness. The flag roughly doubles memory use and slows tests, but the bugs it catches are worth it.

When you derive a child context with a timeout, it can only make the deadline shorter, never longer than the parent's. If the parent is already cancelled or past its deadline, the child is too. This monotonic shrinking guarantees that a sub-operation never outlives the request that spawned it.

keywords: go select to implement timeout loop
facts.answer: You can build a retry-with-overall-timeout loop using a for-select that races a per-attempt timer against an overall ctx.Done(). Each iteration tries the work, and if the context expires the loop returns ctx.Err(). This pattern is common for polling external systems that may need several attempts within a budget.

You must call wg.Add before starting the goroutine, not inside it, otherwise wg.Wait might return before the goroutine even registers. The correct pattern is wg.Add(1) on the calling goroutine, then 'go func(){ defer wg.Done(); ... }()'. Misplacing Add is a subtle bug that causes premature continuation.

Even a buffered channel can deadlock: if the buffer fills and no goroutine ever receives, the next send blocks forever. Buffering only delays, not removes, the need for a consumer. Sizing a buffer to avoid blocking is a tuning aid, but a working consumer is what actually prevents the deadlock.

keywords: go context with cancel always cancel
facts.answer: context.WithCancel returns a cancel function that you must call to release the resources the context holds, even if you never use cancellation. Failing to call it leaks the context's internal goroutine and memory until the parent is cancelled. The idiom 'defer cancel()' right after creation guards against this leak.

keywords: go select to merge with cancel
facts.answer: A cancellable fan-in adds a ctx.Done() case to the merge goroutines so they stop forwarding when the context is cancelled. This prevents merge goroutines from blocking on a full output channel after downstream consumers have quit. Wiring cancellation into the merge is what makes fan-in leak-free under early exit.

Sending SIGQUIT to a Go program (Ctrl+\ on Unix) makes it print the stack traces of all goroutines before exiting. This dump is invaluable for diagnosing deadlocks and leaks, since it shows exactly where each goroutine is blocked. You can also trigger it in code with the runtime's Stack function for a smaller subset.

The goroutine profile from pprof lists every live goroutine grouped by where it is blocked, which is the fastest way to find goroutine leaks. A growing count of goroutines stuck in the same channel receive points straight at the leak. You can fetch it from a server at /debug/pprof/goroutine.

The block profile records where goroutines spend time blocked on synchronization, like waiting for a mutex or channel. You enable it with runtime.SetBlockProfileRate and view it via pprof. It pinpoints contention that slows your program even when CPU usage looks fine.

The mutex profile reports which mutexes goroutines contend on the most, enabled with runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction. When a program is slower than its CPU usage suggests, mutex contention is a likely culprit, and this profile shows the hottest locks. The fix is often finer-grained locking or switching to RWMutex or atomics.

context.AfterFunc, added in Go 1.21, registers a function to run in its own goroutine when a context is cancelled or times out. It returns a stop function to unregister if you no longer need it. It is a tidy way to trigger cleanup on cancellation without manually selecting on ctx.Done().

context.WithoutCancel, added in Go 1.21, derives a context that keeps the parent's values but is not cancelled when the parent is. It is useful when you start background work that should outlive the originating request, such as logging or cleanup that must finish even after the client disconnects. Use it deliberately, since it deliberately breaks cancellation propagation.

Go 1.21 added WithDeadlineCause and WithTimeoutCause, which let you attach a custom error explaining a timeout, readable via context.Cause. This gives more descriptive diagnostics than the generic DeadlineExceeded. It pairs with WithCancelCause to make all cancellation paths self-documenting.

log/slog, added in Go 1.21, is the standard library's structured logging package, producing key-value logs in text or JSON. You attach attributes like slog.Int("count", n) and choose handlers and log levels. Structured logs are far easier for machines to parse and query than free-form text, which matters in production services.

The standard 'maps' package, stabilized in Go 1.21, offers generic helpers like maps.Keys, maps.Values, maps.Clone, and maps.Equal. These replace hand-written loops for common map operations and work on any map type thanks to generics. They make map manipulation more concise and less error-prone.

The standard 'slices' package, added in Go 1.21, provides generic functions like slices.Sort, slices.Contains, slices.Index, and slices.Equal. Before generics, sorting required sort.Slice with a closure; now slices.Sort works directly on ordered element types. It significantly cuts boilerplate for everyday slice work.

The 'cmp' package, added in Go 1.21, defines the Ordered constraint plus helpers like cmp.Compare and cmp.Less for generic comparisons. It underpins the slices and maps packages' sorting and equality functions. cmp.Or, added later, returns the first non-zero of its arguments, handy for defaults.

Go 1.23 introduced range-over-function iterators, letting you write 'for v := range myIterator' where myIterator is a function with a specific signature. This standardizes custom iteration so libraries can offer iterators that plug into the familiar range loop. The iter package defines the Seq and Seq2 iterator types.

The iter package, added in Go 1.23, defines iterator types Seq[V] and Seq2[K,V] used by range-over-function. Functions returning these can be ranged over directly, and the slices and maps packages gained iterator-returning helpers like slices.All and maps.Keys. It gives Go a uniform, lazy iteration story.

Go 1.22 changed loop variables so each iteration of a for loop gets a fresh copy. This fixes the infamous bug where goroutines launched in a loop all captured the same variable and saw the final value. Code that previously needed 'i := i' shadowing inside the loop no longer does.

Go 1.22 added the ability to range over an integer, writing 'for i := range 10' to loop from 0 to 9. It is a small convenience that replaces the classic three-clause for loop for simple counted iteration. The loop variable is the index, just like ranging a slice.

The toolchain directive in go.mod, introduced in Go 1.21, lets a module declare which Go toolchain version it needs, like 'toolchain go1.22.0'. If your installed Go is older, it automatically downloads and uses the requested toolchain. This makes builds reproducible across machines with different Go installations.

Go 1.21 added built-in min and max functions that work on any ordered type and accept two or more arguments, like max(a, b, c). They are evaluated at compile time for constants. These builtins remove the need for tiny helper functions or importing a package for such a basic operation.

The built-in clear function, added in Go 1.21, empties a map or zeroes the elements of a slice in place. For maps, clear(m) deletes all keys; for slices, clear(s) sets each element to its zero value. It is more efficient and clearer than looping to delete keys one by one.

keywords: go context cancel in HTTP client
facts.answer: An http.Request carries a context (set via req.WithContext or r.Context() in a handler), and the HTTP client aborts the request if that context is cancelled. This is how you enforce a timeout on an outbound call or cancel it when the upstream request is cancelled. Forgetting to pass a context means the call can hang past your intended deadline.

Go 1.24 added b.Loop() as a cleaner benchmark loop: 'for b.Loop() { ... }' replaces the manual 'for i := 0; i < b.N; i++'. It automatically handles timer resetting and prevents the compiler from optimizing away the loop body. It makes benchmarks shorter and less error-prone.

Go 1.24 added a Context method on testing.T and B that returns a context cancelled when the test finishes. Passing t.Context() into code under test ensures any goroutines it starts are cancelled at test end, helping catch leaks. It standardizes the previously hand-rolled per-test context.

Go 1.24 added a 'tool' directive in go.mod to track command-line tool dependencies, replacing the old tools.go file trick. You add a tool with 'go get -tool' and run it with 'go tool', and its version is recorded in go.mod. This keeps a project's development tools versioned alongside its code.

b.RunParallel runs a benchmark body across multiple goroutines to measure performance under concurrency. Each goroutine repeatedly calls pb.Next() in a loop until the benchmark's iteration budget is spent. It is the right tool for benchmarking code meant to be hit by many goroutines, like a concurrent cache.

For a context that can never be cancelled (like context.Background), Done() may return nil, and selecting on a nil channel simply never fires—correct behavior with no cost. For cancellable contexts, the Done channel is created lazily on first call. This design keeps non-cancellable contexts cheap.

A common concurrent cache uses a sync.RWMutex around a map, taking the read lock for lookups and the write lock for inserts. To avoid duplicate expensive computations for the same key under load, combine it with singleflight so only one goroutine computes a missing value. This pattern balances read throughput with safe writes.

errgroup.WithContext returns a group and a derived context that is cancelled the moment any goroutine in the group returns an error. Goroutines should watch that context so siblings stop quickly once one fails. This turns a batch of parallel tasks into an all-or-nothing operation that aborts fast on the first failure.

You can throttle a loop by selecting on a time.Ticker so each iteration waits for the next tick before proceeding. This spreads work out at a steady rate, useful for politely polling an API. Combining the ticker case with a ctx.Done() case lets the throttled loop also shut down cleanly.

Starting a goroutine costs only a few hundred nanoseconds and a tiny initial stack, far cheaper than an OS thread. This cheapness is why Go programs freely spawn a goroutine per connection or per request. Still, unbounded goroutine creation can exhaust memory, so high-volume systems use pools or limits.

When many goroutines can fail, one approach is sending each error to a buffered error channel and reading them after all finish. Buffering the channel to the number of goroutines prevents senders from blocking if no one is reading yet. For request-scoped work, errgroup usually handles this collection more cleanly.

Looking up a context value walks the linked chain of parent contexts until it finds the key, so deeply nested contexts make lookups slightly slower. In practice the chains are short and the cost negligible. Still, this is another reason to use context values sparingly and only for genuinely request-scoped data.

keywords: go select with send and receive
facts.answer: A single select can mix send and receive cases, choosing whichever is ready. This lets a goroutine both accept new work and emit results in the same loop without two separate goroutines. Mixing directions in one select is common in mediator or pump goroutines that shuttle data between channels.

runtime.ReadMemStats fills a struct with detailed memory statistics like heap size, number of GC cycles, and total allocations. Programs expose these as metrics to watch memory behavior over time. Reading MemStats triggers a stop-the-world pause, so sample it sparingly rather than in a hot loop.

The GOTRACEBACK environment variable controls how much detail a panic or fatal crash prints. Values range from 'none' to 'all' (every goroutine) to 'crash' (also dumps a core file). Setting GOTRACEBACK=all is useful when diagnosing a crash that involves goroutine interactions.

Receiving from a closed channel never blocks; it returns the element type's zero value immediately, with the ok flag false. This is why a 'for range' over a closed channel ends and why a closed channel can broadcast to many receivers. Relying on the zero value alone is risky, so use the v, ok form to distinguish a real zero from a closed channel.

HTTP middleware in Go commonly enriches the request context, for example adding a request ID or authenticated user with r.WithContext(context.WithValue(...)). Downstream handlers then read those values from r.Context(). This is the canonical, correct use of context values: request-scoped data passing through layers.

keywords: go select to implement worker shutdown
facts.answer: A worker goroutine that should finish current work before stopping selects on both its jobs channel and ctx.Done(), but on cancellation it can choose to drain remaining buffered jobs first. Designing the shutdown semantics—abort now versus finish queued work—is part of correct worker design. Clear shutdown behavior avoids lost or half-processed jobs.

Golden file testing stores expected output in a file (often under a testdata directory) and compares the test's actual output against it. A common pattern adds an -update flag so you can regenerate the golden files when behavior intentionally changes. It suits tests of large outputs like rendered templates or formatted code.

The Go tool ignores any directory named testdata, so you can store fixtures, sample inputs, and golden files there without them being treated as packages. Tests reference these files by relative path since the working directory is the package directory. It is the conventional home for test support files.

Go caches compiled package outputs and test results in a build cache, so unchanged code does not get recompiled or retested. This is why a second 'go build' or 'go test' is dramatically faster. You can inspect or clear it with 'go clean -cache' if you ever suspect a stale entry.

Go caches successful test results keyed by the test binary and inputs, printing '(cached)' when it skips re-running an unchanged test. This speeds up repeated runs but can surprise you if a test depends on outside state. Passing -count=1 forces tests to actually run, bypassing the cache.

The race detector adds significant overhead—memory use can grow several times and execution slows roughly two to ten times. Because of this it is meant for testing and CI, not production builds. The trade-off is worthwhile because the concurrency bugs it surfaces are otherwise extremely hard to find.

When you launch a goroutine for sub-work, you pass the same context into it so it can observe cancellation. The goroutine then selects on ctx.Done() to exit if the parent operation is aborted. Forgetting to pass and check the context is the root cause of goroutines that outlive their request.

Because select randomizes among simultaneously ready cases, repeated runs can pick different branches, which can make tests flaky if they assume an order. The fix is to design code that does not depend on which ready case wins. If determinism matters, structure the channels so only one is ever ready at a time.

You can reuse a sync.WaitGroup after Wait returns, but you must not call Add concurrently with a Wait that has not finished, or call Add with a positive number while the counter is zero and a Wait is in progress. The safe pattern is one full Add-Done-Wait cycle at a time. Misusing reuse leads to panics or races the race detector will flag.

Backpressure is when a slow consumer naturally slows down a fast producer because the connecting channel blocks sends once full. Unbuffered or small-buffer channels provide strong backpressure, keeping memory bounded. Designs that drop or buffer unboundedly to avoid blocking trade backpressure for the risk of runaway memory growth.

A try-send uses select with a default: 'select { case ch <- v: ; default: /* dropped */ }'. If the channel is full or has no receiver, the value is dropped instead of blocking the sender. This pattern suits best-effort signals like metrics or non-critical notifications where blocking is unacceptable.

Context cancellation is cooperative, not forceful: cancelling a context only closes its Done channel, and it is up to each goroutine to check that and stop. Go cannot kill a goroutine that ignores the signal and keeps running. This is why honoring ctx in loops and library calls is essential for cancellation to actually work.

errgroup's TryGo, available when a limit is set, starts a goroutine only if a slot is free and returns false otherwise instead of blocking. It lets you skip or queue work when the group is saturated. This is useful for shedding load gracefully rather than piling up blocked Go calls.

A flame graph from pprof visualizes where a program spends time, with wider bars meaning more time spent in that call stack. You generate it with 'go tool pprof -http=:8080 profile' and explore it interactively in a browser. It is the quickest way to spot a hot function consuming most of the CPU.

Testing concurrent Go is tricky because goroutine scheduling and select randomness make timing non-deterministic. Reliable tests avoid sleeps for synchronization, instead using channels, WaitGroups, or synctest to coordinate. Running tests with -race and many iterations (-count) increases the chance of catching intermittent bugs.

testing/synctest, an experimental package in recent Go versions, runs goroutines in a fake time 'bubble' so concurrent tests are deterministic and fast. Time advances only when all goroutines are blocked, eliminating real sleeps and flaky timing. It makes testing timeouts and tickers reliable without slowing the test suite.

A goroutine should check ctx.Err() or select on ctx.Done() before starting expensive work, because the context may already be cancelled. Skipping this means you might do a long operation whose result is immediately discarded. An early check is a cheap way to honor cancellation that already happened.

A clear concurrency rule is that the goroutine which writes to a channel owns it and is responsible for closing it; receivers never close. This prevents the panic from closing a channel twice or sending on a closed channel. Documenting channel ownership makes pipelines easier to reason about and shut down correctly.

A consumer goroutine often ranges over its input channel until the producer closes it, then exits. This couples shutdown to channel closing: when upstream finishes and closes, the range loop ends naturally. It is cleaner than a separate stop signal when the data stream itself defines completion.

Go deliberately randomizes the iteration order of maps so code cannot accidentally depend on a particular order. Each program run, and even each loop, can visit keys differently. If you need ordered output, collect the keys into a slice and sort them, often with slices.Sort.

An init function runs automatically when a package is loaded, before main, and a package may have several across files. It is used for one-time setup like registering drivers or validating configuration. Because init runs implicitly and ordering between packages depends on imports, heavy logic in init is discouraged in favor of explicit initialization.

Package-level variables shared by goroutines are a common source of data races, since any goroutine can read or write them. Protect them with a mutex, make them atomic, or avoid mutable globals entirely. Read-only globals set during init are safe, but mutable shared state needs synchronization.

A typical pattern stores a request or trace ID in the context at the edge of a service, then logs it at every layer by reading it from ctx. This ties all log lines for one request together for tracing. It is a textbook correct use of context values because the ID is request-scoped and crosses many function boundaries.

keywords: go select to coordinate producers consumers
facts.answer: The producer-consumer pattern in Go connects producing goroutines and consuming goroutines through a channel, decoupling their speeds. Producers send work; consumers receive and process it; the channel buffers any temporary imbalance. Closing the channel after producers finish lets consumers know to stop, completing a clean handoff.

runtime.SetFinalizer attaches a function the garbage collector calls when an object becomes unreachable, used rarely for cleaning up non-memory resources tied to C code. Finalizers are unreliable for timing and may never run before exit, so they are a last resort, not a replacement for explicit Close. Most Go cleanup uses defer and explicit methods instead.

Debouncing collapses rapid bursts of events into one action after a quiet period, implemented with a select that resets a timer each time a new event arrives and only fires when the timer elapses. It is common for things like saving after the user stops typing. The timer-reset-on-event logic is the heart of the pattern.

Go deliberately has no goroutine-local storage, unlike thread-local storage in some languages. The intended way to carry per-operation data is to pass a context or explicit parameters down the call chain. This design keeps data flow visible and avoids hidden state that complicates reasoning about concurrent code.

When running parallel subtests in a loop, the subtest goroutine runs after the loop iteration may have advanced. Before Go 1.22's loop variable fix, you had to copy the loop variable (tc := tc) so each parallel subtest used its own case. With Go 1.22 each iteration has a fresh variable, removing this footgun.

TypeScript uses structural typing, meaning two types are compatible if they have the same shape, not the same name. If an object has all the properties a type requires, it counts as that type even if it was never declared as such. This is different from nominal typing used in languages like Java, where the declared name matters.

A type alias gives a name to any type using the 'type' keyword, like 'type ID = string | number'. Aliases can describe objects, unions, tuples, functions, and more. Unlike interfaces, type aliases can name primitives and unions, but they cannot be reopened to add new members later.

An interface declares the shape of an object in TypeScript, such as 'interface User { name: string }'. Interfaces support extension with 'extends' and can be declared multiple times so the declarations merge together. They are commonly used for public API contracts because the merging and clean extends syntax are convenient.

Interfaces and type aliases overlap heavily, but they differ in a few ways. Interfaces support declaration merging and feel natural for object contracts, while type aliases can also name unions, intersections, tuples, and primitives. A common rule of thumb is to use interfaces for object shapes that might be extended and type aliases for everything else.

A union type means a value can be one of several types, written with the pipe symbol like 'string | number'. You can only safely use members that all union branches share until you narrow the type. Unions are one of TypeScript's most powerful tools for modeling values that change form.

An intersection type combines several types into one using the ampersand, like 'A & B', so the result must satisfy all of them at once. It is often used to merge object shapes, giving you all properties from each part. If the combined types conflict on a property, the result can become 'never' for that property.

A literal type restricts a value to one exact constant, like 'type Yes = "yes"' or 'type One = 1'. Literal types shine when combined into unions, such as 'type Direction = "up" | "down"', which models a fixed set of allowed values. The compiler then rejects any value outside that set.

The 'any' type turns off type checking for a value, letting you do anything with it. It is an escape hatch that should be used sparingly because it silently disables the safety TypeScript provides. Reaching for 'unknown' instead is usually safer because it forces you to check the type before using it.

The 'unknown' type is the type-safe counterpart to 'any': it can hold any value, but you cannot use it until you narrow it with a check or assertion. This forces you to prove what the value is before operating on it. It is the recommended type for values coming from outside your program, like parsed JSON.

The 'never' type represents values that never occur, such as the return type of a function that always throws or loops forever. It is also the type of a variable that has been narrowed away in every branch. Because 'never' is assignable to every type but nothing is assignable to it, it is useful for exhaustiveness checks.

The 'void' type describes a function that does not return a meaningful value. A function typed to return 'void' may still return a value at runtime, but callers are expected to ignore it. This relaxation lets you pass functions that return something into slots expecting 'void', like array forEach callbacks.

Narrowing is how TypeScript refines a broad type to a more specific one inside a code branch. Checks like 'typeof x === "string"', 'if (x)', or 'x instanceof Date' all narrow the type for the block that follows. After narrowing, the compiler lets you use methods that only exist on the narrowed type.

The 'typeof' type guard narrows a value based on its JavaScript runtime type, like 'typeof x === "number"'. It works for the primitive results: string, number, bigint, boolean, symbol, undefined, object, and function. Inside the matching branch, TypeScript treats the variable as that narrowed type.

The 'instanceof' guard narrows a value by checking its constructor, like 'if (err instanceof Error)'. It works for class instances and other things with a prototype chain. Inside the true branch the variable is treated as that class type, so you can access its specific members.

The 'in' operator narrows union types by checking whether a property exists, like 'if ("swim" in animal)'. TypeScript uses the presence of that key to pick which union members are still possible. It is handy when distinguishing object shapes that differ by which properties they carry.

A discriminated union is a union of object types that all share a common literal property, called the discriminant or tag. Switching on that tag, like 'shape.kind', lets TypeScript narrow to the exact member in each branch. This pattern is the idiomatic way to model variants safely in TypeScript.

An exhaustiveness check uses the 'never' type to guarantee you handled every case of a union. In the default branch of a switch you assign the value to a 'never' variable; if a new union member is added, that assignment fails to compile. This turns forgotten cases into compile errors instead of runtime bugs.

Generics let you write code that works with many types while preserving type relationships, using type parameters like '<T>'. A function 'identity<T>(x: T): T' returns exactly the type you pass in, instead of widening to 'any'. Generics power reusable containers, utilities, and data structures without losing type safety.

A generic constraint limits what types a parameter can accept using 'extends', like '<T extends { length: number }>'. This lets you safely access the constrained properties inside the function body. Constraints keep generics flexible yet guarantee the minimum shape your code relies on.

A type parameter can have a default, like '<T = string>', used when the caller does not specify one. Defaults make generic types easier to use in common cases while still allowing customization. They behave much like default function argument values, but at the type level.

The 'keyof' operator produces a union of the property names of a type, so 'keyof { a: 1; b: 2 }' is '"a" | "b"'. It is essential for writing functions that accept a valid key of some object. Combined with generics it lets you build type-safe property accessors.

An indexed access type reads the type of a property using bracket syntax, like 'User["name"]' to get the type of the name field. You can also index with a union of keys to get a union of their types. This keeps derived types in sync with their source type automatically.

A mapped type builds a new object type by transforming each property of an existing one, using syntax like '{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] }'. You can change the value types, add modifiers, or rename keys during the mapping. Mapped types are the engine behind utilities like Partial and Readonly.

A conditional type chooses between two types based on a relationship test, written 'T extends U ? X : Y'. It is like a ternary expression but for types, evaluated by the compiler. Conditional types enable powerful type-level logic such as extracting, filtering, or transforming types.

The 'infer' keyword captures a type from within a conditional type, like 'T extends Array<infer E> ? E : never' to pull out an array's element type. It declares a temporary type variable that the compiler fills in by matching. 'infer' powers many built-in utilities such as ReturnType and Parameters.

The built-in 'Partial<T>' utility makes every property of T optional. It is implemented as a mapped type that adds the '?' modifier to each key. Partial is useful for update functions where the caller supplies only the fields they want to change.

The 'Required<T>' utility makes every property of T mandatory, the opposite of Partial. It strips the optional '?' modifier from each property using the '-?' modifier in a mapped type. This is handy when you receive a partially-filled object and want to assert it is now complete.

The 'Readonly<T>' utility marks every property of T as readonly, preventing reassignment after creation. It is a mapped type that adds the 'readonly' modifier to each key. Note that it is shallow: nested objects are not made readonly unless you apply it recursively.

The 'Record<K, V>' utility builds an object type whose keys are of type K and whose values are of type V, like 'Record<string, number>'. It is a clean way to type dictionaries and lookup tables. When K is a finite union of literals, every key is required.

The 'Pick<T, K>' utility creates a new type by selecting only the keys K from type T. For example 'Pick<User, "id" | "name">' keeps just those two fields. It is useful for narrowing a large type down to the subset a function actually needs.

The 'Omit<T, K>' utility builds a type from T with the keys K removed, the complement of Pick. For instance 'Omit<User, "password">' produces a user type without the password field. It is commonly used to strip sensitive or computed fields from a type.

The 'Exclude<T, U>' utility removes from union T any members that are assignable to U. For example 'Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "a">' yields '"b" | "c"'. It operates on unions of types, not on object keys.

The 'Extract<T, U>' utility keeps from union T only the members assignable to U, the opposite of Exclude. For example 'Extract<string | number, string>' yields 'string'. It is handy for filtering a union down to the parts of interest.

The 'NonNullable<T>' utility removes 'null' and 'undefined' from a type. It is equivalent to 'Exclude<T, null | undefined>'. This is useful after you have already checked a value is present but the type still includes the empty cases.

The 'ReturnType<T>' utility extracts the return type of a function type, like 'ReturnType<() => number>' giving 'number'. It uses 'infer' internally to capture the return type. This keeps derived types tied to a function's actual signature even as it changes.

The 'Parameters<T>' utility extracts a function type's parameter types as a tuple, like 'Parameters<(a: string, b: number) => void>' giving '[string, number]'. It is useful for forwarding arguments or wrapping functions. There is also 'ConstructorParameters' for constructor signatures.

The 'Awaited<T>' utility models the result of awaiting a value, unwrapping Promise types recursively. 'Awaited<Promise<number>>' is 'number', and even nested promises are flattened. It was added so utilities can correctly describe what 'await' produces, including thenables.

The 'InstanceType<T>' utility gets the instance type produced by a class constructor type. Given 'typeof MyClass', it returns the type of 'new MyClass()'. This is useful in factory functions and abstract patterns where you work with constructor types directly.

Template literal types build string types using backtick syntax with embedded type holes, like 'type Greeting = `hello ${string}`'. When you interpolate a union, the compiler expands all combinations. They enable precise typing of things like CSS units, event names, and route patterns.

TypeScript ships intrinsic string types 'Uppercase', 'Lowercase', 'Capitalize', and 'Uncapitalize' that transform string literal types. For example 'Uppercase<"abc">' is '"ABC"'. They are most useful inside template literal types to derive names like event handler keys.

An 'as const' assertion tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest, immutable type for a literal. An object or array gets readonly modifiers and its values become literal types instead of widened ones. This is the easiest way to derive precise union types from a value.

A type assertion uses the 'as' keyword to tell the compiler to treat a value as a specific type, like 'x as string'. It does not change the value at runtime and performs no checking, so an incorrect assertion can hide bugs. Use it only when you know more than the compiler does.

TypeScript originally used angle-bracket syntax for assertions, like '<string>value'. This form is discouraged in .tsx files because it clashes with JSX tag syntax. The 'as' form is preferred everywhere because it always works and reads more clearly.

The non-null assertion operator '!' tells the compiler a value is not null or undefined, like 'element!.value'. It removes 'null' and 'undefined' from the type without any runtime check. Overusing it is risky because it can silence real possibilities of a missing value.

An optional property is marked with '?', like 'name?: string', meaning it may be present or absent. Its type effectively becomes the declared type plus 'undefined'. Optional properties differ from properties explicitly typed as 'T | undefined', which must still be present even if set to undefined.

Optional chaining with '?.' short-circuits a property access or call when the left side is null or undefined, returning 'undefined' instead of throwing. TypeScript narrows the result type to include 'undefined' accordingly. It pairs naturally with the nullish coalescing operator to supply a fallback.

The nullish coalescing operator '??' returns the right side only when the left side is null or undefined, unlike '||' which also triggers on falsy values like 0 or empty string. This makes it safer for supplying defaults to numeric or boolean fields. TypeScript types the result as the union minus null and undefined.

The 'strictNullChecks' compiler option makes 'null' and 'undefined' separate types that are not assignable to other types by default. With it on, you must explicitly include them in a type and handle them before use. It catches a huge class of null-reference bugs and is one of the most valuable strict flags.

The 'strict' compiler flag turns on a bundle of stricter checks at once, including strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, and others. Enabling it is the recommended baseline for new TypeScript projects. You can still toggle individual flags off if a specific one is too disruptive.

The 'noImplicitAny' option flags any place where TypeScript would silently fall back to the 'any' type, such as an untyped function parameter. It forces you to either add an explicit type or accept 'any' deliberately. This keeps accidental loss of type safety from creeping into a codebase.

Type inference is TypeScript's ability to figure out a type without an explicit annotation, such as inferring 'number' for 'let x = 3'. Inference works on variables, return types, generics, and more. Good code leans on inference for local values and adds annotations mainly at public boundaries.

Contextual typing is when TypeScript infers a value's type from the surrounding context rather than the value itself. A common example is a callback whose parameter types are inferred from the function it is passed to. This lets you write 'arr.map(x => x * 2)' without annotating 'x'.

Function overloads let one function present multiple call signatures, declared above a single implementation. Callers see only the overload signatures, while the implementation signature stays hidden and must be compatible with all of them. Overloads model functions whose return type depends on which argument shape you pass.

A readonly array, written 'readonly T[]' or 'ReadonlyArray<T>', forbids mutating methods like push and splice at the type level. It is useful for parameters you promise not to modify. A normal array is assignable to a readonly one, but not the reverse, preventing accidental mutation.

A tuple type describes an array with a fixed number of elements of specific types in order, like '[string, number]'. Tuples can have optional and rest elements too. They are commonly used for returning multiple values, such as React's useState returning a value and a setter.

Tuple elements can carry labels for readability, like '[first: string, second: number]'. The labels do not change the type but show up in editor tooltips and error messages. This makes tuple-based APIs much easier to understand at a glance.

Tuples can include a rest element using spread syntax, like '[string, ...number[]]', allowing a known start and a variable tail. Variadic tuple types let you spread one tuple into another, enabling type-safe argument forwarding. This powers precise typing of functions like 'concat' and 'bind'.

An enum defines a set of named constants, like 'enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }'. Numeric enums auto-increment from zero by default, while string enums require explicit values. Enums generate real runtime objects, which is one reason some teams prefer union literal types instead.

A 'const enum' is fully inlined at compile time, leaving no runtime object behind. Each usage is replaced by its literal value, which reduces output size. Const enums have caveats with isolated module compilation, so some bundlers and the isolatedModules flag discourage them.

A string enum assigns explicit string values to each member, like 'enum Dir { Up = "UP" }'. Unlike numeric enums, string enums have no reverse mapping but produce readable values useful in logs and serialized data. They cannot auto-increment, so every member needs a value.

The 'satisfies' operator checks that a value matches a type without widening the value's inferred type. So 'const config = {...} satisfies Config' validates the shape but keeps the precise literal types for later use. It gives you validation and narrow inference at the same time, which a plain annotation cannot.

A user-defined type guard uses a return type of the form 'param is Type', like 'function isString(x: unknown): x is string'. When the function returns true, the compiler narrows the argument to that type at the call site. This lets you package custom narrowing logic into reusable functions.

An assertion function uses the 'asserts' keyword in its signature, like 'function assert(cond): asserts cond', to tell the compiler that if it returns, the condition held. The form 'asserts x is Type' narrows a value's type for the rest of the scope. These are useful for runtime validation that the type system can then trust.

Declaration merging lets multiple declarations with the same name combine into one. Two interfaces with the same name merge their members, and namespaces can merge with functions or classes. This mechanism is how libraries augment global or third-party types.

Module augmentation adds members to an existing module's types using 'declare module "name"' inside your code. It is commonly used to extend library types, such as adding a property to Express's Request. The augmentation merges with the original declarations rather than replacing them.

A 'declare global' block lets you add or extend types in the global scope from within a module file. It is used to add properties to globalThis, Window, or built-in interfaces. Because it modifies global types, it should be used carefully to avoid surprising other code.

An ambient declaration uses the 'declare' keyword to describe the shape of code that exists at runtime but has no TypeScript source, such as a global variable from a script tag. Ambient declarations have no implementation and generate no output. They live in .d.ts files or in your own type-only declarations.
