A declaration file with a .d.ts extension contains only type information and no executable code. It describes the public types of JavaScript libraries so TypeScript can check code that uses them. Many packages ship their own .d.ts files, and the DefinitelyTyped project provides them for those that do not.

DefinitelyTyped is a large community repository of TypeScript declaration files for JavaScript libraries that lack their own. They are published under the @types scope on npm, so you install types for a library named 'foo' with '@types/foo'. Modern libraries increasingly ship types directly, reducing the need for @types.

An index signature lets an object type have arbitrary keys of a given type, like '{ [key: string]: number }'. It is useful for dictionaries where you do not know the keys ahead of time. All explicitly declared properties must be compatible with the index signature's value type.

TypeScript performs an excess property check when you assign an object literal directly to a typed slot, flagging properties not in the target type. This catches typos like 'colour' instead of 'color'. The check is relaxed if the object first passes through a variable, because structural typing then applies.

A function type describes the parameters and return type of a callable, written 'type Fn = (a: number) => string'. You can also write call signatures inside object types for callable objects. Function types make it easy to pass functions around with full type checking.

TypeScript lets you type the 'this' value of a function by declaring a fake first parameter named 'this', like 'function f(this: Window)'. This parameter is erased at runtime and only exists for type checking. It helps catch cases where a method is called with the wrong receiver.

Method parameters in TypeScript are checked bivariantly by default for historical compatibility reasons, which is technically unsound but convenient. The strictFunctionTypes flag enables stricter contravariant checking, but only for function-typed properties, not methods declared with method syntax. This is why some unsound assignments still slip through with method shorthand.

Covariance means a type relationship is preserved in the same direction; if Dog is a subtype of Animal, then 'Dog[]' is treated as a subtype of 'Animal[]'. Return types of functions are covariant. Covariance is intuitive but can be unsafe for mutable containers, which is one reason readonly types exist.

Contravariance flips a type relationship; a function accepting 'Animal' can be used where one accepting 'Dog' is expected, because it can handle anything a dog handler can. Function parameter positions are contravariant under strictFunctionTypes. Understanding it explains why some function assignments are or are not allowed.

When a conditional type acts on a naked type parameter that is a union, it distributes over each member separately and unions the results. So 'T extends U ? X : Y' applied to 'A | B' becomes the results for A and B combined. Wrapping the parameter in a tuple, like '[T] extends [U]', turns off distribution.

A type can refer to itself to model recursive structures like trees or JSON, such as 'type Json = string | number | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json }'. TypeScript supports bounded recursion in type aliases and conditional types. Very deep recursion can hit an instantiation depth limit and produce an error.

A class can declare type parameters, like 'class Box<T> { value: T }', making it reusable across element types. The type argument is supplied when you create an instance or is inferred from the constructor. Generic classes keep collections and containers type-safe without duplicating code.

An abstract class is declared with the 'abstract' keyword and cannot be instantiated directly. It may contain abstract members that subclasses must implement. Abstract classes are useful for sharing implementation while forcing subclasses to fill in the missing pieces.

TypeScript class members can be marked 'public', 'private', or 'protected' to control visibility. These are compile-time only, so they do not truly hide data at runtime. For runtime privacy, JavaScript's '#' private fields are enforced by the engine itself.

JavaScript private fields use a '#' prefix, like '#count', and are truly private at runtime, unlike TypeScript's 'private' modifier which is only a compile-time check. They cannot be accessed outside the class even via bracket notation. TypeScript supports them fully and recommends them when real encapsulation matters.

A parameter property lets you declare and initialize a class field directly in the constructor by adding a modifier, like 'constructor(private name: string)'. TypeScript creates the field and assigns it automatically. This shorthand removes boilerplate but only works in constructors.

A class can declare 'implements SomeInterface' to promise it satisfies that interface's shape. The compiler then checks the class provides all required members. Note that 'implements' does not change the class's type or import any members; it only verifies compatibility.

TypeScript can type abstract constructors with 'abstract new (...) => T', distinguishing them from concrete constructors. This prevents code from calling 'new' on a class that is abstract. It matters for factory functions that take a constructor type as a parameter.

At the type level, 'typeof someValue' produces the type of that value, like 'typeof config' to get a config object's inferred type. This is different from the runtime 'typeof' operator that returns a string. It is commonly combined with 'keyof' to derive key unions from real objects.

A 'const' type parameter, written '<const T>', tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest literal types for arguments passed to that parameter, as if the caller used 'as const'. This avoids forcing callers to write 'as const' themselves. It is especially useful in library functions that want to preserve literal arrays and objects.

Type widening is when TypeScript broadens a literal type to its base type, such as inferring 'string' instead of '"hello"' for a mutable variable. A 'const' declaration or an 'as const' assertion prevents widening. Understanding widening explains why some inferred types are broader than expected.

Freshness refers to TypeScript treating a brand-new object literal more strictly, applying excess property checks to it. Once the literal is assigned to a variable, it loses its freshness and is checked structurally. This is why a property typo is caught when passing a literal directly but not after storing it first.

Optional chaining also works on method calls, like 'obj.method?.()', which calls the method only if it exists and is not null or undefined. TypeScript types the whole expression with 'undefined' added when the chain might short-circuit. This avoids errors when calling possibly-missing callbacks.

A definite assignment assertion uses '!' after a variable or class field name, like 'let x!: number', to tell the compiler it will be assigned before use even if it cannot prove it. It is useful for fields initialized by a framework or dependency injection. Misusing it can hide genuinely uninitialized values.

A 'unique symbol' is a special subtype of symbol tied to a specific const declaration, enabling symbol-keyed properties with distinct types. It must be declared with 'const' and typed as 'unique symbol'. Each one is treated as its own nominal type, useful for branding and well-known symbols.

A branded type fakes nominal typing in TypeScript's structural system by intersecting a base type with a hidden tag, like 'string & { __brand: "UserId" }'. This makes a UserId incompatible with a plain string even though both are strings at runtime. It is a common technique for preventing mix-ups between IDs and other strings.

An opaque or phantom type carries a type-level marker that has no runtime presence, used to distinguish otherwise identical types. Branded types are one way to build them. They let you encode invariants, like 'validated email' versus 'raw email', purely in the type system.

An 'import type' statement imports only types and is guaranteed to be erased from the JavaScript output. This prevents accidental runtime dependencies and helps bundlers tree-shake. The 'isolatedModules' and 'verbatimModuleSyntax' settings encourage using it for clarity.

An 'export type' statement re-exports types without emitting any runtime code. It pairs with 'import type' to keep type-only references from affecting the runtime module graph. This matters for tools that compile files in isolation and cannot tell types from values otherwise.

The 'isolatedModules' flag ensures each file can be transpiled independently without cross-file type information, which is required by single-file transpilers like Babel and esbuild. It forbids constructs that need whole-program knowledge, such as re-exporting a type without 'export type'. Turning it on keeps your code compatible with fast bundlers.

The 'verbatimModuleSyntax' flag makes TypeScript preserve import and export statements exactly as written, eliding only those marked with 'type'. It replaces older flags like importsNotUsedAsValues and gives predictable output for bundlers. With it on, you must explicitly use 'import type' for type-only imports.

The 'esModuleInterop' flag smooths over differences between CommonJS and ES modules, letting you write 'import x from "cjs-module"' for default-less CommonJS exports. It generates helper code to emulate ES module semantics. It is recommended for most projects that consume both module styles.

The 'moduleResolution' option controls how TypeScript locates imported modules, with modern values like 'bundler', 'node16', and 'nodenext'. The 'bundler' mode matches how tools like Vite and esbuild resolve files and supports package exports without requiring file extensions. Choosing the right mode is key to imports resolving correctly.

The 'paths' option in tsconfig maps import aliases to real folders, like making '@app/*' point to 'src/*'. It is purely a type-checking aid; your bundler or runtime needs matching configuration to resolve the aliases at run time. Combined with 'baseUrl', it cleans up long relative import paths.

The 'skipLibCheck' option tells TypeScript not to type-check declaration files, including those in node_modules. It speeds up builds and avoids errors caused by conflicting third-party types. The tradeoff is that real problems inside .d.ts files can go unnoticed.

The 'lib' option lists which built-in type declaration sets are available, such as 'ES2022' or 'DOM'. It controls whether APIs like Promise, Array methods, or document are known to the compiler. Setting it correctly ensures you only reference features available in your target environment.

The 'target' option sets which JavaScript version TypeScript compiles down to, like 'ES2022'. A lower target makes the compiler downlevel newer syntax into older equivalents. It also influences the default 'lib' and how features like async functions are emitted.

The 'module' option determines the module format of the emitted JavaScript, such as 'ESNext', 'CommonJS', or 'NodeNext'. It affects how import and export statements are compiled. Choosing it depends on where the code will run, like Node, a browser, or through a bundler.

Setting 'declaration' to true makes TypeScript emit .d.ts files alongside the compiled JavaScript. This lets other TypeScript projects consume your library with full type information. Library authors usually enable it so published packages ship their own types.

Project references let you split a large codebase into smaller TypeScript projects that depend on each other, declared with 'references' in tsconfig. Marking a referenced project as 'composite' enables incremental, build-order-aware compilation with 'tsc --build'. This speeds up builds in monorepos by only rebuilding what changed.

The 'incremental' option makes TypeScript save build information to a .tsbuildinfo file so later compilations only redo changed work. It dramatically shortens repeat build times on large projects. Project references build on top of this mechanism for multi-package setups.

TypeScript supports JSX in .tsx files, type-checking elements against the declared component props. The 'jsx' compiler option controls output, with 'react-jsx' using the modern automatic runtime that does not need React in scope. Type errors catch mismatched or missing props at compile time.

In React with TypeScript, a component traditionally returns 'JSX.Element', though 'ReactNode' or 'ReactElement' are also used. The newer automatic JSX runtime uses a 'JSX' namespace from the JSX import source. Typing return values helps catch components that accidentally return the wrong thing.

Writing a generic arrow function in a .tsx file can confuse the parser because '<T>' looks like a JSX tag. The fix is to add a trailing comma, '<T,>', or to use 'extends', which tells TypeScript it is a type parameter. This is a common gotcha when defining generic React hooks.

When a function has multiple overloads, TypeScript tries each signature top to bottom and uses the first one that matches the call. Order matters, so more specific overloads should come before more general ones. If no overload matches, the error reports against the last signature, which can be confusing.

TypeScript infers generic type arguments from the values you pass, so you rarely write them explicitly. Inference considers all argument positions and picks types that satisfy the constraints. When inference fails or chooses too broadly, you can supply the type arguments by hand.

Adding 'as const' to an array literal makes it a readonly tuple of literal types, like '["a", "b"] as const' becoming 'readonly ["a", "b"]'. This is the standard way to derive a union of values, for example 'typeof arr[number]'. Without it, the array would widen to 'string[]'.

Indexing an array type with 'number', like 'typeof colors[number]', produces a union of all its element types. Combined with 'as const' on the source array, it turns a list of values into a string-literal union. This pattern keeps a runtime list and its type in sync from a single source.

Key remapping lets a mapped type rename keys using an 'as' clause, like '{ [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] }'. Mapping a key to 'never' removes it entirely, enabling filtering. This unlocks transformations like generating getter names or stripping certain properties.

Mapped types can add or remove the 'readonly' and '?' modifiers using '+' or '-'. For example '-readonly' strips readonly and '-?' makes properties required. This is exactly how the Required and a mutable-version utility types are built.

A homomorphic mapped type is one of the form '{ [K in keyof T]: ... }' that preserves T's structure, including its modifiers and whether T is an array or tuple. Because it preserves shape, applying Partial to a tuple keeps it a tuple. Non-homomorphic mapped types over an explicit key union do not get this preservation.

Conditional types can be chained like an if-else ladder, with each false branch being another conditional. This lets you classify a type into several cases. While powerful, deeply nested conditionals can become hard to read, so naming intermediate types helps.

A single conditional type can use 'infer' in several positions to capture multiple types at once, such as inferring both parameter and return types of a function. Each 'infer' introduces its own type variable. This is how complex utilities pull apart structured types.

An 'infer' declaration can carry a constraint with 'extends', like 'infer R extends string', so the inferred type is required to satisfy it. This both narrows the inferred type and can reject matches that do not fit. It was added to make type-level extraction more precise.

TypeScript lets you annotate a type parameter's variance with 'in' for contravariant and 'out' for covariant, like 'interface Box<out T>'. These annotations document intent and let the compiler check variance faster and more accurately. They are optional, since TypeScript normally infers variance automatically.

Class constructors can have overloads just like functions, declaring several constructor signatures over one implementation. This lets a class be created with different argument shapes. As with function overloads, the implementation signature must be compatible with every declared overload.

TypeScript allows a getter and setter on the same property to have different types as of recent versions, such as a setter accepting a broader type than the getter returns. The getter's type defines the property type when read. This is useful for fields that normalize input on assignment.

You can combine an index signature with explicitly named properties, but each named property's type must be assignable to the index signature's value type. For example with '[key: string]: number', a property 'count: number' is fine but 'name: string' is not. This keeps the type internally consistent.

An object type can have a numeric index signature, like '{ [index: number]: string }', modeling array-like access. When both string and numeric index signatures exist, the numeric value type must be assignable to the string one. This reflects that JavaScript object keys are ultimately strings.

Index signatures can use 'symbol' keys, like '{ [key: symbol]: number }', alongside string and number signatures. This supports objects keyed by symbols. It complements the older string and number index signatures for fully describing dynamic-key objects.

Template literal types can act as patterns to constrain strings, such as 'type Hex = `#${string}`' to require a leading hash. Combined with infer in conditional types, you can parse parts out of a string at the type level. This enables typing route parameters, units, and structured identifiers.

Using 'infer' inside a template literal type, you can extract substrings, like 'T extends `${infer Key}=${infer Value}` ? ...' to split a key-value string. The compiler matches the literal pattern and binds the holes. This technique underlies type-level parsers for things like query strings.

Conditional types can recurse to process lists or strings character by character, accumulating a result. TypeScript optimizes tail-recursive conditional types so they avoid hitting the recursion limit as quickly. This enables type-level operations like joining tuples into strings.

TypeScript caps how deeply types can be instantiated to keep the compiler from running forever, and exceeding it triggers a 'Type instantiation is excessively deep' error. This usually happens with very recursive conditional or mapped types. Restructuring to be tail-recursive or simplifying the type often resolves it.

Error TS2322, 'Type X is not assignable to type Y', is one of the most common TypeScript errors. It means a value's type does not fit where it is being used. Reading the detailed message, which often points to a specific incompatible property, usually reveals the mismatch.

Error TS2339, 'Property X does not exist on type Y', means you accessed a member the type does not declare. Common causes are typos, missing narrowing on a union, or an outdated type definition. The fix is usually to narrow the type, correct the spelling, or update the declaration.

When you see something is not assignable to type 'never', it often means a value reached a branch the compiler thought was impossible, such as a switch handling all union cases. It is also the expected error in an exhaustiveness check when a new union member appears. The message is a clue that your assumptions about the type no longer hold.

Before using a value typed as 'unknown', you must narrow it with a typeof check, an instanceof check, a type guard, or an assertion. The compiler refuses property access or calls on a raw 'unknown'. This forced checking is exactly why 'unknown' is safer than 'any' for untrusted input.

The type '{}' means 'any non-null, non-undefined value', not 'an object with no properties', which surprises many people. Almost everything except null and undefined is assignable to it. To mean a real empty object, use 'Record<string, never>' or a more specific shape.

The lowercase 'object' type means any non-primitive value, excluding string, number, boolean, and the like. The capitalized 'Object' refers to the JavaScript Object interface and is much broader, so it is rarely what you want. For a real object map, prefer 'Record' or an explicit shape.

The capitalized 'Function' type describes any callable but loses parameter and return type information, so calling it returns 'any'. It is discouraged because it bypasses type safety. Prefer a specific function type signature like '(...args: unknown[]) => unknown' or an exact one.

The TypeScript compiler is invoked with the 'tsc' command, which type-checks and optionally emits JavaScript according to tsconfig.json. Running 'tsc --noEmit' checks types without producing output, useful in CI. The '--watch' flag recompiles on file changes during development.

The tsconfig.json file configures how TypeScript compiles a project, listing compiler options and which files to include. The compiler searches upward from a file to find it. Settings like 'strict', 'target', and 'moduleResolution' live here and shape the entire project's behavior.

A tsconfig.json can inherit from another using the 'extends' field, which points to a base config file or a shared package. This lets teams centralize common compiler options. Local settings override or add to the inherited ones, keeping per-project configs small.

TypeScript types are erased during compilation and have no effect at runtime, a process called type erasure. The output is plain JavaScript with annotations stripped. This is why you cannot check a TypeScript interface with 'instanceof' or rely on types for runtime validation.

Because types vanish at runtime, validating external data needs a runtime validator like Zod, Valibot, or io-ts. These libraries define a schema that both checks values at run time and infers a matching TypeScript type. This bridges the gap between compile-time types and untrusted input.

Libraries like Zod let you write a schema once and derive its TypeScript type with a helper such as 'z.infer<typeof schema>'. This keeps the runtime check and the static type from drifting apart. It is a popular pattern for typing API responses and form data.

A double assertion like 'value as unknown as Target' forces a conversion the compiler would otherwise reject. Routing through 'unknown' bypasses the rule that direct assertions must overlap. It is a last-resort escape hatch and a sign you may be fighting the type system.

Declaring a value with 'const' rather than 'let' makes TypeScript infer a narrower literal type, since a const cannot be reassigned. So 'const x = "a"' infers '"a"' while 'let x = "a"' infers 'string'. This subtle difference often determines whether a value matches a literal union.

TypeScript infers a function's return type from its body, so you usually do not need to annotate it. Annotating the return type anyway can catch mistakes early and document intent at public boundaries. Some teams require explicit return types on exported functions for clarity and stable APIs.

Control flow analysis is how TypeScript tracks a variable's type as it changes through assignments and checks across a function. After an 'if (x === null) return', the compiler knows x is non-null below. This per-branch reasoning is what makes narrowing feel automatic.

Assigning a value to a variable narrows its type to that value's type for the following code. So after 'let x: string | number; x = 5;', the compiler treats x as 'number' until it changes again. This is part of control flow analysis and reduces the need for manual checks.

A truthiness check like 'if (value)' narrows out falsy possibilities such as null, undefined, 0, empty string, and false. Inside the block, the type excludes those. Beware that it also removes valid 0 or empty-string values, so use explicit comparisons when those are meaningful.

Comparing variables with '===' or '!==' narrows their types based on the result. Comparing two union-typed values can narrow both, since equality implies they share a common type. Comparing against a literal narrows to or away from that literal in the respective branches.

TypeScript can narrow based on a boolean stored in a const, like 'const isString = typeof x === "string"', and remember that result when you later use 'isString'. This aliased condition analysis lets you name complex checks. It works for const-bound conditions but not for ones that might change.

Calling an assertion function with an 'asserts' signature narrows a value for the rest of the scope, as if you had checked it inline. For instance 'assertIsString(x)' lets later code treat x as a string. If the function does not throw, the compiler trusts the asserted condition.

Adding 'never' to a union has no effect because 'never' is the empty type; 'string | never' simplifies to 'string'. This property makes 'never' useful in mapped and conditional types to filter members out. Mapping an unwanted key to 'never' effectively deletes it.

Putting 'unknown' in a union collapses the whole thing to 'unknown', since everything is assignable to it; 'string | unknown' is just 'unknown'. This is the dual of how 'never' behaves in unions. It reflects that 'unknown' is the top type and 'never' is the bottom type.

In type theory, the top type is the supertype of all types, and the bottom type is the subtype of all types. In TypeScript, 'unknown' is the top type and 'never' is the bottom type. Knowing this explains many simplification rules, like 'never' vanishing from unions and 'unknown' absorbing them.

Assignability is the core rule deciding whether a value of type A can be placed where type B is expected. TypeScript checks it structurally, comparing shapes rather than names. Most type errors boil down to A not being assignable to B for some specific reason the message explains.

A function is assignable to another if it can be called wherever the target can: it may take fewer parameters but not require more, and its return type must be assignable to the target's. Parameter types are checked contravariantly under strict function checks. This is why a handler taking fewer args can substitute for one taking more.

TypeScript allows a function with fewer parameters to be used where one with more is expected, because ignoring extra arguments is safe. This is why 'arr.forEach(x => ...)' works even though forEach passes three arguments. The reverse, requiring more parameters than provided, is not allowed.

By default, an optional property 'x?: number' allows being absent or explicitly set to undefined. The 'exactOptionalPropertyTypes' flag makes this stricter, distinguishing 'missing' from 'present but undefined'. With it on, you cannot assign undefined to an optional property unless its type explicitly includes undefined.

The 'noUncheckedIndexedAccess' flag adds 'undefined' to the type of any value retrieved through an index signature or array index. This reflects that 'arr[i]' might be out of bounds. It forces you to check before using such values, catching a real class of off-by-one and missing-key bugs.

JavaScript returns 'undefined' for out-of-bounds array access at runtime, but TypeScript ignores this by default and types 'arr[i]' as the element type. Enabling 'noUncheckedIndexedAccess' makes the type include 'undefined' to match reality. Without that flag, indexing can hide a missing-element bug.

A generic parameter can have both a constraint and a default, like '<T extends object = {}>'. The constraint limits valid arguments while the default supplies one when none is given. The default itself must satisfy the constraint.

Built-in Partial is shallow, so deeply nesting optional properties requires a custom recursive type often called DeepPartial. It maps each property and, if the value is an object, applies itself again. This is a common hand-written utility for configuration and patch objects.

A type-safe property getter is typed as 'function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]'. The constraint guarantees the key exists, and the indexed access return type gives back exactly that property's type. This pattern prevents both invalid keys and wrong return types.

You can get the type of a module's default or namespace export using 'typeof import("module")' in a type position. This is handy for typing dynamically imported modules or referencing a module's type without importing its values. It pairs with conditional and indexed types to extract specific exports.

TypeScript supports an 'import("path")' type expression to reference types from another module inline, without a top-level import. This is useful inside .d.ts files and JSDoc comments. It avoids adding a runtime import just to reference a type.

TypeScript can type-check plain JavaScript files using JSDoc comments when 'checkJs' or '@ts-check' is enabled. You annotate with tags like '@param {string} name' and '@returns {number}'. This brings much of TypeScript's safety to JavaScript without converting files.

The 'allowJs' option lets TypeScript include .js files in a project, and 'checkJs' makes it type-check them using inference and JSDoc. Together they enable gradual adoption, letting a JavaScript codebase get type feedback before migrating to .ts. You can opt out per file with a '// @ts-nocheck' comment.

A '// @ts-ignore' comment suppresses the type error on the next line. It is a blunt tool because it hides whatever error appears, even a new unrelated one. Prefer '@ts-expect-error', which both suppresses and warns if the error ever disappears.

A '// @ts-expect-error' comment suppresses the error on the next line but reports a warning if there is no error to suppress. This makes it safer than '@ts-ignore' because it fails loudly when code is fixed. It is also useful in tests that assert certain code should not type-check.

A '// @ts-nocheck' comment at the top of a file disables type checking for the whole file. It is useful for legacy or generated files you do not want to fix yet. Conversely, '// @ts-check' opts a single JavaScript file into checking.

A triple-slash directive like '/// <reference types="node" />' declares a dependency on another declaration file at the top of a file. They were the pre-module way to compose type definitions. Modern code mostly uses import statements instead, but the directives still appear in .d.ts files.

A 'namespace' groups related declarations under a single name, an older alternative to ES modules sometimes called an internal module. Namespaces can span multiple files via merging. For application code, ES modules are preferred, but namespaces still appear in some declaration files and global type definitions.

Numeric enums generate a reverse mapping at runtime, so the enum object maps both names to values and values back to names. This means 'Color[0]' returns '"Red"' for 'enum Color { Red }'. String enums do not get this reverse mapping, keeping their runtime object smaller.

Many TypeScript developers prefer a union of string literals over an enum, like 'type Color = "red" | "green"'. Unions have no runtime footprint, are easier to refactor, and play nicely with tools that compile files in isolation. Enums still help when you need a real runtime object with reverse mapping.

A common enum alternative is a frozen const object plus a derived union: 'const Color = { Red: "red" } as const; type Color = typeof Color[keyof typeof Color]'. This gives both a runtime values object and a literal-union type. It avoids enum quirks while keeping named access to values.

Constraining a generic with 'K extends keyof T' guarantees K is a valid property name of T. This is the foundation of safe property access helpers. The compiler then knows 'obj[k]' has type 'T[K]' and rejects keys that do not exist on T.

A function's return type can be a conditional type that depends on its argument's type, often paired with overloads. For example a function might return an array or a single value depending on a boolean flag's literal type. This lets one function express behavior that varies by input.

Intersecting two function types produces an overloaded function that accepts either signature, an alternative to declaring overloads. For example '((x: string) => string) & ((x: number) => number)' is callable with a string or a number. This trick is sometimes used in generated or higher-order type code.

An abstract method in an abstract class declares a signature without an implementation, forcing subclasses to provide one. The compiler errors if a concrete subclass omits it. Abstract methods let a base class call into behavior that only its subclasses define.

The 'override' keyword marks a method that is meant to replace a base class method, and with 'noImplicitOverride' enabled it is required. If the base method is renamed or removed, the override no longer matches and the compiler flags it. This prevents silent drift between a subclass and its parent.

The 'noImplicitOverride' flag requires the 'override' keyword on any method that overrides a base class method. It catches mistakes where a base method is renamed but a subclass still defines the old name, accidentally creating a new method. Turning it on makes inheritance refactors much safer.

A property marked 'readonly' can be set during initialization but not reassigned afterward, like 'readonly id: string'. It is a compile-time guarantee with no runtime enforcement. Readonly is great for fields meant to stay constant after construction, such as identifiers.

'const' applies to variable bindings and prevents reassignment of the binding, while 'readonly' applies to object properties and array contents. A 'const' object can still have its mutable properties changed. They address immutability at different levels: the binding versus the members.

The built-in Readonly is shallow, so making nested structures immutable requires a recursive DeepReadonly type. It maps each property to readonly and recurses into object values. This is a common custom utility for guaranteeing a config or state tree is not mutated.

When a template literal type interpolates two unions, the compiler produces every combination, like '`${"a"|"b"}-${"x"|"y"}`' yielding four strings. This cross-product can explode quickly with large unions, so use it carefully. It is powerful for generating things like all valid event names.

Template literal types can derive event handler names from event names, mapping 'click' to 'onClick' with 'Capitalize'. This pattern types component prop names or DOM event maps precisely. It keeps a single source of event names and generates the derived handler keys automatically.

Node.js APIs are typed by the '@types/node' package, which you install to use globals like 'process' and 'Buffer' in TypeScript. Set the 'types' or 'lib' options so the compiler includes them. Without it, Node-specific globals will be reported as unknown.

Browser APIs like document, window, and fetch are typed by the 'DOM' library, included via the 'lib' option. In Node-only projects you may omit DOM to avoid pretending browser globals exist. Choosing the right libs keeps the available API surface honest for your environment.

A generic factory can take a constructor type and produce an instance, typed with 'new (...args) => T' or 'InstanceType'. The return type is tied to the class you pass in. This pattern underlies dependency injection containers and plugin registries.

A mixin in TypeScript is a function that takes a base class and returns a new class extending it with extra features. It is typed using a constructor type constraint like 'T extends new (...args: any[]) => {}'. Mixins compose behavior horizontally where single inheritance is too limiting.

A constructor or newable type describes something you can call with 'new', written 'new (args) => Instance'. It is distinct from a plain function type. Constructor types are used to type class references passed as values, such as in factories and DI.

Mixins typically constrain the base to a concrete constructor type 'new (...args: any[]) => object'. Using an abstract constructor type allows abstract base classes to participate too. Choosing the right constructor type determines which classes can be mixed in.

TypeScript flags a 'weak type' error when you assign an object to a type whose properties are all optional, but the object shares none of them. This catches passing a completely unrelated object to an all-optional options type. It is a special heuristic since structurally the empty match would otherwise be allowed.

Intersecting incompatible primitives like 'string & number' produces 'never' because no value can be both. This is occasionally useful as a deliberate impossibility marker. More often it appears accidentally when over-combining types and signals a logic error.

A clever conditional type called UnionToIntersection converts a union like 'A | B' into the intersection 'A & B' by exploiting contravariance of inferred function parameters. It is an advanced type-level utility used in libraries. Understanding it requires knowing how inference distributes over function parameter positions.

Indexing a tuple type with 'number', like 'T[number]', collapses it into a union of its element types. This converts a tuple of literals into a union, often after using 'as const' on an array. It is a frequent step in deriving unions from value lists.

A tuple type exposes its length as a literal number via the 'length' property type, so '[a, b, c]["length"]' is '3'. This is used in advanced type-level arithmetic where tuple lengths stand in for numbers. Counting with tuples is a workaround since TypeScript has no native type-level number math.

TypeScript has no built-in number arithmetic at the type level, so libraries simulate it by building and measuring tuple lengths. Adding numbers means concatenating tuples and reading the resulting length. These tricks power advanced types but can be slow and hit recursion limits.

Unlike 'as', the 'satisfies' operator validates that a value conforms to a type without changing or widening the value's inferred type, and without forcing an unsafe conversion. 'as' can silence real errors, while 'satisfies' only confirms compatibility. Use 'satisfies' when you want a check but still need the precise literal type.

A common 'satisfies' use is validating an object against 'Record<Key, Value>' while keeping each property's exact type. For example a config object can be checked to have all required keys yet still report literal value types when read. This combines completeness checking with precise inference.

User-defined type guards let you encapsulate narrowing logic and reuse it, such as 'isNonNull' used to filter arrays. Passing such a guard to 'array.filter' narrows the resulting array's element type. This makes filtering out null values type-safe in one expression.

Filtering null and undefined out of an array does not change the element type unless you use a type guard. Writing 'arr.filter((x): x is T => x != null)' tells the compiler the result excludes null and undefined. Without the guard, the filtered array keeps the original wider type.

The 'strictBindCallApply' flag, enabled by strict mode, type-checks the arguments to a function's bind, call, and apply methods. Without it, these methods accept any arguments and return loosely typed results. With it on, mismatched arguments to call or apply are caught at compile time.

The 'useDefineForClassFields' flag makes class field declarations use the standard JavaScript define semantics, creating own properties with [[Define]]. This matches the ECMAScript class fields proposal and affects how fields interact with getters in base classes. It is on by default for modern targets.

A decorator is a function that modifies a class, method, accessor, property, or parameter, applied with '@' syntax. TypeScript supports the standardized ECMAScript decorators, with the older experimental ones behind a flag. Frameworks like Angular and NestJS rely heavily on decorators for metadata.

Experimental decorators paired with 'emitDecoratorMetadata' and the reflect-metadata library let frameworks read parameter and property types at runtime. This is how some dependency injection systems infer what to provide. The newer standard decorators do not include this metadata emission, so patterns differ.

The 'accessor' keyword declares an auto-accessor field that creates a getter and setter backed by a private storage slot. It was introduced alongside standard decorators to give them a natural target. Decorators applied to an accessor can intercept reads and writes.

Calling 'Array.isArray(x)' narrows x to an array type within the true branch, because its return type is a built-in type predicate. This is the reliable way to check for arrays since 'typeof' reports 'object' for them. It is especially useful when narrowing a union that might be an array or a single value.

A function that always throws can be typed to return 'never', signaling it never completes normally. This helps the compiler's control flow analysis treat code after a call to it as unreachable. Helper functions like 'fail(msg): never' use this to act as type-level guarantees.

A common pattern is an 'assertNever(x: never): never { throw ... }' helper placed in a switch's default branch. If every case is handled, x is 'never' and the call type-checks; if a case is missing, the argument is not 'never' and it errors. This gives compile-time exhaustiveness for free.

A function can accept a readonly tuple parameter and spread it into another call using variadic tuple types. This preserves the exact element types through the forwarding. It is how typed wrappers around functions keep precise argument types.

To forward arguments with full typing, you can use a rest parameter typed as a generic tuple, like 'function wrap<A extends any[]>(...args: A)'. Combined with 'Parameters', this lets wrappers accept and pass through exactly the original function's arguments. It powers memoization and logging decorators.

The TypeScript Playground is an online editor at the official site where you can write TypeScript and see the compiled JavaScript, type errors, and emitted .d.ts. It supports changing compiler options and sharing code via URL. It is the best place to experiment with type-level tricks quickly.

A type annotation like 'const x: Foo = value' checks that the value fits Foo, while a type assertion 'value as Foo' tells the compiler to trust you. The annotation is safer because it verifies assignability. Prefer annotations and reserve assertions for cases the compiler genuinely cannot know.

Object literals widen their property value types unless you use 'as const'. So '{ kind: "a" }' infers 'kind: string', which can break discriminated unions expecting a literal. Adding 'as const' or annotating the property keeps the literal type intact.

A 'const' type parameter makes a generic preserve the literal, readonly tuple type of an array argument without the caller writing 'as const'. This is great for functions that map over a fixed list of options and want to keep each element's literal type. It moves the burden of precise inference from the caller to the function author.

Complex generic and conditional types can produce long, nested error messages that are hard to read. Naming intermediate types, simplifying conditionals, and using the '--noErrorTruncation' flag for full output can help diagnose them. Tools and the Playground also help by letting you hover to expand types step by step.

A 'Prettify' helper type, written '{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {}', forces TypeScript to flatten and display a computed type's resolved shape in tooltips. It does not change the type, only its presentation. Developers use it to make intersections and mapped results readable in editor hovers.

You can filter a union by mapping unwanted members to 'never' inside a distributive conditional type, then letting them vanish. For example 'T extends Function ? never : T' removes function members from a union. This is the core technique behind Exclude and many custom filters.

The built-in 'NoInfer<T>' utility blocks a type parameter from being inferred from a particular argument position. It is useful when you want one argument to determine a generic and another to merely be checked against it. For example it can stop a default value's type from widening the inferred parameter.

The 'this' type refers to the current type and is polymorphic, so a method returning 'this' returns the subclass type when called on a subclass. This enables fluent builder APIs where chained methods keep the most specific type. It is more precise than naming the class explicitly.

Returning 'this' from a method makes a builder chainable while preserving the subclass type through the chain. So a subclass method can be called after a base method without casting. This polymorphic 'this' is the idiomatic way to type fluent or chainable APIs.

TypeScript allows template literal types in index signatures, like '{ [key: `data-${string}`]: string }', restricting keys to a pattern. This precisely types objects whose keys must follow a naming scheme, such as data attributes. Keys not matching the pattern are rejected.

When you spread objects with the spread operator, TypeScript computes the resulting type by overlaying later properties on earlier ones. Optional and conditional spreads are handled by widening appropriately. This lets immutable update patterns like 'const next = { ...prev, count: 1 }' stay fully typed.

Typing curried or partially applied functions uses generic tuples and the spread/rest features to track which arguments remain. This can get intricate with variadic tuple types. Libraries provide pre-typed curry helpers so you rarely write these signatures by hand.

The 'Awaited' utility unwraps nested promises recursively, so 'Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>' is 'number'. It mirrors how 'await' flattens thenables at runtime. This recursion correctly types code that awaits a value which itself resolves to another promise.

A promise is typed 'Promise<T>' where T is the resolved value type, like 'Promise<string>'. An async function automatically wraps its return value in a promise, so returning a number gives 'Promise<number>'. Awaiting a 'Promise<T>' yields a 'T'.

An async function always returns a promise, so its declared return type must be a 'Promise<T>', and 'Promise<void>' if it returns nothing. The compiler enforces this even if you forget to wrap the value. Awaiting the result unwraps the promise back to T.

A generator function is typed with 'Generator<YieldType, ReturnType, NextType>', capturing what it yields, what it ultimately returns, and what 'next' accepts. Async generators use 'AsyncGenerator' with the same parameters. These types make iterating and driving generators type-safe.

The 'Iterable<T>' type describes anything with a Symbol.iterator method producing values of type T, like arrays and sets. 'IterableIterator<T>' combines being iterable and being an iterator. Typing custom iterables with these lets them work in for-of loops and spreads with full type checking.

A function returning 'void' completes normally but produces no useful value, while one returning 'never' does not complete at all, because it throws or loops forever. They look similar but mean opposite things about whether the function returns. Control flow analysis treats code after a 'never' call as unreachable, but not after a 'void' call.

You can extract an array's element type with a conditional type: 'T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never'. This pattern generalizes to extracting type parameters from any generic container. It is the building block for utilities like 'Flatten' and element-wise transformations.

A Flatten utility uses 'T extends Array<infer E> ? E : T' to reduce an array type to its element type, leaving non-arrays unchanged. Recursing makes it flatten nested arrays. It demonstrates how conditional types and 'infer' compose to reshape types.

'keyof any' evaluates to 'string | number | symbol', the set of all valid property key types. It is used as a constraint for generic key parameters, as in 'K extends keyof any'. The built-in Record utility uses it to allow any key type.

The built-in 'PropertyKey' type is an alias for 'string | number | symbol', the types that can be object keys. It is handy when writing generic code over arbitrary keys. Using 'PropertyKey' is clearer than spelling out the union each time.

When narrowing with 'instanceof' across a class hierarchy, TypeScript narrows to the checked class even if the variable was a union of subclasses. This works because each class is a distinct constructor. It enables clean handling of polymorphic values without manual casts.

Passing a literal directly as a function argument keeps its literal type if the parameter expects a literal or union, but widens if the parameter is a broad type. This interaction decides whether 'fn("a")' is seen as '"a"' or 'string'. Annotating the parameter with a union or using a 'const' type parameter controls the outcome.

Overloads are best when the return type depends on which argument shape is passed, while a single signature with a union parameter suffices when the return type is the same. Overloads add complexity, so reach for them only when one signature cannot express the relationship. Misusing overloads where a union works just adds noise.

React is a free JavaScript library made by Facebook (now Meta) for building user interfaces, like the buttons and screens you see in apps. Instead of describing every tiny step to change a page, you describe what the screen should look like and React updates it for you. It's one of the most popular tools for making websites and is used by sites like Netflix and Airbnb.

A component in React is a reusable piece of a webpage, like a button, a card, or a whole menu. You write it once and use it many times, just like a LEGO brick you can snap in wherever you need it. Components can hold other components inside them, so you build big pages out of small pieces.

JSX is a special syntax in React that lets you write HTML-looking tags right inside your JavaScript code, like writing

Hello

. It isn't real HTML; a tool called a transpiler turns it into normal JavaScript function calls before the browser runs it. JSX makes components easier to read because the markup sits next to the logic that controls it.

Props are how you pass information into a React component, kind of like settings or ingredients you hand it. A component reads its props but should never change them, because they belong to the parent that sent them. For example, a Greeting component could take a name prop and show 'Hello, Sam!'.

State is data that a React component remembers and can change over time, like a counter that goes up when you click. When state changes, React automatically re-draws the part of the screen that depends on it. This is what makes React apps feel alive and interactive.

useState is a React Hook that gives a function component a piece of memory plus a way to change it. You call it like const [count, setCount] = useState(0), getting the current value and a setter function. Calling the setter tells React to remember the new value and redraw the screen.

useEffect is a React Hook for running code as a side effect, such as fetching data, setting a timer, or talking to the outside world after the screen draws. You give it a function and a list of dependencies, and it runs again whenever those values change. Returning a cleanup function lets you stop timers or cancel work when the component goes away.

Hooks are special functions in React whose names start with 'use', like useState and useEffect, that let function components use features such as memory and side effects. They were added in React 16.8 in 2019 so you no longer need class components for most things. The two main rules are: only call hooks at the top level, and only call them inside React functions.

The virtual DOM is a lightweight copy of the real webpage that React keeps in memory. When your data changes, React updates this copy first, compares it to the previous version, and figures out the smallest set of real changes to make. This makes updates faster than rewriting the whole page every time.

Reconciliation is the process React uses to compare the new virtual DOM with the old one and decide what really needs to change on screen. It uses smart shortcuts, like assuming elements of different types are completely different, to do this quickly. The result is that only the parts of the page that actually changed get updated.

When you show a list of items in React, each one needs a unique 'key' prop so React can tell them apart between updates. Good keys are stable IDs from your data, not the array index, because indexes can shift when items are added or removed. Without proper keys, React may mix up which item is which and show bugs.

Rendering in React means calling your component functions to figure out what the screen should look like. React does this whenever state or props change, then commits only the differences to the real page. A render does not always mean the browser repaints; React often skips work when nothing visible actually changed.

A function component is the modern way to write React components: it's a JavaScript function that returns JSX describing what to show. With Hooks, function components can hold state and run effects, so they can do everything older class components could. They are shorter and easier to read, which is why most new React code uses them.

A class component is an older style of React component written as a JavaScript class that extends React.Component and has a render method. They use lifecycle methods like componentDidMount and this.state. Function components with Hooks have mostly replaced them, but you'll still see class components in older codebases.

A controlled component is a form input whose value is stored in React state, so React is the single source of truth for what's typed. You set the input's value from state and update state in the onChange handler. This lets you validate, format, or reset the input easily because React always knows its current value.

An uncontrolled component lets the browser keep the form input's value instead of React state, and you read it later using a ref. It's handy for quick forms or when integrating non-React code. Controlled inputs are usually preferred because they make it easy to react to every keystroke.

useRef gives you a box that holds a value which stays the same between renders without causing a re-render when it changes. A common use is grabbing a real DOM element, like focusing an input box with inputRef.current.focus(). You can also store values you want to remember but don't want to display.

useContext is a Hook that lets a component read data from a React Context without passing props down through every layer. You wrap part of your app in a Context Provider and any component inside can grab the value. It's great for things many components need, like the current theme or logged-in user.

Context is a React feature for sharing data across many components without manually passing props at every level, a problem called prop drilling. You create a context, provide a value at the top, and consume it anywhere below. It's best for global-ish data like theme, language, or user info, not for everything.

Prop drilling is when you pass a prop down through many components that don't use it themselves, just to reach a deeply nested one that does. It clutters your code and makes changes harder. Context or state management libraries are common ways to avoid drilling props through every layer.

useMemo is a Hook that remembers the result of an expensive calculation and only redoes it when its inputs change. This can speed up a component that would otherwise recompute heavy work on every render. Don't overuse it, though, since memoizing cheap things can cost more than it saves.

useCallback returns a memorized version of a function that stays the same between renders unless its dependencies change. This is useful when passing callbacks to child components that skip re-rendering when their props are unchanged. Like useMemo, it's an optimization and shouldn't be sprinkled everywhere by default.

useReducer is a Hook for managing more complex state by sending 'actions' to a reducer function that returns the next state. It's like a tiny version of Redux built into React and is handy when state changes follow clear rules. You get a state value and a dispatch function to fire off actions.

A custom hook is your own function whose name starts with 'use' and that calls other hooks to share reusable logic between components. For example, useWindowSize could track the browser size for any component. Custom hooks let you package up behavior without copying and pasting code.

A React Fragment lets you return several elements from a component without wrapping them in an extra div. You write <>...</> or <React.Fragment>...</React.Fragment>. This keeps your HTML clean by avoiding pointless wrapper tags that can mess up layouts.

Conditional rendering means showing different things on screen depending on the situation, like a loading spinner before data arrives. In React you commonly use the ternary operator (condition ? a : b) or the && operator inside JSX. Returning null from a component renders nothing at all.

To show a list in React, you usually call .map() on an array and return a JSX element for each item. Each returned element needs a unique key prop so React can track them. This pattern turns data like an array of names into a list of <li> elements on screen.

React handles events with camelCase props like onClick, onChange, and onSubmit that take a function. The function receives a synthetic event object that works the same across browsers. Unlike plain HTML, you pass a function reference, not a string, for example onClick={handleClick}.

A SyntheticEvent is React's cross-browser wrapper around the browser's native event, so onClick and friends behave the same everywhere. It has the familiar methods like preventDefault() and stopPropagation(). React used to reuse these objects in a pool, but since React 17 it no longer does, so you can use them more freely.

Lifting state up means moving shared state to the closest common parent of the components that need it. The parent holds the state and passes it down as props, often with a function to update it. This keeps two components in sync, like two inputs that must always show the same number.

React uses one-way data flow, meaning data moves down from parent to child through props. Children can't directly change a parent's data; instead they call functions the parent passed down. This predictable direction makes it easier to understand where data comes from and why the screen looks the way it does.

In React you should treat state as immutable, meaning you make a new copy with changes instead of editing the old object or array. For example, use [...items, newItem] rather than items.push(newItem). This helps React detect changes correctly and avoids confusing bugs.

StrictMode is a special wrapper component that helps you find problems during development by adding extra checks and warnings. In development it intentionally runs some functions twice to surface bugs like accidental side effects. It doesn't render anything visible and has no effect in the production build.

Create React App (CRA) was an old tool that set up a new React project with one command so you didn't configure the build yourself. As of 2025 the React team officially recommends frameworks like Next.js or Vite instead, and CRA is considered retired. New projects should start with Vite or a full framework.

Vite is a fast modern build tool often used for React apps that starts your dev server almost instantly. It uses native browser modules during development so it doesn't bundle everything up front, and it uses Rollup to build for production. Many teams switched from older tools to Vite for its speed.

Next.js is a popular React framework that adds routing, server rendering, and other features so you don't build them yourself. It can render pages on the server for speed and search engines, and supports the App Router with React Server Components. It's made by Vercel and is one of the most recommended ways to build full React apps.

Server-side rendering (SSR) means the server builds the HTML for a page before sending it to the browser, so users see content faster and search engines can read it. The browser then 'hydrates' the page to make it interactive. Frameworks like Next.js make SSR easy with React.

Client-side rendering (CSR) means the browser downloads a mostly empty page plus JavaScript, then builds the content with React in the browser. It can feel slower on the first load and harder for search engines, but makes later navigation snappy. Many single-page apps use CSR.

Hydration is when React takes server-rendered HTML and attaches its event listeners and state so the page becomes interactive. The HTML shows up fast, then hydration 'wakes it up' so buttons and inputs work. If the server and client HTML don't match, React warns about a hydration mismatch.

Static site generation (SSG) builds your pages into plain HTML files ahead of time, during the build, instead of for each request. This makes pages extremely fast and easy to host since there's no work to do when a visitor arrives. It's great for content that doesn't change often, like blogs or docs.

React Router is a popular library that adds page navigation to React apps without a full page reload. You define routes that map URLs to components, so visiting /about shows the About component. It keeps the browser address bar in sync so back and forward buttons still work.

A single page application (SPA) loads one HTML page and then uses JavaScript to swap the content as you navigate, instead of fetching new pages from the server. This makes the app feel fast and app-like with no full reloads. React is commonly used to build SPAs, often with a router for navigation.

The component lifecycle describes the stages a component goes through: mounting (appearing), updating (changing), and unmounting (going away). In function components you handle these with useEffect, for example running setup when it mounts and cleanup when it unmounts. Understanding the lifecycle helps you start and stop work at the right time.

Mounting is when a React component is created and added to the page for the first time. This is a good moment to fetch data or start a subscription, which you do inside a useEffect with an empty dependency array. The effect's cleanup function runs later when the component unmounts.

Unmounting is when React removes a component from the page, for example when you navigate away. This is when you should clean up timers, listeners, or network requests so they don't keep running. In function components, the function you return from useEffect handles this cleanup.

The dependency array is the list you pass as the second argument to useEffect, telling React which values the effect depends on. An empty array means run once after the first render; no array means run after every render. Listing the right values keeps the effect in sync and avoids stale data.

A stale closure happens when a function inside a component captures an old value of state or props and keeps using it after it should have updated. It often shows up in timers or event handlers set up in useEffect. The fix is usually to include the value in the dependency array or use the functional form of a state setter.

Batching is when React groups several state updates together and re-renders just once instead of once per update, which is faster. Since React 18, this happens automatically even inside promises and timeouts, not only during event handlers. That's why calling setCount twice in a row may only trigger one render.

React 18, released in 2022, introduced concurrent features that let React pause and resume rendering to keep the app responsive. It added automatic batching, the new createRoot API, useTransition, and improved Suspense. These features help apps stay smooth even when doing heavy work.

React 19, released in late 2024, added official support for Actions to handle form submissions and async updates, plus new hooks like useActionState, useOptimistic, and the use API. It also lets you read context with use and improves Server Components support. It streamlines common patterns that used to need extra code.

Suspense is a React feature that lets you show a fallback, like a loading spinner, while a component waits for something such as data or code to load. You wrap components in <Suspense fallback={...}> and React shows the fallback until they're ready. It makes loading states cleaner than scattering spinners everywhere.

React.lazy lets you load a component only when it's actually needed instead of including it in the first download. Combined with Suspense, you can show a loading state while the chunk downloads. This is called code splitting and it makes the initial page load faster by shipping less JavaScript up front.

Code splitting breaks your app's JavaScript into smaller chunks that load on demand instead of one giant file. This means users download only what they need for the current page. React.lazy plus dynamic import() and bundlers like Vite or webpack make code splitting straightforward.

React Server Components (RSC) run only on the server and send their result to the browser, so their code and big libraries never get downloaded by the user. They can read databases or files directly and reduce the JavaScript shipped to the client. Frameworks like Next.js use them, often mixed with regular client components.

In frameworks using Server Components, the 'use client' directive at the top of a file marks that file's components to run in the browser, where they can use state and event handlers. Without it, a component is treated as a server component. You add 'use client' when you need interactivity like onClick or useState.

The 'use server' directive marks a function as a Server Action, code that runs on the server but can be called from the client, often from a form. It lets you handle things like saving data without writing a separate API endpoint. React 19 and Next.js support this pattern for forms and mutations.

useTransition lets you mark some state updates as low-priority 'transitions' so React can keep the interface responsive during heavy work. It gives you an isPending flag and a startTransition function. For example, you can keep typing smooth while a big filtered list updates in the background.

useDeferredValue lets you show a slightly delayed version of a value so urgent updates, like typing, stay fast while expensive renders catch up afterward. You pass it a value and it returns a deferred copy. It's useful for keeping an input responsive while a heavy list re-renders behind it.

An error boundary is a component that catches JavaScript errors in the components below it and shows a fallback UI instead of a blank crashed screen. They're built with class components using componentDidCatch or getDerivedStateFromError, or you use a library wrapper. They don't catch errors in event handlers or async code, though.

A React portal lets you render a child into a different part of the page's HTML than its parent, while keeping it connected in React. It's commonly used for modals, tooltips, and popups that need to escape a container's overflow or z-index. You create one with ReactDOM.createPortal(child, domNode).

React.memo wraps a component so it skips re-rendering when its props haven't changed, which can speed up parts of your app. It does a shallow comparison of props by default. Use it for components that render often with the same props; wrapping everything can actually slow things down.

forwardRef lets a parent component pass a ref down to a DOM element inside a child component, so the parent can focus or measure it. Before React 19 you needed forwardRef to do this; in React 19 you can often pass ref as a normal prop. It's useful when building reusable input components.

The children prop holds whatever you put between a component's opening and closing tags, letting you nest content inside it. For example, a Card component can render {props.children} so anything inside <Card>...</Card> appears in the card. This makes flexible wrapper components like layouts and panels.

Composition in React means building complex UIs by combining simple components, often by nesting them or passing them as props. React favors composition over inheritance, so instead of one component extending another, you wrap or include components. This keeps pieces flexible and reusable.

Default props give a component a fallback value when a prop isn't provided. In modern function components you usually set defaults with JavaScript default parameters, like function Button({ color = 'blue' }). This prevents errors and undefined values when a prop is left out.

Prop spreading uses the spread operator to pass many props at once, like <Button {...rest} />. It's handy for forwarding leftover props to an inner element. Be careful, though, since spreading can accidentally pass props the component doesn't expect.

A render prop is a technique where a component takes a function as a prop and calls it to decide what to render, sharing logic while letting the caller control the look. For example, a Mouse component could call props.render(position). Hooks have replaced many render-prop use cases, but you'll still see the pattern.

A higher-order component (HOC) is a function that takes a component and returns a new one with extra behavior added, like withAuth(Profile). HOCs were a common way to reuse logic before Hooks. Today custom hooks usually handle the same jobs more simply, but HOCs still appear in libraries.

The component tree is the nested structure of all your components, with the root at the top and children branching below. React uses this tree to know what to render and how data flows down through props. Tools like React DevTools let you explore the tree to debug your app.

React DevTools is a free browser extension that lets you inspect your component tree, see each component's props and state, and check why things re-rendered. It adds Components and Profiler tabs to your browser's developer tools. It's one of the most useful tools for debugging React apps.

The React Profiler, part of React DevTools, records how long your components take to render so you can find slow spots. It shows which components re-rendered and why during an interaction. Using it helps you decide where optimizations like memo or useMemo are actually worth adding.

Controlled inputs store their value in React state, giving React full control and easy validation, while uncontrolled inputs let the DOM hold the value and you read it with a ref. Controlled is the common choice for interactive forms; uncontrolled can be simpler for basic or one-off cases. Both can be used in the same form.

Handling forms in React usually means tracking input values in state and running a function on submit that calls event.preventDefault() to stop the page from reloading. You can validate values and show messages before sending data. React 19 also adds Actions and useActionState to simplify form submissions.

Calling event.preventDefault() inside an event handler stops the browser's default behavior, like a form reloading the page or a link navigating away. In React forms you call it at the start of your onSubmit handler so you can handle the data yourself. It works on the synthetic event React passes you.

React expects your components to be pure, meaning given the same props and state they always return the same output and don't change things outside themselves during rendering. Side effects like fetching data belong in useEffect, not in the render. Purity is what lets React safely re-render and optimize components.

A side effect is anything a component does that reaches outside of just calculating the UI, like fetching data, setting a timer, or changing the document title. These belong inside useEffect, not in the main body of the component. Keeping the render pure and effects separate avoids surprising bugs.

The initial render, or mount, is the very first time React runs a component and puts its output on the page. State starts at the values you give to useState, and effects with an empty dependency array run right after this first paint. Later updates are re-renders, not initial renders.

A re-render is when React runs a component again because its state or props changed, or its parent re-rendered. React then compares the new output to the old and updates only what differs on screen. Too many unnecessary re-renders can slow an app, which is when tools like memo help.

React Native lets you build real mobile apps for iPhone and Android using React and JavaScript, rendering actual native components instead of a webpage. You write components much like in React for the web, but use elements like View and Text. Apps like Instagram and Discord have used React Native.

styled-components is a popular CSS-in-JS library that lets you write CSS inside your JavaScript and attach it directly to components. You create a styled element like const Button = styled.button`color: blue;`. It scopes styles to each component so they don't accidentally affect other parts of the page.

Tailwind CSS is a popular styling framework where you add small utility classes like 'p-4' or 'text-center' directly in your HTML or JSX instead of writing separate CSS files. It speeds up styling and keeps designs consistent. Many React developers pair Tailwind with their components for fast, tidy layouts.

CSS Modules let you write normal CSS in a file like Button.module.css and import it into a component, with class names automatically made unique. This keeps styles scoped so a 'title' class in one component won't clash with another. It's a popular way to avoid global CSS conflicts in React apps.

In React you can apply inline styles using the style prop with a JavaScript object, like style={{ color: 'red', fontSize: 16 }}. Property names use camelCase instead of dashes, so background-color becomes backgroundColor. Inline styles are handy for dynamic values but can't do things like hover states or media queries.

In JSX you set CSS classes with className instead of the HTML 'class' attribute, because 'class' is a reserved word in JavaScript. For example, <div className="card">. This is one of the small differences between JSX and plain HTML.

Redux is a library for managing app-wide state in a single central store, useful for big apps with lots of shared data. You change state by dispatching actions to pure reducer functions. Modern Redux uses Redux Toolkit, which cuts down the boilerplate that older Redux was known for.

Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, recommended way to use Redux, designed to remove the boilerplate that made classic Redux tedious. It provides helpers like createSlice to define state and reducers in one place, and includes good defaults. The Redux team now steers everyone toward Redux Toolkit instead of writing Redux by hand.

Zustand is a small, simple state management library for React that uses a single hook to read and update a shared store. It needs far less setup than Redux and doesn't require wrapping your app in a provider. It's popular for apps that want global state without heavy boilerplate.

React Query, now called TanStack Query, is a library that handles fetching, caching, and updating server data in React apps. It manages loading and error states, caches results, and refetches stale data automatically. It saves you from writing lots of manual useEffect-and-useState data-fetching code.

Fetching data in React traditionally happens inside a useEffect that calls fetch or axios, then stores the result in state. You usually track loading and error states too. Today many teams use libraries like TanStack Query or framework features so caching and refetching are handled for them.

A loading state is a piece of state that tracks whether data is still arriving, so you can show a spinner or skeleton while waiting. A common pattern is setting isLoading to true before a fetch and false when it finishes. Good loading states make apps feel responsive instead of frozen.

An error state tracks when something went wrong, like a failed network request, so you can show a friendly message instead of a broken screen. You typically catch the error and store it in state, then render it. Pairing loading and error states makes data fetching feel polished.

An optimistic update changes the UI immediately as if an action succeeded, before the server confirms, to make the app feel instant. If the server later fails, you roll the change back. React 19 added the useOptimistic hook to make this pattern easier.

useOptimistic is a React 19 Hook that lets you show an instant, expected result while a real update is still in progress. For example, a sent message can appear right away before the server confirms it. If the action fails, React reverts to the actual state automatically.

useActionState is a React 19 Hook that manages state tied to a form action, returning the current state, an action to attach to a form, and a pending flag. It makes handling form submissions and their results cleaner. It works well with Server Actions and the new form features.

useFormStatus is a React 19 Hook that tells a component whether the form it's inside is currently submitting. A submit button can use it to disable itself and show 'Saving...' while the action runs. It must be used in a component that's a child of the form.

The 'use' API in React 19 lets you read the value of a promise or a context directly during render. When you use a promise that isn't ready, React suspends and shows the nearest Suspense fallback until it resolves. Unlike other hooks, use can be called conditionally.

Concurrent rendering is React 18's ability to prepare multiple versions of the UI at once and pause or abandon work to stay responsive. It lets urgent updates like typing interrupt less urgent ones like rendering a big list. Features like useTransition and Suspense build on this.

createRoot is the React 18 way to attach your app to the page, replacing the older ReactDOM.render. You call ReactDOM.createRoot(domNode).render(<App />). Using createRoot turns on React 18's concurrent features like automatic batching.

dangerouslySetInnerHTML is React's way to insert raw HTML strings into the page, named scary on purpose because it can open security holes. If you put untrusted text in it, an attacker could inject scripts, a problem called XSS. Only use it with content you fully trust or have sanitized.

React protects against cross-site scripting (XSS) by automatically escaping text you put in JSX, so user input shows up as plain text rather than running as code. The main risk comes from dangerouslySetInnerHTML or building HTML by hand. Always sanitize any HTML you insert that came from users.

Accessibility (often shortened to a11y) means building apps everyone can use, including people who rely on screen readers or keyboards.
