In React, use proper HTML elements like button and label, add aria attributes when needed, and make sure things work without a mouse. Accessible apps are better for all users.

In JSX you connect a label to an input using htmlFor instead of the HTML 'for' attribute, since 'for' is a reserved word in JavaScript. For example, <label htmlFor="email">. Linking labels to inputs improves accessibility and lets users click the label to focus the field.

ARIA attributes, like aria-label and aria-hidden, give assistive technologies extra information about elements that plain HTML can't express. In React you write them as normal props, such as aria-label="Close menu". Use them to fill gaps, but prefer real semantic HTML when you can.

Semantic HTML means using tags that describe their meaning, like <button>, <nav>, <header>, and <main>, instead of stuffing everything in <div>. This helps screen readers, search engines, and other developers understand your page. React lets you use all these semantic tags directly in JSX.

In React, a dropdown is a <select> element, and to control it you set its value from state and update state in onChange. Unlike plain HTML, you don't add 'selected' to an option; you set the select's value instead. This keeps the chosen option in sync with your state.

A controlled checkbox in React uses the 'checked' prop tied to a boolean in state, not 'value', and updates state in onChange using event.target.checked. For example, checked={isOn} onChange={e => setIsOn(e.target.checked)}. This keeps the checkbox's on/off state managed by React.

For a form with many fields, you can keep one state object and update it with a single handler that reads event.target.name. The handler spreads the old object and overrides the changed field, like setForm({...form, [name]: value}). This avoids writing a separate handler for every input.

Debouncing delays running a function until the user stops doing something, like waiting until they finish typing before searching. In React you often set a timer in useEffect and clear it on the next keystroke. Debouncing reduces wasted work, like firing one search instead of one per letter.

Throttling limits how often a function can run, like handling a scroll event at most once every 100 milliseconds. It's useful for events that fire very rapidly, such as scrolling or resizing. Unlike debouncing, throttling runs at a steady rate rather than waiting for activity to stop.

When you start a timer with setInterval in a React effect, you must clear it in the effect's cleanup function with clearInterval, or it'll keep running after the component leaves. Forgetting cleanup causes memory leaks and bugs like multiple timers stacking up. Always return a cleanup function from useEffect when starting timers.

AbortController lets you cancel a fetch request, which is useful in React when a component unmounts before the data arrives. You create a controller, pass its signal to fetch, and call abort() in the effect's cleanup. This prevents updating state on a component that's gone, avoiding warnings and leaks.

useLayoutEffect works like useEffect but runs synchronously right after the DOM updates and before the browser paints. Use it for measuring elements or making visual changes that must happen before the screen shows, to avoid flicker. Because it blocks painting, prefer regular useEffect unless you specifically need this timing.

useImperativeHandle customizes what a parent can access through a ref to your component, exposing specific methods like focus() or reset(). It's used with forwardRef (or ref as a prop in React 19) to give a controlled, limited API. It's an advanced tool you rarely need in everyday code.

useId is a Hook that generates a unique, stable ID safe for server-side rendering, useful for connecting labels and inputs. It avoids mismatches between the server and client that random IDs would cause. You typically use it to build matching id and htmlFor values.

useSyncExternalStore is a Hook that lets you safely read from an external data store outside React, like a custom state library or browser API. It keeps React in sync with that store during concurrent rendering. Most app developers don't call it directly; library authors use it under the hood.

Derived state is information you can calculate from existing state or props, like a filtered list from a search term. You should compute it during render instead of storing it in its own state, which can get out of sync. Keeping only the minimum state and deriving the rest avoids bugs.

A good React rule is to keep state minimal: only store values you can't compute from other values. For example, store the list and the search text, but compute the filtered results during render rather than storing them. Less duplicated state means fewer chances for things to disagree.

To update an object in React state, make a new object with the spread operator and change just the fields you need, like setUser({...user, name: 'Sam'}). Don't edit the existing object directly, because React may not notice the change. This keeps state immutable and updates reliable.

To change an array in React state, create a new array instead of mutating the old one. Add with [...items, newItem], remove with filter, and change one with map. Avoid push, splice, or sort directly on state because those mutate the original and can confuse React.

When new state depends on the old state, pass a function to the setter, like setCount(c => c + 1), instead of using the current variable. This guarantees you work from the latest value, which matters when updates are batched. It's the safe way to increment counters or toggle flags repeatedly.

For animations in React, many developers use libraries like Framer Motion (now called Motion) or React Spring instead of writing raw CSS transitions by hand. These let you animate components as they appear, change, or leave the screen. They handle the tricky timing and physics for smooth motion.

Framer Motion, now known as Motion, is a popular animation library for React that makes it easy to animate components with simple props. You wrap an element in motion.div and set animate, initial, and exit values. It can also animate components leaving the page using AnimatePresence.

A bundler is a tool that combines your many JavaScript, CSS, and asset files into a few optimized files the browser can load efficiently. Popular bundlers include Vite (using Rollup and esbuild), webpack, and esbuild. Bundlers also handle things like minifying code and splitting it into chunks.

A transpiler converts code written in one form into another, like turning JSX and modern JavaScript into older JavaScript browsers understand. Babel is the classic transpiler for React, though faster tools like SWC and esbuild are now common. This step is why you can write JSX even though browsers don't read it directly.

npm is the default package manager for JavaScript, used to install libraries like React and run project scripts. Packages live in a folder called node_modules, and your dependencies are listed in package.json. You install React with a command like npm install react react-dom.

package.json is a file at the root of a JavaScript project that lists its name, version, dependencies, and scripts you can run. When you install a package, npm records it here so others can recreate the same setup. Scripts like 'npm run dev' are defined in its scripts section.

node_modules is the folder where npm installs all your project's libraries and their dependencies. It can get very large, so it's usually excluded from version control with .gitignore and rebuilt from package.json. You don't edit files inside it; you change versions through package.json instead.

Modern JavaScript splits code into modules using export to share things and import to bring them in. In React you import the library and components at the top of files, like import React from 'react'. There are named exports (import { useState }) and default exports (import App from './App').

A default export is the single main thing a module shares, imported without curly braces and with any name you like. For React components you often write export default App and then import App from './App'. A file can have only one default export but many named exports.

A named export shares a specific named value from a module, imported with curly braces using its exact name, like import { useState } from 'react'. A module can have many named exports. React itself exports hooks and utilities as named exports.

A common React pattern is filtering a list as the user types: store the search text in state, then compute the filtered list during render with .filter(). You don't store the filtered result; you derive it each render. This keeps the displayed list always in sync with the search box.

React component names must start with a capital letter, like MyButton, so React knows to treat them as components rather than plain HTML tags. A lowercase name like <button> is treated as a built-in element. This rule is easy to forget and a common source of confusing bugs.

A React component must return a single root element, though it can contain many children. If you want to return several siblings without an extra wrapper, use a Fragment (<>...</>). Trying to return two top-level elements without a wrapper causes an error.

Inside JSX you can embed any JavaScript expression by wrapping it in curly braces, like {user.name} or {2 + 2}. You can put variables, function calls, and ternaries there, but not statements like if or for. This is how you mix dynamic data into your markup.

To write a comment inside JSX, you wrap a JavaScript comment in curly braces, like {/* this is a comment */}. Regular HTML comments don't work in JSX. Outside of JSX, in normal JavaScript code, you use the usual // or /* */ comments.

In JSX, tags that have no children must be self-closed with a slash, like or
, even ones that are sometimes left open in HTML. Forgetting the slash causes a syntax error. This stricter rule is part of how JSX keeps the structure clear.

When a boolean prop should be true, you can write just its name, like <input disabled />, which is shorthand for disabled={true}. To set it false you write disabled={false} or leave it out. This shortcut keeps simple on/off props tidy.

A modal in React is usually a component shown or hidden based on a boolean in state, often rendered with a portal so it sits on top of the page. You toggle the state to open and close it, and add a backdrop and a close button. Good modals also trap focus and close on the Escape key for accessibility.

A toast is a small pop-up message that briefly appears to confirm an action or show an error, then disappears. In React you typically keep a list of active toasts in state and remove each after a timer. Libraries like react-hot-toast handle the queue and animations for you.

A skeleton loader is a gray placeholder shaped like the content that's coming, shown while data loads instead of a spinner. It makes the wait feel shorter because the layout appears stable. In React you render the skeleton component while isLoading is true, then swap in the real content.

A tabs component in React tracks which tab is active in state and shows the matching panel. Clicking a tab updates the state, and you highlight the active one with a class. For accessibility, tabs should use the right ARIA roles and respond to arrow keys.

An accordion is a list of sections that expand and collapse when clicked, often allowing only one open at a time. In React you store which section is open in state and toggle it on click. Each header should be a real button for keyboard and screen-reader support.

A carousel shows one slide at a time with controls to move forward and back. In React you keep the current slide index in state and change it with next and previous buttons. Accessible carousels also let users pause auto-play and navigate with the keyboard.

Infinite scroll loads more content automatically as the user nears the bottom of a list, instead of using page buttons. In React you can detect the bottom with the IntersectionObserver API and then fetch the next batch. It keeps state for the loaded items and whether more remain.

IntersectionObserver is a browser API that tells you when an element scrolls into view, useful for lazy-loading images or triggering infinite scroll. In React you set it up in a useEffect and clean it up when the component unmounts. It's more efficient than listening to every scroll event.

Virtualization, or windowing, renders only the list items currently visible on screen instead of thousands at once, which keeps long lists fast. Libraries like react-window and TanStack Virtual handle the math of which items to show. It's essential for huge lists like big tables or chat histories.

Drag and drop in React lets users move items by dragging them, often to reorder a list. You can use the browser's native drag events or libraries like dnd-kit that handle accessibility and touch. The component updates the array order in state when an item is dropped in a new spot.

React Hook Form is a popular library that makes building forms easier and faster by using refs to avoid re-rendering on every keystroke. It handles validation, error messages, and submission with a simple useForm hook. It's known for good performance on large forms.

Form validation checks that what users type is correct before submitting, like requiring an email format or a minimum length. In React you can validate in state on each change, on submit, or with libraries like Zod plus React Hook Form. Showing clear error messages near each field helps users fix mistakes.

Zod is a TypeScript-friendly library for describing the shape of data and checking that real data matches, often used for form and API validation. You define a schema, then call .parse() or .safeParse() to validate. It pairs well with React Hook Form to validate user input.

TypeScript adds types to JavaScript, helping catch mistakes before you run the code, and it's widely used with React. You can type props with interfaces, like type Props = { name: string }, and React provides types for hooks and events. Many modern React projects start with TypeScript by default.

In TypeScript React, you describe a component's props with a type or interface, then use it in the function signature. For example, function Greeting({ name }: { name: string }). This makes the editor warn you if you pass the wrong props or forget a required one.

useState often infers the type from its initial value, so useState(0) is a number. When the initial value can't tell the whole story, you provide the type, like useState<User | null>(null). This helps catch errors when you read or update the state later.

Environment variables let you configure your app per environment, like a different API URL in development and production. In Vite they must start with VITE_ and you read them with import.meta.env, while older setups used REACT_APP_ and process.env. Remember that anything bundled into the frontend is visible to users, so never put secrets there.

You should never store passwords, API secret keys, or other private data in frontend React code, because anything sent to the browser can be read by users. Secrets belong on the server. The frontend should only hold values that are safe to be public, like a public API URL.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule that controls whether your React app can call an API on a different domain. The server must send headers allowing your site, or the browser blocks the request. CORS errors are common when a frontend and backend run on different addresses during development.

During development, a dev server proxy lets your frontend forward API calls to your backend so you avoid CORS issues. In Vite you set this up in the server.proxy option of vite.config. The browser thinks it's calling the same origin, and the dev server quietly relays the request.

React build tools support different modes like development and production, changing things like error messages and optimizations. The production build strips out helpful dev warnings and minifies code so it's small and fast. You create it with a command like 'npm run build'.

A production build of a React app is optimized: code is minified, dead code is removed, and dev-only warnings are stripped, making the files small and fast. You should always deploy the production build, not the development version. Tools like Vite create it with 'npm run build', outputting files to a dist folder.

To avoid unnecessary re-renders in React, you can wrap components in React.memo, memoize callbacks with useCallback, and keep values stable. But first make sure the re-renders are actually a problem, since most are cheap. Measure with the Profiler before optimizing.

Components re-render when their state or props change or their parent re-renders. A common surprise is passing a fresh object or function as a prop each render, which breaks memoization. Tools like React DevTools Profiler help you see what triggered a render so you can fix wasteful ones.

When a Context value changes, every component reading that context re-renders, which can be slow if the value updates often. To limit this, split contexts by concern or memoize the provided value. For very frequent updates, a dedicated state library may perform better than context.

The function you return from useEffect is its cleanup, run before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts. Use it to remove event listeners, clear timers, or cancel subscriptions. Cleanup prevents leaks and stops old effects from interfering with new ones.

Passing an empty array [] as the second argument to useEffect makes it run only once, right after the component first appears. This is the common spot to fetch initial data or set up a one-time subscription. Its cleanup then runs when the component unmounts.

React's lint rule warns when a useEffect uses a value it doesn't list in its dependency array, which can cause stale data bugs. The fix is usually to add the value, or restructure so you don't need it. Ignoring the warning often leads to effects using outdated state.

A classic data-fetching pattern is calling fetch inside a useEffect with an empty dependency array, then storing the result in state. You should guard against setting state after unmount, often with an AbortController or an isMounted flag. Many teams now use TanStack Query to skip this manual work.

Changing a component's key prop makes React throw away the old one and create a fresh instance, resetting all its state. This is a handy trick to reset a form or animation when some value changes. It's simpler than manually clearing every piece of state.

Fiber is the internal architecture React uses since version 16 to render the UI in small, interruptible units of work. It lets React pause, resume, and prioritize rendering, which powers concurrent features. Most developers never touch Fiber directly, but it's why React can stay responsive during big updates.

Accessible modals should trap keyboard focus inside while open, return focus to the trigger when closed, and close on the Escape key. They also need ARIA roles like role="dialog" and aria-modal. Many React modal libraries handle these details so you don't have to wire them up by hand.

Managing focus means deciding where the keyboard cursor lands, which matters for accessibility, like focusing the first field when a form opens. In React you use a ref and call element.focus(), often inside a useEffect. Good focus management makes apps usable without a mouse.

React handles keyboard events with props like onKeyDown and onKeyUp that give you a synthetic event with the key pressed in event.key. You can check for keys like 'Enter' or 'Escape' to trigger actions. This is how you add keyboard shortcuts or close a modal with Escape.

Responsive design makes a layout work on phones, tablets, and big screens. While CSS media queries do most of the work, React components can also read the window size with a custom hook to change behavior. Frameworks like Tailwind make responsive styling easy with prefixes like md: and lg:.

A common custom hook called useWindowSize tracks the browser window's width and height in state, updating on the resize event. You set up the listener in useEffect and remove it in the cleanup. Components can then change layout or behavior based on the current size.

localStorage lets a React app save small bits of data in the browser that survive page reloads, like a theme preference. You read and write it with localStorage.getItem and setItem, usually syncing it with state in a useEffect. It only stores strings, so you JSON.stringify objects before saving.

A dark mode toggle in React stores the chosen theme in state, applies it with a CSS class or data attribute on the page, and often saves the choice in localStorage. You can also respect the user's system setting with a media query. Context is handy so any component can read the current theme.

Persisting state means saving it so it survives reloads, commonly using localStorage for small data. A typical pattern reads the saved value as the initial state and writes back whenever it changes via useEffect. For bigger or shared data, you'd use a backend instead.

fetch is the browser's built-in way to make network requests, while axios is a popular library that adds conveniences like automatic JSON parsing and easier error handling. Both work fine in React. Many newer projects use fetch directly or a data library like TanStack Query that wraps it.

async/await is JavaScript syntax for writing asynchronous code, like network requests, in a clean step-by-step style. In React you can't make the component function itself async, so you put the async function inside useEffect and call it. Using await makes fetching data read like ordinary sequential code.

A promise represents a value that will be ready later, like the result of a network request, and can be pending, fulfilled, or rejected. You handle it with .then and .catch, or with async/await. React data fetching is built on promises returned by fetch or axios.

When an error boundary catches a crash, it shows a fallback UI you provide instead of a broken screen. A good fallback explains something went wrong and may offer a retry button. Error boundaries protect the rest of the app from one component's failure.

Suspense can show a fallback while data loads if the data source integrates with it, which frameworks like Next.js and libraries provide. The component reads the data and Suspense holds the spinner until it's ready. React 19's use API makes reading promises with Suspense more straightforward.

Streaming server rendering sends the page's HTML in pieces as it becomes ready, so users see the top of the page before slow parts finish. React 18's renderToPipeableStream and Suspense make this possible. It improves how fast a page feels by not waiting for everything at once.

Progressive or selective hydration makes pages interactive piece by piece instead of all at once, so important parts respond sooner. React 18 can hydrate components wrapped in Suspense as they're ready and prioritize where the user interacts. This reduces the wait before a page becomes usable.

A meta-framework builds on React to add routing, data loading, and server rendering out of the box, so you don't assemble them yourself. Examples include Next.js, Remix (now part of React Router), and Astro. The React team recommends starting new apps with a framework rather than bare React.

Remix is a React framework focused on web standards, server rendering, and great data loading with loaders and actions tied to routes. In 2024 the Remix team merged much of its work into React Router. It emphasizes fast page loads and forms that work even before JavaScript loads.

Astro is a web framework that ships zero JavaScript by default and lets you use React components only where you need interactivity, an approach called islands. It's great for content sites like blogs that should load fast. You can mix React, Vue, and Svelte components in the same Astro project.

Islands architecture means a mostly static HTML page with small interactive 'islands' of JavaScript, each hydrated independently. This sends far less JavaScript than making the whole page a single app. Astro popularized the idea, and it pairs well with React components for the interactive parts.

Search engines read HTML, so pure client-rendered React apps can be harder to index because content arrives via JavaScript. Server rendering or static generation, like Next.js provides, sends real HTML that's easy for search engines to read. This is a big reason teams reach for frameworks instead of plain client-side React.

To change the browser tab's title in plain React, you set document.title inside a useEffect. Frameworks like Next.js provide built-in ways to manage the title and other head tags per page. React 19 also lets you place <title> and <meta> tags directly in components.

React 19 lets you render document metadata tags like <title>, <meta>, and <link> right inside your components, and React automatically hoists them into the page's head. This makes per-page titles and descriptions easier without a separate helmet library. It works during both server and client rendering.

react-helmet was a popular library for managing the document head, like the title and meta tags, from inside components. With React 19's built-in metadata support, you often no longer need it. Frameworks like Next.js also offer their own head management.

Web Vitals are Google's metrics for real user experience, like Largest Contentful Paint (loading), Interaction to Next Paint (responsiveness), and Cumulative Layout Shift (visual stability). React apps can measure them and report them to analytics. Good scores help both users and search ranking.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures how much content jumps around as a page loads, which is annoying to users. You reduce it by reserving space for images and ads with set dimensions and avoiding inserting content above what's already visible. In React, render skeletons sized like the real content to keep layout stable.

Optimizing images means serving the right size and modern formats like WebP or AVIF so pages load faster. Next.js offers an Image component that resizes and lazy-loads images for you. In plain React you can use the loading="lazy" attribute and proper width and height to avoid layout shift.

Adding loading="lazy" to an tells the browser to wait until the image is near the screen before downloading it, saving bandwidth. This works the same in React JSX as in HTML. It's an easy win for pages with many images below the fold.

Tree shaking is when a bundler removes code you never use, like unused functions from a library, so the final bundle is smaller. It relies on ES module imports and exports to know what's actually needed. Importing only the pieces you use, rather than a whole library, helps tree shaking work well.

Bundle size is how much JavaScript users must download, and smaller is faster. You shrink it with code splitting, tree shaking, and avoiding huge libraries. Tools like a bundle analyzer show which packages take up the most space so you can trim them.

A dynamic import() loads a module only when needed, returning a promise, which enables code splitting. React.lazy uses dynamic import to load a component on demand. This keeps the initial download small and fetches extra code as users explore the app.

JSX looks like HTML but has differences: use className instead of class, htmlFor instead of for, camelCase event and style names, self-closing tags, and curly braces for JavaScript. These exist because JSX compiles to JavaScript, where some words are reserved. Knowing them avoids common beginner errors.

To toggle CSS classes based on conditions, developers often build a class string with template literals or use a tiny library like clsx or classnames. For example, clsx('btn', isActive && 'btn-active'). These libraries make conditional class lists clean and avoid extra spaces or undefined values.

Compound components are a pattern where related components work together, like <Menu> with <Menu.Item> children sharing state through context. It gives a clean, flexible API where the parent manages shared logic. Many UI libraries use this pattern for things like tabs and dropdowns.

Headless components provide behavior and accessibility without any built-in styling, so you control the look entirely. Libraries like Radix UI, Headless UI, and React Aria offer accessible building blocks like dropdowns and dialogs. You add your own CSS, getting correct behavior plus full design freedom.

Radix UI is a library of unstyled, accessible React components like dialogs, dropdowns, and tooltips that handle keyboard support and ARIA for you. Because they're unstyled, you bring your own design, often with Tailwind. It's a popular base for custom design systems.

shadcn/ui is a popular collection of React components you copy into your own project rather than install as a dependency, built on Radix UI and Tailwind CSS. Because you own the code, you can fully customize each component. It became a common starting point for building design systems in 2024 and 2025.

A component library provides ready-made UI pieces like buttons, inputs, and dialogs so you don't build them from scratch. Examples include Material UI, Chakra UI, Ant Design, and Mantine. They speed up development and keep designs consistent, though they add to your bundle size.

A design system is a shared set of components, styles, and rules that keep a product looking and behaving consistently. In React it's often a package of reusable components with agreed-upon colors, spacing, and typography. Building one helps teams move faster and avoid one-off styles.

Storybook is a tool for building and viewing UI components in isolation, outside your full app. You write 'stories' showing each component in different states, which helps with development, testing, and documentation. It's widely used to develop and showcase React component libraries.

Testing React apps usually combines a test runner like Vitest or Jest with React Testing Library to render components and check behavior. The goal is to test what users see and do, like clicking a button and seeing a result, not internal details. Good tests catch bugs before users do.

React Testing Library is a popular tool for testing React components by interacting with them the way a user would, finding elements by visible text or roles. Its philosophy is to avoid testing implementation details so tests don't break on small refactors. You render a component, simulate events, and assert on the result.

Jest is a widely used JavaScript testing framework that runs your tests, checks results with matchers like expect(x).toBe(y), and can mock modules. It's been a standard for testing React, often paired with React Testing Library. Newer Vite projects frequently use Vitest, which has a similar API.

Vitest is a fast test runner built for Vite projects, with an API very similar to Jest so it's easy to switch. It reuses your Vite config and is quick because of Vite's speed. It's a common choice for testing modern React apps that already use Vite.

A snapshot test saves a component's rendered output to a file and compares future runs against it, flagging any change. It's quick to add but can break on harmless changes, so use it sparingly. Testing visible behavior is usually more valuable than snapshotting everything.

End-to-end (E2E) tests drive a real browser through your app like a user, checking whole flows such as logging in and buying something. Tools like Playwright and Cypress are popular for React E2E tests. They catch bugs that unit tests miss but run slower.

Playwright is a modern tool for automating browsers to test web apps end-to-end across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. You write scripts that click, type, and check the page just like a user. It's a popular choice for testing React apps in real browsers.

When testing or developing without a real backend, you can mock API responses so your React app gets fake data. Tools like Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercept network requests and return canned responses. This lets you build and test the UI before the API exists.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts your app's network requests and returns mock responses, working in both the browser and tests. Because it mocks at the network level, your app code calls fetch normally and doesn't know it's faked. It's popular for developing and testing React apps offline.

A linter like ESLint scans your code for likely mistakes and style problems, including React-specific rules such as the Hooks rules. It catches things like missing useEffect dependencies before they cause bugs. Most React projects run ESLint automatically while you code or before committing.

The eslint-plugin-react-hooks package enforces the Rules of Hooks: call hooks only at the top level and only in React functions, plus checks effect dependencies. These rules catch a whole class of subtle bugs. They're included by default in most React starter setups.

Prettier is a code formatter that automatically arranges your code's spacing, line breaks, and quotes in a consistent style. It ends arguments about formatting because everyone's code looks the same. Many React projects run Prettier on save or before commits, often alongside ESLint.

A monorepo keeps several related projects, like an app and its shared component library, in one repository. Tools like Turborepo and Nx manage building and caching across the packages. Teams use monorepos so shared React components and utilities stay in sync.

Turborepo is a build tool that speeds up monorepos by caching task results and running them in parallel, only redoing work that actually changed. It's made by Vercel and often used with multiple React apps and shared packages. Caching means a second build can be nearly instant.

Fast Refresh updates your React app in the browser the instant you save a file, usually keeping the current state intact so you don't lose your place. It's built into Vite and Next.js. This quick feedback loop makes building UIs much faster than full reloads.

Hot Module Replacement (HMR) swaps changed code into a running app without a full page reload, preserving state where possible. React's Fast Refresh is HMR tuned for components. It's a big reason modern dev servers feel so quick when you edit and save.

The Next.js App Router organizes pages using folders in an app directory, where special files like page.js and layout.js define routes and shared layouts. It supports React Server Components and streaming by default. It replaced the older Pages Router as the recommended approach in recent Next.js versions.

In the Next.js App Router, a layout.js file wraps the pages inside its folder with shared UI like a header or sidebar, and it stays mounted as you navigate between those pages. This avoids re-rendering the shared parts on every navigation. You can nest layouts for sections of your site.

Next.js uses file-based routing, where the folder and file structure decides your URLs, so a file at app/about/page.js becomes the /about route. This means you create pages just by adding files, no separate route config. Dynamic routes use folders with brackets, like [id].

A dynamic route in Next.js uses square brackets in a folder name, like [id], to match any value in that part of the URL. Visiting /posts/5 maps id to '5', which your page can read. This lets one page template handle many items, like every blog post.

Next.js lets you write backend API endpoints inside the same project, using route handlers in the App Router or files in pages/api. They run on the server, so they can safely use secrets and talk to a database. This means a Next.js app can include both frontend and backend code.

In the older Next.js Pages Router, getServerSideProps fetched data on the server for each request before rendering a page. The newer App Router fetches data by simply using async Server Components and await. New projects use the App Router approach, but you'll still see getServerSideProps in older code.

A hydration mismatch happens when the HTML the server rendered doesn't match what React produces in the browser, causing a warning. Common causes include using random values, dates, or browser-only APIs during the initial render. The fix is to make the first render the same on both sides, sometimes by waiting until after mount.

In server-rendered React, code like window or document doesn't exist on the server, so using them during render causes errors. You should access browser-only APIs inside useEffect, which runs only in the browser. This keeps server rendering from crashing on browser-specific code.

If you render a list without unique keys, React logs a warning that each child should have a unique key prop. The fix is giving each item a stable, unique key, usually an ID from your data. Ignoring it can lead to wrong items being reused or animated incorrectly.

The 'Too many re-renders' error usually means you called a state setter directly during render instead of inside an event handler or effect. For example, writing onClick={setCount(1)} runs immediately and loops; you need onClick={() => setCount(1)}. React stops the runaway loop and shows this error to protect your app.

React compares props and state by reference for objects and arrays, so a new object with the same contents counts as 'changed'. That's why creating a fresh object each render can defeat memoization and cause extra re-renders. Stable references, sometimes via useMemo, keep things steady when needed.

A shallow comparison checks each top-level property for equality but doesn't look deep inside nested objects. React.memo and many optimizations use shallow comparison on props. Knowing this explains why a changed nested object can be missed unless you replace the outer reference too.

Effects run after React has updated the DOM and the browser has painted, so users see the screen first and then effects fire. Multiple effects in one component run in the order you wrote them. useLayoutEffect runs earlier, before paint, when you need to avoid visible flicker.

When a useEffect's dependencies change, React first runs the previous effect's cleanup, then runs the effect again with new values. This keeps things tidy, like removing an old event listener before adding a new one. Understanding this order helps you reason about effects that depend on changing values.

Defining a function inline in JSX, like onClick={() => doThing()}, creates a new function on every render. This is fine for most cases and keeps code readable. It only matters when a memoized child re-renders because of the changing function, where useCallback can help.

If computing the initial state is expensive, pass a function to useState instead of a value, like useState(() => heavyCompute()). React calls it only on the first render, not every render. This avoids wasting work recomputing an initial value React already has.

Use state for values that should update the screen when they change, and use a ref for values you want to remember without triggering a re-render. For example, store a timer ID in a ref, but a counter you display in state. Changing a ref's .current never re-renders the component.

In relational database theory, a 'relation' is the formal name for a table. It is an unordered set of rows (tuples), each made of the same named columns (attributes). Because a relation is a set, the rows have no inherent order and there are no duplicate rows in the pure mathematical model, though real SQL tables can have duplicates unless you add a key.

A tuple is the formal term for a single row in a relational database. It is one record holding a value for each column of the table. The word comes from math, where a tuple is just an ordered list of values like (3, 'cat', true).

A primary key is a column (or set of columns) whose value uniquely identifies each row in a table, and it can never be NULL. Databases automatically build an index on the primary key so lookups by it are fast. A table can have only one primary key, though that key may span several columns (a composite key).

A foreign key is a column in one table that points to the primary key of another table, linking the two. For example an 'orders' table might have a customer_id foreign key referencing the 'customers' table. The database can enforce that every foreign key value actually exists in the target table, which is called referential integrity.

Referential integrity is the rule that a foreign key must point to a row that really exists (or be NULL). Databases enforce it so you cannot, say, create an order for a customer that was deleted. You can control what happens to children when a parent is removed using ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL, or RESTRICT.

A composite key is a primary or unique key made of two or more columns together. No single column is unique, but the combination is. A common example is a join table where the pair (student_id, course_id) uniquely identifies an enrollment.

A surrogate key is an artificial primary key with no business meaning, like an auto-incrementing id or a UUID. It is used instead of a 'natural key' (such as an email or SSN) so the key never changes even if real-world data does. Surrogate keys keep joins simple and stable.

A natural key is a primary key built from real-world data that already uniquely identifies a row, such as a country's ISO code or a book's ISBN. Its advantage is meaning; its risk is that real-world values sometimes change or turn out not to be unique, which can break references.

A candidate key is any column or set of columns that could serve as the primary key because it uniquely identifies every row. A table can have several candidate keys; you pick one as the primary key, and the rest become 'alternate keys' that you can still enforce with UNIQUE constraints.

Normalization is organizing tables to reduce duplicated data and avoid update anomalies. You split data into smaller related tables so each fact is stored once. The classic steps are first, second, and third normal form (1NF, 2NF, 3NF), each removing a specific kind of redundancy.

First normal form (1NF) requires that each column holds a single atomic value, not a list or a nested table. A column storing 'red,green,blue' violates 1NF; you would instead store one color per row in a related table. 1NF makes querying and indexing individual values possible.

Second normal form (2NF) applies to tables with composite keys: every non-key column must depend on the whole key, not just part of it. If a column depends on only one part of a two-column key, you move it to its own table. 2NF removes redundancy caused by partial dependencies.

Third normal form (3NF) says no non-key column may depend on another non-key column (no transitive dependencies). For example, if a table stores zip_code and also city, and city is determined by zip_code, you should move that to a separate table. 3NF is the practical target for most operational databases.

Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) is a stricter version of 3NF: every determinant (anything that decides another column's value) must be a candidate key. It fixes rare anomalies that 3NF allows when a table has overlapping candidate keys. Most well-designed 3NF schemas are already in BCNF.

Denormalization deliberately stores redundant or pre-joined data to make reads faster, trading away some of normalization's tidiness. For example you might copy a customer's name into the orders table so a report avoids a join. The cost is that you must keep the duplicated copies in sync on updates.

An update anomaly happens when the same fact is stored in many rows, so changing it requires updating every copy and missing one leaves the data inconsistent. Normalization prevents this by storing each fact exactly once. Insert and delete anomalies are the related problems of not being able to add or remove data cleanly.

ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability, the four guarantees a reliable transaction database provides. Atomicity means all-or-nothing; Consistency means rules stay satisfied; Isolation means concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other; Durability means committed data survives a crash. Relational databases like PostgreSQL are built around ACID.

Atomicity is the 'A' in ACID: a transaction either fully completes or has no effect at all. If a transfer debits one account but crashes before crediting the other, atomicity rolls back the debit so money is never lost. The database tracks changes so it can undo a partial transaction.

Durability is the 'D' in ACID: once a transaction commits, its changes survive even a power loss or crash. Databases achieve this by writing changes to a durable log on disk before reporting success. After a crash, the database replays that log to restore committed work.

A transaction groups several database operations into one unit of work that either all succeed or all fail. You start it with BEGIN, finish with COMMIT to save, or ROLLBACK to discard. Transactions are what let a bank transfer move money out of one account and into another safely as a single step.

COMMIT permanently saves all the changes made inside a transaction, making them visible to other users and durable on disk. Until you commit, your changes are private to your transaction and can be undone. Many database tools 'autocommit' each statement unless you explicitly start a transaction.

ROLLBACK cancels every change made since the transaction began, returning the database to its prior state. You use it when something goes wrong partway through, like a constraint violation. A SAVEPOINT lets you roll back to a marked point instead of undoing the whole transaction.

A savepoint is a named marker inside a transaction that you can roll back to without abandoning the whole transaction. You set one with SAVEPOINT name, and later ROLLBACK TO name undoes only the work after that point. It is useful for trying a risky step that you might want to retry.

An isolation level controls how much one transaction can see of another's in-progress changes. SQL defines four levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE, from loosest to strictest. Higher levels prevent more anomalies but can reduce concurrency and increase the chance of conflicts.

A dirty read is when a transaction reads data another transaction has changed but not yet committed. If that other transaction rolls back, you acted on data that never really existed. The READ UNCOMMITTED isolation level allows dirty reads; READ COMMITTED and above prevent them.

A non-repeatable read happens when you read a row twice in one transaction and get different values because another transaction committed a change in between. The REPEATABLE READ isolation level prevents it by keeping the rows you read stable for the whole transaction.

A phantom read is when a transaction re-runs a query and finds new rows that another transaction inserted and committed in between. Unlike a non-repeatable read (which is about changed values), phantoms are about added or removed rows. The SERIALIZABLE isolation level prevents phantoms.

SERIALIZABLE is the strictest isolation level: transactions behave as if they ran one after another, with no concurrency anomalies at all. It prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms. The trade-off is more locking or more conflict aborts, so it is the slowest under heavy contention.

Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC) lets readers and writers avoid blocking each other by keeping multiple versions of a row. A reader sees a consistent snapshot from when its transaction (or statement) started, while a writer creates a new version. PostgreSQL, Oracle, and MySQL's InnoDB all use MVCC.

Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a frozen view of the database as it looked when the transaction started, using MVCC. Reads never block and never see other transactions' uncommitted changes. It prevents most anomalies but can allow a subtle one called write skew, which true serializable isolation avoids.

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely, so it locks rows before changing them, forcing other transactions to wait. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is a common way to grab such a lock. It avoids lost updates but can cause waiting and deadlocks under heavy contention.

Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare, so it does not lock; instead it checks at write time whether the row changed since you read it, often using a version number or timestamp column. If the version no longer matches, the update fails and the app retries. It scales well when conflicts are uncommon.

A deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so both wait forever. Databases detect deadlocks and automatically abort one transaction (the 'victim') so the other can proceed. Acquiring locks in a consistent order across your code helps avoid them.

A lost update happens when two transactions read the same row, both modify it, and one's change overwrites the other's. For example two users each add $10 to a balance but only $10 gets added. Locking, atomic UPDATE ... SET balance = balance + 10, or optimistic version checks prevent it.

A row lock restricts access to a single row rather than the whole table, letting other transactions work on different rows at the same time. Most modern databases use row-level locking by default for high concurrency. Locking too many rows, though, can escalate toward locking large portions of a table.

A table lock blocks access to an entire table, which is simple but limits concurrency since everyone competes for the one lock. Some operations like certain schema changes need a table lock. Modern databases prefer fine-grained row locks for normal reads and writes to keep many users working at once.

An index is a separate data structure that lets the database find rows fast without scanning the whole table, much like a book's index. It maps column values to the locations of matching rows. Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes slightly and use extra storage, so you add them where they help most.

A B-tree (technically B+tree) index is the default index type in most databases, storing keys in a balanced, sorted tree so lookups, range scans, and ordered reads are all fast (about log n steps). Because keys stay sorted, a B-tree supports equality, range queries, and ORDER BY on the indexed column. It is the workhorse index for relational data.

A hash index stores keys in a hash table, giving very fast exact-match lookups but no support for range queries or sorting, since hashing scrambles order. It shines for equality checks like WHERE id = 5. PostgreSQL supports hash indexes, but B-trees are usually preferred because they handle both equality and ranges.

A composite index covers more than one column, like (last_name, first_name). Column order matters: the index helps queries that filter on a leftmost prefix (last_name alone, or both), but not first_name alone. Designing the column order to match your common queries is key to making it effective.

A partial index covers only rows matching a condition, like WHERE active = true. It is smaller and faster to maintain than a full index, and useful when queries always filter on that condition or when most rows are irrelevant. PostgreSQL calls them partial indexes; SQL Server calls them filtered indexes.

A unique index both speeds up lookups and enforces that no two rows share the same value in the indexed column(s). Primary keys and UNIQUE constraints are implemented with unique indexes under the hood. Inserting a duplicate value triggers a constraint violation error.

A clustered index determines the physical order in which rows are stored on disk, so the table itself is sorted by that key. A table can have only one clustered index because data can be physically sorted just one way. SQL Server and MySQL's InnoDB cluster by the primary key by default.

A non-clustered (secondary) index is stored separately from the table and points back to the rows, so a table can have many of them. Looking up a row through it may require a second step to fetch the actual row data (a 'bookmark lookup'). Covering indexes avoid that extra step.

Selectivity measures how well an index narrows results: a highly selective column (like a unique id) points to few rows per value, while a low-selectivity column (like a boolean) points to many. The planner prefers highly selective indexes because they eliminate the most rows. Indexing a column with only a couple of distinct values often is not worth it.

A full table scan (or sequential scan) reads every row in a table to find matches. It is unavoidable when no useful index exists, or it is actually the fastest choice when a query returns most of the table. The planner sometimes picks a scan over an index on purpose when the index would not save enough work.

An index scan walks part of an index to find matching rows, then usually fetches those rows from the table. It is efficient when a query targets a small fraction of rows. If the index alone has all needed columns, the database can do an index-only scan and skip the table fetch entirely.

The query planner (or optimizer) decides how to actually run your SQL: which indexes to use, what join order, and which join algorithm. SQL is declarative, so you say what you want and the planner figures out how. It compares estimated costs of many plans and picks the cheapest based on statistics about your data.

EXPLAIN shows the plan the database intends to use for a query without running it, listing scans, joins, and estimated costs. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports real timings and row counts, which is invaluable for finding why a query is slow. Comparing estimated vs actual rows reveals bad statistics.

Query cost is the planner's abstract estimate of how expensive a plan is, combining disk page reads and CPU work into one number. Lower estimated cost wins. The numbers are not seconds; they are relative units the planner uses to compare alternative plans, tuned by parameters like random_page_cost.

Statistics are summaries the database keeps about each table: row counts, distinct values per column, value distributions (histograms), and null fractions. The planner relies on them to estimate how many rows a filter will return. Stale statistics cause bad plans, which is why you run ANALYZE (Postgres) or update statistics regularly.

ANALYZE (in PostgreSQL) scans a table to collect fresh statistics about its data distribution for the query planner. Without up-to-date statistics, the planner may badly misjudge how many rows a query touches and pick a slow plan. Autovacuum runs ANALYZE automatically, but you can run it manually after big data changes.

A histogram is a statistic that buckets a column's values to describe their distribution, so the planner can estimate how many rows fall in a range like price BETWEEN 10 AND 20. Without it, the planner would only know the min, max, and count. Histograms make range and inequality estimates much more accurate.

A nested loop join takes each row from one table and looks for matches in the other, ideally using an index on the inner table. It is fast when the outer side is small and the inner side is indexed, but slow if both sides are large. The planner picks it for selective joins.

A hash join builds an in-memory hash table from the smaller input, then probes it with rows from the larger input to find matches. It is excellent for joining two big tables on equality with no useful index. It only works for equality (=) join conditions, not ranges.

A merge join (sort-merge join) requires both inputs sorted on the join key, then walks them together like merging two sorted lists. It is efficient for large datasets and supports range as well as equality joins. If the data is already sorted (for instance from an index), it avoids the sort step.

An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables on the join condition. Rows in either table with no partner are dropped. It is the most common join, used to combine related data like orders with their customers.

A LEFT JOIN (left outer join) returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right; where there is no match, the right-side columns come back as NULL. It is how you find, say, all customers and their orders including customers who never ordered. A WHERE on the right table can accidentally turn it back into an inner join.

A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row from the right table and fills NULLs where the left has no match, the mirror image of a LEFT JOIN. In practice people rewrite right joins as left joins by swapping table order, since left joins read more naturally. The result sets are equivalent.

A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, matching where it can and filling NULLs on whichever side has no partner. It is useful for reconciling two datasets and spotting rows that exist in only one. MySQL lacks it natively, so you simulate it with a UNION of a left and a right join.

A CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of another, producing a Cartesian product. With 100 and 50 rows you get 5,000 result rows. It is rarely intended; an accidental cross join (from forgetting a join condition) is a classic cause of runaway queries.

A self join joins a table to itself, using table aliases to tell the two copies apart. It is handy for hierarchical data, like an employees table where each row has a manager_id pointing to another employee. You write FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id.

Join order is the sequence in which the planner combines tables in a multi-table query, and it can hugely affect performance. The optimizer searches many orderings to find the one that keeps intermediate result sets small. For queries with many tables, the search space is huge, so planners use heuristics or limit how far they search.

A subquery is a query nested inside another, often in a WHERE, FROM, or SELECT clause. For example WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders) filters using results of an inner query. Subqueries can sometimes be rewritten as joins, which the optimizer may handle more efficiently.

A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query, so conceptually it re-runs for each outer row. For example, finding employees who earn more than their department's average uses the outer row's department. They can be slow on large data; rewriting as a join or window function is often faster.

A Common Table Expression (CTE), written with the WITH keyword, names a temporary result set you can reference in the main query. It makes complex queries readable by breaking them into named steps. CTEs can also be recursive, which is how you query hierarchies and graphs in SQL.

A recursive CTE references itself to traverse hierarchical or graph data, like an org chart or a folder tree. It has a base case (the anchor) and a recursive part that repeatedly joins back to the CTE until no new rows appear. It is the standard SQL way to do 'walk the tree' queries.

A window function computes a value across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them into one row like GROUP BY does. Examples include ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), running totals with SUM() OVER, and LAG/LEAD for comparing to neighboring rows. The OVER clause defines the 'window' of rows it considers.

PARTITION BY inside a window function's OVER clause splits rows into groups, and the function restarts for each group. For instance ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers employees within each department separately. It is like GROUP BY but keeps all the rows.

GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same values in the listed columns into one row per group, so you can apply aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM, or AVG per group. Every selected column must either appear in GROUP BY or be wrapped in an aggregate. It is the foundation of summary reports.

HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, the way WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. You use HAVING to keep, say, only departments with more than 10 employees: GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 10. You cannot use aggregates in WHERE, which is exactly why HAVING exists.

Aggregate functions compute a single value over many rows: COUNT counts rows, SUM adds, AVG averages, MIN and MAX find extremes. They are usually paired with GROUP BY to summarize per group. COUNT(*) counts all rows while COUNT(column) skips NULLs, a common source of confusion.

DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from a query's result, returning only unique combinations of the selected columns. SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers lists each city once. It can be expensive on large results because the database must sort or hash to detect duplicates.

UNION stacks the results of two queries into one, removing duplicate rows. UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is faster because it skips the deduplication step. Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types.

INTERSECT returns only the rows that appear in both query results, like the overlap of two sets. EXCEPT (or MINUS in Oracle) returns rows in the first query that are not in the second. These set operators are handy for comparing datasets.

NULL represents an unknown or missing value, not zero or an empty string. Any comparison with NULL using = returns 'unknown', so you must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test for it. NULLs also propagate: 5 + NULL is NULL, and they behave specially in aggregates and joins.

SQL uses three-valued logic: a condition can be TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN because of NULLs. WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is TRUE, so a row where the test is UNKNOWN is dropped. This is why WHERE salary <> 100 surprisingly excludes rows where salary is NULL.

COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value from its list of arguments, so COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Anonymous') falls back gracefully. It is the standard way to provide defaults for missing data in queries. NULLIF is its cousin, returning NULL when two values are equal.

Whether NULLs appear in an index depends on the database: PostgreSQL B-trees do index NULLs, while some others omit them. This matters because a WHERE col IS NULL query may or may not use an index. A partial index WHERE col IS NULL can make such lookups fast where they otherwise scan the table.

A constraint is a rule the database enforces on data, rejecting any change that breaks it. Common kinds are NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, and CHECK. Constraints keep data valid at the database level, which is more reliable than trusting every application to validate correctly.

A CHECK constraint enforces a condition on a column's values, such as CHECK (price >= 0) or CHECK (status IN ('open','closed')). Any insert or update that violates it is rejected. It pushes validation into the database so bad data cannot sneak in through any code path.

A NOT NULL constraint forbids a column from holding NULL, meaning every row must supply a value. It is the simplest way to mark a field as required at the database level. Primary key columns are implicitly NOT NULL.

A UNIQUE constraint guarantees no two rows share the same value(s) in the specified column(s), though it allows multiple NULLs in many databases since NULLs are considered distinct. It is backed by a unique index. Use it for things like email addresses that must not repeat.

A DEFAULT clause supplies a value for a column when an insert omits it, such as DEFAULT now() for a created_at timestamp or DEFAULT 0 for a counter. Defaults keep inserts simple and ensure columns are never accidentally left NULL when a sensible value exists.

Auto-increment columns generate a unique increasing integer for each new row, perfect for surrogate primary keys. MySQL uses AUTO_INCREMENT, PostgreSQL uses SERIAL or the newer GENERATED AS IDENTITY, and SQL Server uses IDENTITY. The database hands out the next number automatically so you never collide.

A UUID is a 128-bit identifier so large that you can generate one anywhere without coordination and not collide. It is useful for distributed systems where multiple servers create ids independently. The downside is that random UUIDs scatter inserts across a B-tree index; UUIDv7, which is time-ordered, fixes that locality problem.

A view is a saved query that behaves like a virtual table; selecting from it runs the underlying query. Views simplify complex queries, present a stable interface, and can restrict which columns users see. A plain view stores no data of its own and is recomputed each time it is read.

A materialized view stores the actual results of a query on disk, so reading it is fast like reading a table. The trade-off is staleness: it does not auto-update, so you must REFRESH it to pick up new data. They are great for expensive reports that tolerate being slightly out of date.

A stored procedure is a named block of SQL (and procedural logic) stored in the database and called by name. It can take parameters, run multiple statements, and encapsulate business logic close to the data. Procedures reduce round-trips and centralize logic, though they can scatter business rules across app and database.

A trigger is code that runs automatically in response to an event on a table, like BEFORE INSERT or AFTER UPDATE. Triggers can enforce rules, maintain audit logs, or keep derived columns in sync. They are powerful but can make behavior hard to trace, since effects happen invisibly behind ordinary statements.

A sequence is a database object that hands out an ordered series of unique numbers, used to feed auto-increment columns. You call nextval() to get the next number. Sequences are not transactional in the usual sense: a rolled-back transaction still 'uses up' its number, so id columns can have gaps.

In SQL a schema is a namespace that groups related tables, views, and other objects under one name, like 'sales' or 'auth'. It helps organize large databases and control permissions per area. Note 'schema' is also used loosely to mean the overall structure of a database.

DDL (Data Definition Language) is the subset of SQL that defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and TRUNCATE for tables, indexes, and other objects. It is contrasted with DML, which manipulates the data inside those structures. In many databases DDL statements implicitly commit the current transaction.

DML (Data Manipulation Language) is the part of SQL that works with the data itself: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. These statements run inside transactions so you can commit or roll them back. DML is the day-to-day language of querying and changing rows.

DCL (Data Control Language) handles permissions with GRANT and REVOKE, deciding who may do what to which database objects. For example GRANT SELECT ON orders TO analyst lets a role read the orders table. It is how databases implement access control.

DELETE removes rows one at a time and can have a WHERE clause and fire triggers, while TRUNCATE quickly empties an entire table by deallocating its storage. TRUNCATE is much faster for clearing everything but cannot be filtered and may reset auto-increment counters. In many databases TRUNCATE is harder to roll back than DELETE.

An upsert inserts a row, or updates it instead if a row with the same key already exists, in one atomic step. PostgreSQL writes INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, MySQL uses INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, and standard SQL has MERGE. It avoids the race condition of checking-then-inserting in two separate statements.

MERGE is a standard SQL statement that compares a source and target table and, per row, inserts, updates, or deletes based on whether matches exist. It is the formal way to synchronize two datasets or do upserts. It is powerful but its syntax is verbose, and historically some implementations had subtle bugs.

INSERT adds new rows to a table. You can insert one row with VALUES, many rows at once with multiple value lists (much faster than separate statements), or rows produced by a SELECT. Multi-row inserts reduce round-trips and let the database batch the work efficiently.

UPDATE changes existing rows' column values, using SET to assign new values and WHERE to choose which rows. Forgetting the WHERE clause updates every row in the table, a classic and costly mistake. Wrapping updates in a transaction lets you verify the result before committing.

Bulk inserting many rows in one statement or with a dedicated loader like PostgreSQL's COPY is far faster than thousands of single-row inserts, because it avoids per-statement overhead and round-trips. Temporarily dropping indexes and re-creating them after a large load can speed it up further. Batching also lets the database group disk writes.

A prepared statement is a query parsed and planned once, then executed many times with different parameter values. It saves repeated parsing work and, crucially, prevents SQL injection because parameters are sent separately from the query text. Most database drivers offer prepared statements with placeholders like ? or $1.

SQL injection is an attack where user input is concatenated into a query, letting an attacker change its meaning, like passing ' OR '1'='1 to bypass a login. The fix is parameterized queries (prepared statements), which send data separately from SQL so it can never be interpreted as code. Never build SQL by string-concatenating untrusted input.

A parameterized query uses placeholders for values and passes the actual data separately, so the database treats it strictly as data, not code. This is the single most important defense against SQL injection. It also enables plan reuse and avoids quoting bugs with strings containing apostrophes.

A connection pool keeps a set of open database connections ready to reuse, instead of opening a new one for every request, which is slow. The app borrows a connection, uses it, and returns it to the pool. Pools cap the total connections so the database is not overwhelmed; sizing the pool right is key to stability.

The N+1 problem is running one query to fetch a list, then one extra query per item to fetch related data, ending up with N+1 round-trips. For example loading 100 posts then fetching each post's author separately. The fix is to fetch related data in a single join or batched query (eager loading).

Eager loading fetches related records up front in as few queries as possible, the cure for the N+1 problem. ORMs offer it through methods like 'includes', 'with', or 'joinedload'. It trades a slightly bigger initial query for far fewer round-trips, usually a big win.

Lazy loading defers fetching related data until you actually access it, which saves work if you never use it but causes the N+1 problem if you do in a loop. ORMs often default to lazy loading. The trick is knowing when to switch to eager loading for collections you will iterate.

An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) lets you work with database rows as objects in your programming language, generating SQL for you. Examples include Hibernate, Django ORM, SQLAlchemy, Prisma, and ActiveRecord. ORMs boost productivity but can hide inefficient queries, so understanding the SQL they emit remains important.

Sharding splits a large table across multiple database servers, each holding a subset of rows chosen by a shard key (like user_id mod N). It scales writes and storage beyond one machine. The cost is complexity: cross-shard queries and transactions are hard, and picking a good shard key to avoid hot spots is critical.

Partitioning splits one logical table into smaller physical pieces by a key, such as by date range or hash, while still querying it as a single table. It speeds up queries that target one partition and makes dropping old data (a whole partition) instant. Unlike sharding, partitions usually live on the same server.

Range partitioning divides a table by value ranges of a key, commonly dates, so each month or year lives in its own partition. Queries filtered to one period read only the relevant partition (partition pruning), and you can drop an entire old month in one cheap operation. It suits time-series and log data.

Hash partitioning assigns rows to partitions by hashing a key, spreading data evenly to avoid hot spots. It is good when you want balanced partitions but have no natural range to split on. The downside is that range queries cannot prune partitions, since hashing scatters nearby values.

Partition pruning is the planner's ability to skip partitions that cannot contain matching rows. If a table is partitioned by month and you query WHERE date = '2025-03-15', the planner reads only the March partition. Pruning is the main performance payoff of partitioning, so write queries that filter on the partition key.

A read replica is a copy of a database that receives all changes from the primary and serves read-only queries, spreading read load across machines. Writes still go to the primary. Replicas often lag slightly behind, so they may return data a moment out of date (eventual consistency).

Replication lag is the delay between a write committing on the primary and that change appearing on a replica. Under heavy load, lag can grow to seconds, so a user might write data and then not see it when a later read hits a stale replica. Apps handle this by routing reads-after-writes to the primary.

In primary-replica (leader-follower) replication, one node accepts all writes and streams them to follower nodes that serve reads. It is the most common setup because there is only one writer, avoiding write conflicts. If the primary fails, a failover promotes a replica to become the new primary.

Synchronous replication makes the primary wait until at least one replica has confirmed receiving a write before reporting success, guaranteeing no committed data is lost if the primary crashes. The cost is higher write latency. Asynchronous replication is faster but risks losing the last few writes on failure.

The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a distributed datastore can guarantee at most one of Consistency (every read sees the latest write) or Availability (every request gets a response). When the network is healthy you can have both. The theorem forces designers to choose CP or AP behavior when partitions happen.

Eventual consistency means that if no new writes happen, all replicas will eventually agree, but for a short window different reads may return different values. Many distributed and NoSQL systems choose it to stay highly available. It works well for things like social feeds where a brief delay is acceptable.

Strong consistency (linearizability) guarantees that once a write completes, every later read sees it, as if there were a single up-to-date copy. It makes reasoning easy but is harder to scale and can hurt availability during network partitions. Single-node relational databases naturally provide it.

NoSQL refers to databases that depart from the strict relational table model, including document stores, key-value stores, wide-column stores, and graph databases. They often trade some consistency or query flexibility for scale, schema flexibility, or specific access patterns. 'NoSQL' really means 'not only SQL', not 'no SQL'.

A document database stores data as flexible, self-contained documents, usually JSON-like, instead of rows in fixed tables. MongoDB and Couchbase are examples. It suits data that varies in shape or nests naturally, and lets you fetch a whole object in one read, but it makes cross-document joins and consistency harder.

A key-value store maps unique keys to opaque values, offering extremely fast get and put by key but little query power beyond that. Redis and DynamoDB (in its simplest mode) are examples. They excel at caching, sessions, and simple lookups where you always know the exact key.

A wide-column store like Cassandra or HBase organizes data into rows that can each have a huge, varying number of columns grouped into families. It scales writes across many nodes and suits time-series and very large datasets. You design tables around the queries you will run, since flexible ad-hoc querying is limited.

A graph database stores data as nodes and edges (relationships) and excels at queries that traverse connections, like 'friends of friends' or shortest paths. Neo4j is a well-known example, queried with Cremlin or Cypher. It avoids the expensive multi-join chains that the same query would need in a relational database.

Columnar storage keeps each column's values together on disk rather than each row's values together. This is ideal for analytics, where queries scan a few columns over millions of rows, because you read only the needed columns and they compress extremely well. Row storage, by contrast, is better for transactional reads and writes of whole rows.

OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) is the workload of short, frequent read-write transactions that run an application, like placing an order or updating a profile. It favors row storage, normalized schemas, and quick indexed lookups. PostgreSQL and MySQL are classic OLTP databases.

OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) is the workload of large, complex read queries that scan and aggregate huge amounts of data for analytics and reporting. It favors columnar storage and denormalized or star-schema designs. Warehouses like Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse, and Redshift are built for OLAP.

A data warehouse is a database optimized for analytics: it aggregates data from many sources into a structure tuned for big read-only queries and reporting. It typically uses columnar storage and a star or snowflake schema. Examples include Snowflake, BigQuery, and Amazon Redshift.

A star schema is a data-warehouse design with one central fact table (measurements like sales amounts) surrounded by dimension tables (descriptive context like date, product, store). Its simple, mostly denormalized shape makes analytical queries fast and easy to write. A snowflake schema further normalizes the dimensions into sub-tables.

A fact table in a data warehouse holds the numeric measurements of business events, like quantity and revenue per sale, along with foreign keys to dimension tables. It is usually the largest table, with many rows but few columns. Queries aggregate its measures grouped by dimension attributes.

A dimension table stores descriptive attributes you slice and filter analytics by, such as a product's name and category or a date's month and quarter. Dimensions are wide but have relatively few rows. They connect to the fact table and provide the human-readable labels for reports.

ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load: pulling data from source systems, cleaning and reshaping it, then loading it into a warehouse. The modern variant ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse, leaning on cheap cloud compute. Pipelines often run on schedules or in response to new data.

ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into a powerful warehouse first, then transforms it there using SQL, reversing the order of traditional ETL. It became popular because cloud warehouses like Snowflake and BigQuery make in-database transformation cheap and scalable. Tools like dbt manage these in-warehouse transformations.
