A write-ahead log (WAL) records every change before it is applied to the data files, so the database can recover committed work after a crash by replaying the log. It is the mechanism behind durability in ACID. The log also feeds replication, since replicas can apply the same change stream.

Write-Ahead Logging is the rule that changes are written to a sequential log on disk before they touch the actual table pages. Sequential log writes are fast, and the log lets the database recover after a crash and stream changes to replicas. PostgreSQL's WAL and the equivalent redo logs in other databases are central to reliability.

A checkpoint is the point at which the database flushes accumulated in-memory changes (dirty pages) to the data files and records that the log up to here is safely applied. Checkpoints bound how much of the log must be replayed after a crash. Frequent checkpoints shorten recovery but add I/O; the database balances this automatically.

In PostgreSQL, VACUUM reclaims space from dead row versions left behind by MVCC after updates and deletes, and updates visibility information. Without it, tables bloat and slow down. Autovacuum runs it automatically, but heavy-write tables sometimes need tuning so it keeps up with the dead-tuple churn.

Table bloat is wasted space from dead row versions and partially filled pages, common in MVCC databases after many updates and deletes. Bloat makes scans read more pages than necessary, slowing queries. Routine vacuuming controls it; severe bloat may need VACUUM FULL or pg_repack to physically compact the table.

Index bloat is the index equivalent of table bloat: dead entries and fragmentation that make an index larger and slower than needed. Frequent updates to indexed columns are a common cause. Rebuilding the index (REINDEX) or using REINDEX CONCURRENTLY restores it to a compact form.

A query cache stores the results of queries so identical repeat queries can be answered without re-running them. MySQL once had a built-in query cache but removed it because invalidating it on every write hurt more than it helped at scale. Today caching usually happens in the application layer or a separate cache like Redis.

The buffer pool (or shared buffers) is the database's in-memory cache of recently used data pages, so hot data is served from RAM instead of disk. A high buffer-cache hit ratio is crucial for performance, since disk is far slower than memory. Sizing the buffer pool appropriately for the working set is a key tuning step.

A page (or block) is the fixed-size unit, often 8KB or 16KB, in which a database reads and writes data on disk and caches in memory. Rows are packed into pages, and indexes point to pages. The database always moves whole pages, so storing related data on the same page reduces I/O.

A heap is a table whose rows are stored in no particular order, just wherever there is free space. PostgreSQL stores all tables as heaps and relies on indexes for ordered access. In SQL Server, a table without a clustered index is a heap, and lookups must scan or go through nonclustered indexes.

Fill factor sets how full a database leaves each index or table page when building it, reserving free space for future updates. A lower fill factor leaves room so updates can fit in place, reducing page splits and fragmentation on write-heavy tables. The default near-100% suits read-mostly or append-only data.

A page split happens when an index page is full and a new key must be inserted, so the database splits the page into two and moves half the entries. Splits cause extra writes and fragmentation, hurting performance on write-heavy indexes. Inserting keys in ascending order (or leaving free space via fill factor) reduces splits.

Index fragmentation is when an index's pages become physically out of order or partly empty, often from page splits, so scanning it requires more scattered I/O. Heavily fragmented indexes slow range scans. Rebuilding or reorganizing the index restores a compact, ordered layout.

A statement (query) timeout aborts a query that runs longer than a set limit, protecting the database from a runaway query holding resources. PostgreSQL's statement_timeout and similar settings elsewhere enforce it. Setting sensible timeouts prevents one bad query from monopolizing connections.

LIMIT/OFFSET pagination fetches a page of results by skipping OFFSET rows and returning LIMIT rows, like LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 for page 3. It is simple but slow for deep pages, because the database still scans and discards all the skipped rows. Large offsets get progressively more expensive.

Keyset (cursor) pagination fetches the next page using a WHERE filter on the last seen value, like WHERE id > 1000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20, instead of OFFSET. Because it seeks straight to the right spot using an index, it stays fast even on the millionth page. The trade-off is you cannot jump to an arbitrary page number.

An index hint tells the database to use (or avoid) a specific index, overriding the planner's choice. It is a last resort for when the planner picks a bad plan despite good statistics. Hints are fragile because they assume data and the planner never change, so prefer fixing statistics or rewriting the query first.

A plan cache stores compiled execution plans so repeated queries skip the planning step. It helps performance but can cause 'parameter sniffing' problems, where a plan optimized for one parameter value is reused poorly for very different values. Databases offer ways to recompile or to detect skewed parameter distributions.

Parameter sniffing is when the database builds a cached plan based on the first parameter values it sees, then reuses that plan for later, very different values where it performs badly. For example a plan tuned for a rare value being reused for a common one. Fixes include recompiling per execution or using optimizer hints.

Cardinality estimation is the planner's guess of how many rows each step of a query will produce, driving its choice of join order and algorithms. It relies on table statistics like histograms and distinct counts. Bad estimates, often from correlated columns or stale stats, are the most common cause of bad plans.

Columns are correlated when their values move together, like city and zip_code. Planners assume columns are independent by default, so they badly underestimate rows when you filter on correlated columns together. PostgreSQL's extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS) let you teach the planner about such correlations.

An index-only scan answers a query entirely from the index without visiting the table, because the index contains every column the query needs. It is dramatically faster since it touches fewer pages. In PostgreSQL it also requires the rows' visibility info to be current, which good vacuuming maintains.

A bitmap scan, used by PostgreSQL, builds a bitmap of which pages contain matching rows from one or more indexes, then visits those pages in physical order. It is efficient when a query matches a medium number of scattered rows and can combine multiple indexes with AND/OR. It sits between a plain index scan and a full scan.

A covering query is one where every column it touches is present in an index, letting the database serve it without reading the table. You design covering indexes by adding the columns a hot query selects and filters on. The payoff is fewer page reads and faster results, at the cost of a larger index.

A LIKE pattern with a leading wildcard, like '%cat', cannot use a normal B-tree index because the index is sorted by the start of the string. So the query falls back to scanning. Trailing-wildcard patterns ('cat%') can use the index; for general substring search you need full-text search or a trigram index.

Full-text search indexes the words inside text so you can search by terms, with ranking, stemming, and stop-word handling, rather than exact string matching. PostgreSQL has tsvector/tsquery with GIN indexes; dedicated engines include Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. It powers search boxes far better than LIKE patterns.

A GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) in PostgreSQL maps each contained element to the rows that hold it, making it ideal for searching inside composite values like full-text documents, JSONB keys, and array elements. It answers 'which rows contain this term' fast. GIN indexes are slower to update than B-trees, which suits read-heavy search data.

A GiST (Generalized Search Tree) index in PostgreSQL is a flexible framework for indexing complex data like geometric shapes, ranges, and nearest-neighbor searches. It powers geospatial queries via PostGIS and overlap checks on range types. Unlike B-trees, GiST supports 'is near' and 'overlaps' style operators.

A BRIN (Block Range Index) stores only the min and max value per block range rather than per row, making it tiny and cheap to maintain. It works beautifully for huge tables where data is naturally ordered, like time-series appended by timestamp, letting the planner skip block ranges that cannot match. It is far smaller than a B-tree but only helps when data is physically clustered by the column.

A trigram index (PostgreSQL's pg_trgm extension) breaks text into overlapping three-character chunks, enabling fast fuzzy and substring searches, including LIKE '%middle%' and similarity matching. It powers typo-tolerant search and autocomplete. You back it with a GIN or GiST index on the trigram representation.

JSONB is PostgreSQL's binary JSON type that stores parsed JSON for fast access and supports indexing of keys and values via GIN. It lets you keep flexible, schema-less data inside a relational table and query into it with operators like ->> and @>. JSON (text) preserves exact formatting but is slower to query than JSONB.

Some databases, notably PostgreSQL, let a column hold an array of values, like integer[] or text[]. You can query with operators such as ANY, @> (contains), and unnest() to expand an array into rows. Arrays can model simple lists without a separate table, though heavy relational use usually still warrants a join table.

An enum type restricts a column to a fixed set of named values, like mood AS ENUM ('happy','sad','ok'). It documents allowed values and stores them compactly. The downside is that adding or reordering values can require schema changes, so a lookup table is sometimes more flexible.

A generated (computed) column derives its value from other columns by a formula, like full_name from first and last name, or area from width times height. Stored generated columns persist the value on disk; virtual ones compute on read. They keep derived data consistent and let you index the computed result.

Isolation (the I in ACID) is about how concurrent transactions affect each other, while consistency (the C) is about each transaction leaving the database satisfying all rules and constraints. They are related but distinct: weak isolation can still keep individual transactions internally consistent. Choosing an isolation level trades concurrency against the anomalies you tolerate.

Write skew is a concurrency anomaly allowed by snapshot isolation: two transactions read overlapping data, make decisions based on it, and write disjoint rows that together violate an invariant. A classic case is two on-call doctors each checking 'someone else is on duty' and both going off duty. True serializable isolation prevents it.

Two-phase commit (2PC) coordinates a transaction across multiple databases: a coordinator first asks all participants to PREPARE (promise they can commit), then, if all agree, tells them to COMMIT. It guarantees all-or-nothing across systems but blocks if the coordinator fails mid-protocol. Many modern systems avoid it in favor of sagas for this reason.

The saga pattern breaks a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. Instead of locking across services, you roll forward and, on failure, run compensations in reverse. It trades strict atomicity for availability, common in microservices.

An operation is idempotent if running it multiple times has the same effect as running it once. This matters for databases and APIs because retries after a timeout might apply the same write twice. Designing inserts with unique idempotency keys (so a duplicate is ignored) makes retries safe.

A soft delete marks a row as deleted (often a deleted_at timestamp or is_deleted flag) instead of physically removing it, so the data can be recovered or audited. The catch is every query must filter out soft-deleted rows, and unique constraints get tricky. Hard deletes physically remove the row.

An audit table records who changed what and when, often populated by triggers on insert/update/delete of the main table. It supports compliance, debugging, and undo features. Designs range from a generic history table to per-table shadow tables; temporal tables automate this in some databases.

A system-versioned (temporal) table automatically keeps the history of every row, recording when each version was valid. You can query the table 'as of' a past time to see how data looked then. SQL Server and the SQL standard support it natively, removing the need to hand-roll audit triggers for time-travel queries.

Foreign key columns are usually worth indexing because joins and lookups by them are common, and because deleting a parent row scans children to enforce the constraint. Many databases index the referenced (parent) key automatically but not the referencing (child) column. An un-indexed FK can make parent deletes do slow full scans of the child table.

ON DELETE CASCADE makes deleting a parent row automatically delete its child rows that reference it, keeping referential integrity without manual cleanup. It is convenient but dangerous: one delete can wipe out huge related trees. ON DELETE SET NULL or RESTRICT are safer alternatives when cascading is too aggressive.

Referential actions define what happens to child rows when a referenced parent key is deleted or updated: CASCADE propagates the change, SET NULL clears the foreign key, SET DEFAULT resets it, RESTRICT or NO ACTION block the change if children exist. They let the database maintain integrity automatically. Choose based on whether children make sense without a parent.

A scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column, so it can be used wherever a single value is expected, such as in a SELECT list or comparison. For example SELECT name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id = c.id) FROM customers c. If it accidentally returns multiple rows, the database raises an error.

EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns any rows at all, stopping as soon as it finds one, which makes it efficient for 'is there a related record' checks. WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE orders.cust_id = c.id) finds customers with at least one order. NOT EXISTS is the standard way to find rows with no match.

IN checks if a value appears in a list or subquery result, while EXISTS checks if a correlated subquery returns any rows. Modern optimizers often produce identical plans for the two, but EXISTS can be safer with NULLs: NOT IN behaves surprisingly when the subquery contains a NULL, sometimes returning no rows. When in doubt, NOT EXISTS is more predictable.

A CASE expression returns different values based on conditions, the SQL equivalent of if/else inside a query. You write CASE WHEN status='A' THEN 'Active' ELSE 'Inactive' END. It is useful in SELECT lists, ORDER BY, and even inside aggregates to do conditional counting like SUM(CASE WHEN paid THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

Pivoting turns row values into columns, like transforming monthly sales rows into one row with a column per month. Some databases have a PIVOT operator; otherwise you use conditional aggregation with CASE inside SUM or COUNT. Unpivot does the reverse, turning columns back into rows.

ROLLUP extends GROUP BY to produce subtotals and a grand total alongside the detailed groups. GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, product) gives totals per product, per region, and overall in one query. CUBE goes further, producing every combination of subtotals, useful for cross-tab reports.

The FILTER clause restricts which rows an aggregate considers, like COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='paid'). It is a cleaner standard-SQL alternative to the SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END) trick. It lets one query compute several conditional counts side by side.

A LATERAL join lets a subquery in the FROM clause reference columns from earlier tables in the same FROM, effectively running it per row of the left side. It is perfect for 'top N per group' queries, like getting each customer's three most recent orders. CROSS APPLY in SQL Server is the equivalent.

Finding the top N rows within each group (like the highest-paid employee per department) is a classic SQL puzzle. Clean solutions use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY value DESC) and filter rn <= N, or a LATERAL join. Naive correlated subqueries work but are usually slower.

ORDER BY can be costly because the database may have to sort the whole result, spilling to disk if it exceeds the sort memory limit. If an index already provides the requested order, the planner can skip the sort entirely. So an index matching your ORDER BY (and any leading WHERE columns) speeds up sorted queries.

An index whose column order matches a query's WHERE filter followed by its ORDER BY can let the database return sorted results without a separate sort step. For example an index on (user_id, created_at) serves WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at directly. This is one of the highest-impact indexing techniques for paginated, sorted lists.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) in PostgreSQL runs the query and reports both real timings and how many pages came from cache versus disk. The BUFFERS data reveals whether slowness is from disk I/O or pure computation. Comparing the planner's estimated rows to the actual rows pinpoints where statistics are misleading it.

keywords: seq scan vs index scan choice
facts.answer: The planner picks a sequential scan over an index when it estimates the query will return a large fraction of the table, because reading sequentially is cheaper than many scattered index lookups. If it wrongly thinks a query is non-selective (bad statistics), it may choose a slow scan. Updating statistics often flips it to the right choice.

Query rewriting is transforming a query into a logically equivalent one that runs faster, done both by the optimizer and by developers. Examples include turning correlated subqueries into joins, pushing filters down before joins, and replacing OR conditions with UNION. The optimizer does much of this automatically, but understanding it helps you write planner-friendly SQL.

Predicate pushdown is moving filter conditions as early as possible in query execution, so fewer rows flow through later joins and aggregations. The optimizer does this automatically, applying WHERE filters at the data source or before joins. In federated and columnar systems, pushing predicates down to the storage layer dramatically cuts I/O.

A sargable (Search ARGument ABLE) predicate is one the database can satisfy using an index, typically because the indexed column appears alone on one side of a comparison. WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01' is sargable; WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025 is not, because wrapping the column in a function hides it from the index. Rewriting to avoid functions on indexed columns restores index use.

Applying a function to an indexed column in a WHERE clause, like WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com', usually prevents the index from being used because the index stores the raw values. Fixes include a functional index (an index on LOWER(email)) or storing a normalized column. This is one of the most common hidden performance bugs.

A functional (expression) index indexes the result of an expression rather than a raw column, such as an index on LOWER(email) or on a JSON field. It makes otherwise non-sargable queries fast by precomputing the expression for every row. The query must use the exact same expression to benefit from it.

Implicit type conversion happens when you compare columns of different types, like an integer column to a string literal, and the database silently casts one side. This can prevent index use if the column itself gets converted, quietly turning a fast query into a full scan. Matching parameter types to column types avoids the trap.

Updating or deleting millions of rows in one statement can lock heavily, bloat the transaction log, and run for a long time. Processing in batches (for instance, 10,000 rows per transaction in a loop) keeps locks short, lets the log and vacuum keep up, and allows progress to be observed. It trades a single big operation for many small, safer ones.

Opening a fresh database connection for every request is slow because connection setup involves TCP, authentication, and session initialization. Under load it can exhaust the database's connection limit. The fix is a connection pool that reuses a bounded set of warm connections.

Every database has a cap on simultaneous connections because each one consumes memory and a process or thread. Exceeding it rejects new connections, taking down the app. A connection pooler like PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections onto a few database connections, letting thousands of clients share a small backend pool.

PgBouncer is a lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL that sits between applications and the database, reusing a small set of server connections for many clients. Its transaction pooling mode hands a server connection to a client only for the duration of a transaction, greatly increasing how many clients one database can serve. It is essential for serverless and high-concurrency apps.

Plan stability is keeping a query's execution plan predictable so performance does not suddenly regress when statistics or data shift. Sudden plan flips can turn a fast query slow overnight. Techniques include keeping statistics fresh, sometimes pinning plans, and writing queries the optimizer handles consistently.

READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server. Each statement sees only data committed before that statement began, so it never reads dirty data, but two statements in the same transaction can see different snapshots. It allows non-repeatable reads and phantoms in exchange for high concurrency.

REPEATABLE READ guarantees that rows you read once will return the same values for the whole transaction, preventing non-repeatable reads. In PostgreSQL it is implemented as snapshot isolation, freezing your view at transaction start. The standard still allows phantoms at this level, though PostgreSQL's implementation prevents many of them.

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads rows and locks them so other transactions cannot modify them until you commit, implementing pessimistic locking. It is used to read-then-write safely, like reserving inventory. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets a worker grab the next unlocked row, a neat trick for queue tables.

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED makes a query lock and return rows, silently skipping any that are already locked by another transaction. This turns a regular table into a concurrent job queue: many workers each grab different un-locked jobs without blocking each other. It is a simple, reliable alternative to dedicated queue systems for moderate scale.

An advisory lock is a named lock the application chooses to take, not tied to any row, used to coordinate work like ensuring only one server runs a scheduled job. PostgreSQL offers session and transaction-scoped advisory locks via pg_advisory_lock. The database does not enforce what the lock 'means'; the app honors it by convention.

COUNT(*) on a large table can be slow in MVCC databases like PostgreSQL because it must check each row's visibility, so it scans the table or a covering index. For exact counts of huge tables, that is expensive; an estimated count from table statistics (pg_class.reltuples) is near-instant when an approximation suffices. Keeping a maintained counter is another option.

When an exact count is too slow on a giant table, an approximate count is often good enough. PostgreSQL exposes a fast estimate via the planner statistics in pg_class.reltuples, refreshed by ANALYZE. Analytics systems use probabilistic structures like HyperLogLog to estimate distinct counts using tiny memory.

HyperLogLog is a probabilistic algorithm that estimates the number of distinct values in a huge dataset using only kilobytes of memory, by analyzing patterns in hashed values. It trades a small error (a few percent) for enormous memory savings versus storing every value. Databases like Redis and analytics engines use it for fast distinct counts.

A materialized view must be refreshed to reflect new data because it stores a snapshot. A plain REFRESH locks the view while rebuilding; REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY in PostgreSQL rebuilds without blocking reads but requires a unique index. Choosing refresh frequency balances data freshness against the cost of recomputation.

A database migration is a versioned, repeatable change to the schema, like adding a column or table, tracked in code alongside the application. Tools like Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, and built-in framework migrators apply them in order and record which have run. Migrations make schema changes reviewable and deployable like any other code.

An online schema change alters a table without locking out reads and writes, essential for large tables in production. Techniques include adding nullable columns (cheap), backfilling in batches, and tools like pg-online-schema-change or gh-ost that build a shadow table and swap it in. Naively running ALTER TABLE on a huge table can lock it for a long, painful time.

Historically, adding a column with a default value rewrote the whole table to set the default on every row, locking it. Modern PostgreSQL (11+) stores the default as metadata so adding a column with a constant default is instant. Volatile defaults or backfilling existing rows with computed values still require careful batched updates.

In most SQL databases a UNIQUE constraint treats NULLs as distinct, so a column can hold many NULL values even though it must be unique otherwise. This follows from NULL meaning 'unknown', so two unknowns are not considered equal. PostgreSQL 15+ adds NULLS NOT DISTINCT to change this when you need only one NULL allowed.

A deferrable constraint can have its checking postponed until the end of a transaction (COMMIT) rather than after each statement. This lets you temporarily violate it mid-transaction, for example swapping two rows' unique values, as long as it holds by commit time. You declare it DEFERRABLE and switch behavior with SET CONSTRAINTS.

An exclusion constraint (PostgreSQL) generalizes uniqueness: it forbids two rows whose values overlap by some operator, not just equal. The classic use is preventing overlapping bookings, with EXCLUDE USING gist on a time range and '&&' (overlaps). It is enforced with a GiST index and catches conflicts no simple UNIQUE could.

PostgreSQL range types like int4range and tstzrange store a value range (lower and upper bound with inclusivity) in one column. Operators test containment, overlap, and adjacency, and you can index them with GiST. They model things like valid time periods or numeric bands cleanly, instead of two separate start/end columns.

The primary SQL injection defense is parameterized queries, but layered defenses add safety: validating and allow-listing input formats, using least-privilege database accounts, escaping output, and running web application firewalls. Stored procedures help only if they too use parameters internally. No single layer is sufficient if dynamic SQL builds queries from raw input.

Running an application with a database account that has only the permissions it needs limits the damage if it is compromised or injected. A web app rarely needs DROP TABLE or superuser rights. Separate accounts for migrations (more powerful) and runtime (read/write only on needed tables) is a common, safer pattern.

Row-Level Security (RLS) lets the database restrict which rows a user can see or change based on policies, enforced no matter how the query is written. In PostgreSQL you enable RLS on a table and define policies referencing the current user or session variables. It centralizes multi-tenant isolation in the database instead of trusting every query to filter correctly.

Column-level encryption protects specific sensitive fields, like SSNs or tokens, by encrypting them before storage so even a database dump leaks nothing readable. The application or a database feature handles the keys, ideally in a separate key-management service. It is finer-grained than encrypting the whole disk and protects against more threats, at the cost of not being searchable in plaintext.

Encryption at rest scrambles the database's files on disk so a stolen drive or backup is useless without the key. It is often handled transparently at the storage or filesystem level (Transparent Data Encryption). It protects against physical theft but not against an attacker who already has valid database access, which is why it is combined with access control and encryption in transit.

Encryption in transit uses TLS to protect data moving between the application and the database from eavesdropping on the network. Most databases support requiring SSL/TLS connections and verifying certificates. It complements encryption at rest, since data is vulnerable both while stored and while traveling over the wire.

A full backup copies the entire database; an incremental backup copies only what changed since the last backup, saving time and space. Restoring from incrementals requires the last full backup plus all the increments since. A good strategy balances backup speed against restore complexity, often a periodic full plus frequent incrementals.

Point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores a database to any exact moment, like just before an accidental DELETE, by replaying the write-ahead log on top of a base backup up to the chosen timestamp. It needs continuous archiving of the WAL. PITR limits data loss to seconds and lets you recover from human mistakes, not just crashes.

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much recent data you can afford to lose, measured in time, while RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how quickly you must be back online. A 5-minute RPO means backups or replication must capture changes at least that often. These targets drive your backup frequency, replication strategy, and failover design.

A hot standby is a replica that can serve read queries while it continuously applies changes from the primary, unlike a cold standby that only stands ready. It both offloads reads and provides a target for fast failover. PostgreSQL's hot standby lets you run analytics on the replica without touching the primary.

Failover is switching to a standby when the primary database fails, promoting the standby to become the new primary. It can be manual or automatic via tools like Patroni or managed-cloud orchestration. The key concerns are not promoting two primaries at once (split-brain) and minimizing data loss based on whether replication was synchronous.

Split-brain is a failure where a network partition causes two nodes to each believe they are the primary and accept writes, leading to divergent, conflicting data. It is a serious risk in automatic failover. Quorum-based coordination and fencing (forcibly stopping the old primary) prevent it by ensuring only one node can be primary at a time.

A quorum is the minimum number of nodes that must agree for a distributed operation to proceed, usually a majority. Requiring a majority for both reads and writes guarantees they overlap, so a read always sees the latest committed write. Quorum-based systems like Raft keep a cluster consistent even when a minority of nodes fail.

Raft is a consensus algorithm that keeps a cluster of nodes agreeing on a replicated log, even as nodes fail. One node is elected leader and orders all writes; followers replicate its log, and a majority must acknowledge each entry. Raft underpins systems like etcd, CockroachDB, and many distributed databases needing strong consistency.

Distributed SQL (NewSQL) databases like CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, and Google Spanner offer the familiar SQL interface and ACID transactions while automatically sharding and replicating across many nodes for horizontal scale. They use consensus protocols like Raft or Paxos to stay consistent. They aim to give relational guarantees at NoSQL scale, trading some latency for that combination.

A vector database stores high-dimensional embedding vectors and finds the nearest ones to a query vector, powering semantic search and AI retrieval. It uses approximate nearest-neighbor indexes like HNSW to search billions of vectors quickly. PostgreSQL's pgvector extension adds this to a relational database; dedicated options include Pinecone, Milvus, and Qdrant.

pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector column type and similarity operators, letting you do AI embedding search inside your existing relational database. It supports exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search with HNSW and IVFFlat indexes. Keeping vectors alongside relational data avoids syncing to a separate vector store for many applications.

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a graph-based index for approximate nearest-neighbor search over vectors, giving fast, high-recall similarity queries. It builds layered proximity graphs you traverse from coarse to fine. It is the default high-quality index for vector databases and pgvector, trading a bit of accuracy and memory for speed.

A time-series database is optimized for timestamped data like metrics, sensor readings, and logs, where you mostly append and query by time ranges. Examples include TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, and Prometheus. They use time-based partitioning, heavy compression, and downsampling (rolling up old fine-grained data) to handle huge write volumes efficiently.

On Linux filesystems, every file is tracked by an inode, a small record holding metadata like size, permissions, owner, and pointers to the data blocks. The filename itself lives in a directory, which just maps names to inode numbers. That's why you can have several names (hard links) for the same file: they all point to one inode. Run 'ls -i' to see a file's inode number.

A hard link is a second directory entry pointing at the same inode as an existing file. Created with 'ln target linkname', both names are equally 'real' — deleting one doesn't remove the data until the last link is gone. Hard links can't cross filesystems or point to directories. The inode keeps a link count, visible in 'ls -l' as the number right after the permissions.

A symbolic link (symlink) is a tiny file whose contents are just a path to another file, created with 'ln -s target linkname'. Unlike hard links, symlinks can cross filesystems and point to directories. If the target is deleted, the symlink becomes 'dangling' and breaks. 'ls -l' shows symlinks with an arrow, like 'link -> /real/path'.

A file descriptor is a small non-negative integer the kernel gives a process to refer to an open file, socket, or pipe. By convention 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output, and 2 is standard error. Each process has its own table of descriptors. You can inspect a running process's open descriptors under /proc/PID/fd on Linux.

Every Unix program starts with three standard streams: stdin (descriptor 0) for input, stdout (1) for normal output, and stderr (2) for error messages. Keeping errors on a separate stream means you can pipe a program's real output while still seeing warnings. Redirect them separately, like 'cmd > out.txt 2> err.txt'.

A pipe connects one program's standard output to the next program's standard input using the '|' symbol, like 'ls | sort'. The shell runs both programs at once and the kernel streams data between them in memory, no temp file needed. Pipes are a core Unix idea: small tools chained together do big jobs. Data flows left to right through the pipeline.

Redirection sends a program's streams to or from files instead of the terminal. '>' overwrites a file with stdout, '>>' appends to it, and '<' feeds a file in as stdin. To capture errors use '2>' for stderr, and '&>' (or '> file 2>&1') to grab both streams together. These are handled by the shell before the program even runs.

The notation '2>&1' tells the shell to send stderr (descriptor 2) to wherever stdout (descriptor 1) currently points. Order matters: 'cmd > file 2>&1' first points stdout at the file, then routes stderr to that same file. Writing '2>&1 > file' instead would send errors to the old terminal and only stdout to the file. It's a classic gotcha.

A heredoc lets you feed a block of inline text to a command as its standard input, using '<<WORD' until a line containing just WORD. For example 'cat <<EOF ... EOF' prints everything between the markers. Quoting the marker like <<'EOF' stops the shell from expanding variables inside. Use <<- to strip leading tabs for indentation.

A process ID (PID) is a unique number the Linux kernel assigns to each running process. PID 1 is the init system (usually systemd), the ancestor of all other processes. PIDs are reused over time once a process exits and is reaped. A shell can see its own PID in the '$$' variable.

fork() is the system call that creates a new process by duplicating the calling one. The child gets a copy of the parent's memory and an almost identical state, differing mainly in its PID and fork()'s return value (0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent). Modern kernels use copy-on-write so the memory isn't actually copied until one side writes to it. fork is usually followed by exec to run a new program.

The exec family of system calls replaces the current process's program image with a new one, keeping the same PID. After a successful exec, the old code is gone and the new program starts at its entry point. Shells combine fork and exec: fork to make a child, then exec to run the command in it. In a script, 'exec command' replaces the shell itself with that command.

A zombie (or defunct) process is one that has finished running but whose parent hasn't yet read its exit status with wait(). It holds almost no resources — just an entry in the process table to report how it died. Zombies show up as 'Z' or '<defunct>' in ps. They clear once the parent reaps them; if the parent dies first, init adopts and reaps them.

An orphan is a process whose parent exited before it did. The kernel re-parents orphans to PID 1 (init/systemd), which then waits on them when they finish so they don't become permanent zombies. Daemons are sometimes created deliberately as orphans so they detach from the launching terminal. This 'double fork' trick hands the daemon off to init.

Signals are short asynchronous messages the kernel or a process sends to another process to notify it of events or ask it to act. Common ones include SIGINT (Ctrl+C, interrupt), SIGTERM (polite terminate request), and SIGKILL (force kill, can't be caught). A program can install handlers for most signals to clean up, but SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can never be ignored.

Despite its name, 'kill' just sends a signal to a process by PID; the default signal SIGTERM asks it to shut down nicely. 'kill -9 PID' sends SIGKILL, which the kernel enforces immediately and the process can't block. Use 'kill -l' to list signal names and numbers. 'pkill' and 'killall' target processes by name instead of PID.

SIGTERM (signal 15) politely asks a process to terminate, giving it a chance to flush files, close connections, and clean up. SIGKILL (signal 9) is the kernel forcibly ending the process with no warning and no cleanup. Always try SIGTERM first; reach for SIGKILL only when a process is truly stuck. systemd sends SIGTERM, waits, then escalates to SIGKILL.

SIGHUP originally meant a terminal's modem had hung up, so processes attached to that terminal got the signal. Today it's commonly repurposed: many daemons treat SIGHUP as 'reload your config without restarting'. When you log out, processes in your session may receive SIGHUP, which is why 'nohup' exists to shield long jobs from it.

'nohup command &' runs a command immune to SIGHUP, so it keeps going after you log out or close the terminal. Its output is redirected to a file called nohup.out by default unless you redirect it yourself. nohup is a simple way to detach a long task, though tools like tmux, screen, or systemd services give more control.

Appending '&' to a command runs it in the background, returning your shell prompt immediately while the job continues. The shell prints a job number and PID. Background jobs still share the terminal for output unless redirected. List them with 'jobs', bring one forward with 'fg %1', or push a stopped one back with 'bg %1'.

Job control lets a shell manage multiple programs in one terminal. Press Ctrl+Z to suspend the foreground job (sending SIGTSTP), then 'bg' resumes it in the background or 'fg' brings it back to the foreground. 'jobs' lists them with %-prefixed numbers. This is handy when you need a prompt without killing what you started.

'ps' reports a snapshot of running processes. 'ps aux' (BSD style) shows every process with user, CPU, memory, and command; 'ps -ef' is the equivalent System V style. Unlike 'top', ps is a one-shot view, perfect for grepping. Combine it like 'ps aux | grep nginx' to find a specific program.

'top' shows a live, continuously updating view of processes sorted by CPU usage, along with load average, memory, and per-process stats. Inside it you can press 'M' to sort by memory, 'k' to kill a PID, or 'q' to quit. It's the quickest way to see what's hogging a machine right now. The header also summarizes total CPU and memory use.

htop is a friendlier, colorful alternative to top with per-core CPU bars, a scrollable process list, and mouse support. You can tag processes, kill them by selecting from a menu, and view a tree of parent/child relationships with F5. It isn't installed by default on most systems, so you usually add it via the package manager. Many admins prefer it for everyday monitoring.

Load average is the average number of processes that are running or waiting to run over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes, shown by 'uptime' or 'top'. On a machine with N CPU cores, a load near N means it's fully busy; well above N means tasks are queuing up. On Linux it also counts processes in uninterruptible I/O wait, so high load can mean disk pressure, not just CPU.

A process's 'nice' value nudges the scheduler on how much CPU to give it, ranging from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). Higher nice means 'nicer' to others, so it yields CPU. Start a command at lower priority with 'nice -n 10 cmd', and change a running one with 'renice'. Only root can set negative (more aggressive) nice values.

Environment variables are named values the shell passes to programs it launches, like PATH, HOME, and LANG. Set one for a single command with 'VAR=value cmd', or export it with 'export VAR=value' so child processes inherit it. View them all with 'env' or 'printenv'. Each process gets its own copy, so changing one in a child doesn't affect the parent.

PATH is a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches, in order, to find the program you typed. If a command 'isn't found', it usually just isn't in any PATH directory. Check it with 'echo $PATH' and locate a command with 'which' or 'type'. Putting '.' (the current directory) in PATH is discouraged for security reasons.

In a shell, a plain assignment like 'X=5' creates a variable only the current shell sees. 'export X' (or 'export X=5') marks it for export so any program the shell launches inherits it as an environment variable. Without export, child processes never see the value. 'export -p' lists everything currently exported.

'which name' tells you which file the shell would run for a command by searching PATH, printing its full path. It only finds executables on PATH, not shell builtins or aliases. The shell builtin 'type name' is often more accurate because it also reports builtins, functions, and aliases. 'command -v name' is the portable POSIX way to do the same check.

An alias is a shell shortcut that expands to a longer command, like 'alias ll="ls -alF"'. Aliases only work in interactive shells and are usually defined in a file like ~/.bashrc so they load each session. Run 'alias' with no arguments to list them, and 'unalias name' to remove one. For anything needing arguments in the middle, a shell function is better.

A shell function bundles commands under a name you can call like a command, defined as 'name() { commands; }'. Inside, positional parameters $1, $2, and so on hold the arguments, and 'return' sets an exit status. Functions are more powerful than aliases because they take arguments and contain logic. They live in your shell config or scripts.

Every command returns an exit status: 0 means success, and any nonzero value (1-255) means some kind of failure. The shell stores the last command's status in the special variable '$?'. Scripts and 'if' statements use this to decide what to do next. By convention 0 is the only 'true' value, the opposite of most programming languages.

'chmod' changes a file's permission bits for owner, group, and others. You can use symbolic mode like 'chmod u+x script.sh' to add execute for the owner, or octal mode like 'chmod 755 file' where each digit packs read(4)+write(2)+execute(1). 755 means owner can read/write/execute and everyone else can read/execute. Only the owner or root can change a file's mode.

'chown' changes which user (and optionally group) owns a file, like 'chown alice:devs file'. Changing ownership generally requires root because it could be used to dodge disk quotas or hide files. Add '-R' to recurse through a directory tree. The related 'chgrp' changes only the group.

The umask is a mask that removes permission bits from newly created files and directories. With a umask of 022, new files default to 644 (rw-r--r--) and directories to 755, because the masked bits (write for group and others) are turned off. Set it with 'umask 027' in your shell config. It only subtracts permissions; it never adds them.

The setuid bit on an executable makes it run with the file owner's privileges instead of the user who launched it. The classic example is 'passwd', which is owned by root so any user can update the password file safely through it. It appears as an 's' in the owner's execute position in 'ls -l'. Misused setuid programs are a common security risk.

The setgid bit on a program makes it run with the file's group privileges. On a directory, setgid does something different: new files created inside inherit the directory's group, which is handy for shared team folders. It shows as 's' in the group execute slot of 'ls -l'. Set it with 'chmod g+s'.

The sticky bit on a directory restricts deletion so users can only remove their own files, even if the directory is world-writable. /tmp is the canonical example: everyone can write there, but you can't delete someone else's files. It shows as 't' in the 'others' execute slot of 'ls -l'. Set it with 'chmod +t dir'.

cron is the classic Unix job scheduler that runs commands at set times. The cron daemon reads 'crontab' files, where each line has five time fields (minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week) followed by the command. Edit your jobs with 'crontab -e' and list them with 'crontab -l'. An entry like '0 3 * * * backup.sh' runs every day at 3 AM.

A crontab line uses five fields before the command: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day of month (1-31), month (1-12), and day of week (0-7, where 0 and 7 are Sunday). An asterisk means 'every', '*/5' means 'every 5', and lists like '1,15' work too. So '*/15 * * * * cmd' runs every fifteen minutes. Special strings like @daily and @reboot are also accepted.

systemd timers are a modern alternative to cron for scheduling. A .timer unit defines when to run and triggers a matching .service unit that does the work. Timers support calendar expressions via OnCalendar, monotonic delays like OnBootSec, randomized delays, and missed-run catch-up with Persistent=true. List active ones with 'systemctl list-timers'.

systemd is the init system and service manager on most modern Linux distributions, running as PID 1. It starts and supervises services (called units), handles dependencies and parallel startup, manages logging via the journal, and controls timers, sockets, and mounts. You interact with it mainly through 'systemctl' and 'journalctl'. It replaced older SysV init scripts on most distros.

'systemctl' is the command to control systemd units. Common uses: 'systemctl start/stop/restart name' to control a service now, 'systemctl enable/disable name' to set whether it autostarts at boot, and 'systemctl status name' to see its state and recent logs. Add 'sudo' for system services. 'systemctl daemon-reload' tells systemd to re-read changed unit files.

A systemd service is described by a unit file (ending in .service) with sections like [Unit] for description and dependencies, [Service] for how to start the program (ExecStart) and restart policy, and [Install] for when to enable it. System units live in /etc/systemd/system or /usr/lib/systemd/system. After editing one, run 'systemctl daemon-reload'.

'journalctl' reads the systemd journal, a structured binary log of system and service messages. 'journalctl -u nginx' shows one service's logs, '-f' follows new entries live like 'tail -f', and '-b' limits output to the current boot. You can filter by time with '--since' and '--until'. By default the journal may be memory-only unless persistent storage is configured.

A daemon is a long-running background process that provides a service rather than interacting with a user directly, like a web server or the print spooler. Traditionally daemons detach from the terminal and run with PID 1 as parent. By convention many daemon names end in 'd', such as sshd, crond, and systemd. Modern systems supervise daemons with systemd rather than letting them self-detach.

'sudo' lets a permitted user run a single command as another user, usually root, after entering their own password. It logs each use and is far safer than logging in as root directly. Who can run what is configured in /etc/sudoers, edited with 'visudo' to catch syntax errors. 'sudo -i' or 'sudo su' starts a root shell when you need several commands.

root is the all-powerful administrative account on Linux, with user ID 0 and the ability to bypass file permission checks. Because root can do anything, including destroy the system, best practice is to log in as a normal user and elevate only when needed with sudo. Many distributions lock the root login entirely and rely on sudo. Be especially careful running recursive deletes as root.

Mounting attaches a filesystem (on a disk, partition, or image) to a directory in the existing tree, called the mount point. After 'mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data', the disk's contents appear under /mnt/data. Run 'mount' with no arguments or 'findmnt' to see what's mounted. Linux has a single unified tree rather than drive letters like Windows.

/etc/fstab lists filesystems to mount automatically at boot. Each line has the device (often by UUID), mount point, filesystem type, options, and two numeric flags for dump and fsck order. Using UUIDs instead of /dev names keeps mounts stable even if disk ordering changes. A typo here can stop a system from booting, so edit carefully.

'df' reports how much disk space each mounted filesystem uses and has free. 'df -h' shows human-readable sizes like 12G, and 'df -i' shows inode usage instead of bytes. It's the first tool to reach for when a system complains it's out of space. Remember a filesystem can run out of inodes even with bytes to spare.

'du' estimates the disk space used by files and directories, walking the tree. 'du -sh dir' gives a single human-readable total for a directory, while 'du -h --max-depth=1' breaks it down one level deep. It's the go-to for finding what's eating space, often piped into 'sort -h'. Unlike df, du measures actual files rather than filesystem-level totals.

'grep' searches input for lines matching a pattern and prints them, like 'grep error log.txt'. Useful flags: '-i' ignores case, '-r' recurses through directories, '-n' shows line numbers, '-v' inverts to show non-matching lines, and '-c' counts matches. With '-E' it uses extended regular expressions. The name comes from the old editor command g/re/p.

sed is a stream editor that transforms text line by line as it flows through. Its most common use is substitution: 'sed "s/old/new/g"' replaces every 'old' with 'new'. Add '-i' to edit a file in place. sed can also delete lines, print specific ranges, and apply changes only to lines matching a pattern. It shines in pipelines and scripts.

awk is a small programming language for processing columnar text. It splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) on whitespace by default and runs your program per line. 'awk "{print $1, $3}"' prints the first and third columns; 'awk -F,' changes the separator to comma for CSV. It supports patterns, math, and BEGIN/END blocks for totals.

'cut' pulls out parts of each line. 'cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd' uses ':' as the delimiter and prints the first field (usernames). '-c' selects by character position instead, like 'cut -c1-10'. It's simpler than awk for straightforward column slicing but only handles a single-character delimiter. It does not collapse repeated delimiters.

'sort' orders lines of text. By default it sorts alphabetically; '-n' sorts numerically, '-r' reverses, '-k2' sorts by the second field, and '-u' removes duplicates. '-h' understands human sizes like 2K and 1G. Sorting before 'uniq' is essential because uniq only collapses adjacent duplicate lines.

'uniq' filters adjacent duplicate lines, so it's almost always paired with 'sort' first. 'uniq -c' prefixes each line with how many times it occurred, great for counting. 'uniq -d' shows only the duplicated lines and '-u' only the unique ones. A common idiom is 'sort file | uniq -c | sort -rn' to rank lines by frequency.

'wc' counts things in its input: '-l' counts lines, '-w' words, '-c' bytes, and '-m' characters. With no flag it prints lines, words, and bytes together. It's frequently used to count results, like 'grep error log | wc -l' to count error lines. Counting lines of a pipe is one of the most common shell measurements.

'head' prints the beginning of a file or stream, ten lines by default. 'head -n 5 file' shows the first five lines, and 'head -c 100' shows the first 100 bytes. It pairs naturally with pipes to peek at the top of large output. The opposite tool, 'tail', shows the end.

'tail' prints the end of a file, ten lines by default; 'tail -n 20' shows the last twenty. Its standout feature is 'tail -f', which follows a file and prints new lines as they're appended — perfect for watching logs in real time. 'tail -F' also re-opens the file if it's rotated. Press Ctrl+C to stop following.

'find' walks a directory tree looking for files matching tests. 'find . -name "*.log"' finds log files, '-type d' restricts to directories, '-mtime -7' finds things changed in the last week, and '-size +100M' finds big files. The powerful '-exec cmd {} \;' runs a command on each match. It's the Swiss Army knife of filesystem searching.

'xargs' reads items from standard input and turns them into arguments for another command, which is useful when a tool doesn't read stdin directly. 'find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs rm' deletes the found files. Use 'find ... -print0 | xargs -0' to handle filenames with spaces safely. '-n' limits items per command and '-P' runs jobs in parallel.

tar bundles many files into a single archive, optionally compressed. 'tar -czf backup.tar.gz dir/' creates a gzip-compressed archive (c=create, z=gzip, f=file), and 'tar -xzf backup.tar.gz' extracts it (x=extract). Add 'v' for verbose listing and 't' to list contents without extracting. The name dates back to tape archives, though it's used for everything now.

gzip compresses a single file using the DEFLATE algorithm, replacing 'file' with 'file.gz' by default. 'gzip file' compresses and 'gunzip file.gz' or 'gzip -d' restores it. It's fast and ubiquitous but only handles one file, which is why it's usually combined with tar. Newer alternatives like zstd often compress faster with similar ratios.

SSH (Secure Shell) gives you an encrypted remote login and command channel to another machine, like 'ssh user@host'. All traffic is encrypted, replacing insecure tools like telnet. Beyond shells, SSH can copy files (scp/sftp), forward ports, and tunnel other protocols. Key-based authentication is more secure and convenient than passwords.

SSH key authentication uses a key pair: a private key you keep secret and a public key you place on servers in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Generate a pair with 'ssh-keygen', preferably an Ed25519 key, then copy the public half with 'ssh-copy-id user@host'. Logins then need no password and resist guessing attacks. Protect the private key with a passphrase.

'scp' copies files over SSH, using the same authentication. 'scp file user@host:/path' uploads, and 'scp user@host:/path/file .' downloads. Add '-r' to copy directories recursively. Many people now prefer rsync or sftp for large or repeated transfers, but scp is simple for one-off copies.

rsync efficiently synchronizes files between locations, copying only the differences it detects. 'rsync -av src/ dest/' archives recursively while preserving permissions and times; add '-z' to compress over the network and '--delete' to mirror exactly. Over SSH it's the standard for backups and deploys. The trailing slash on the source matters: it copies contents rather than the folder itself.

tmux is a terminal multiplexer that lets one terminal host multiple windows and panes, and keeps sessions alive after you disconnect. Start with 'tmux', detach with the prefix (default Ctrl+B) then 'd', and reattach later with 'tmux attach'. It's essential for long remote jobs because the session survives a dropped SSH connection. Panes split the screen for side-by-side work.

GNU screen is an older terminal multiplexer, the predecessor to tmux. It keeps sessions running after detach so remote work survives disconnects. The default prefix key is Ctrl+A; 'Ctrl+A d' detaches and 'screen -r' reattaches. Many admins have switched to tmux, but screen is still widely installed and useful.

bash (Bourne Again SHell) is the most common interactive shell and scripting language on Linux. It reads commands, expands variables and globs, runs pipelines, and supports loops, conditionals, and functions for scripting. Its config files include ~/.bashrc for interactive shells and ~/.bash_profile at login. Scripts usually start with the shebang '#!/bin/bash'.

zsh is a feature-rich shell, the default on macOS and popular on Linux. Compared to bash it adds smarter tab completion, spelling correction, powerful globbing, and themeable prompts, often extended with frameworks like Oh My Zsh. It's largely compatible with bash scripts but has its own extensions. Many developers use it interactively while keeping bash for scripts.

A shebang is the first line of a script starting with '#!', telling the kernel which interpreter to run, like '#!/bin/bash' or '#!/usr/bin/env python3'. When you execute the script directly, the kernel reads this line and launches the named program with the script as input. Using '/usr/bin/env' makes scripts more portable by finding the interpreter on PATH. The file also needs execute permission.

Globbing is the shell expanding wildcard patterns into matching filenames before running a command. '*' matches any characters, '?' matches a single character, and '[abc]' matches one listed character. So 'rm *.tmp' deletes all .tmp files. The shell, not the program, does this expansion, so a command never sees the '*' itself unless no file matches (or globbing is disabled).

Quotes control how the shell treats special characters. Single quotes preserve everything literally — no variable or wildcard expansion happens inside. Double quotes still expand variables ($VAR) and command substitution but protect spaces and most wildcards. So 'echo "$HOME"' prints your home path while 'echo '\''$HOME'\''' prints the literal text. Quoting variables prevents word-splitting bugs.

Command substitution runs a command and inserts its output into the surrounding command line, written as $(command) or the older backticks. For example 'echo "Today is $(date)"' embeds the date. The modern $() form nests cleanly and is easier to read than backticks. The output's trailing newline is stripped during substitution.

'pwd' prints your current working directory, the folder commands act on by default. Every process has its own working directory, inherited from its parent. The shell tracks it and updates the PWD environment variable. With logical vs physical options, pwd can show the path through symlinks or the resolved real path.

'cd' changes the shell's working directory. 'cd ..' goes up one level, 'cd ~' or just 'cd' returns home, and 'cd -' jumps back to the previous directory. Because changing directory must affect the shell itself, cd is a shell builtin, not an external program. It updates the PWD and OLDPWD variables.

'ls' lists directory contents. '-l' gives the long format with permissions, owner, size, and date; '-a' includes hidden dotfiles; '-h' makes sizes human-readable; and '-t' sorts by modification time. Combined as 'ls -lath', it's one of the most-typed commands on Linux. Colors usually indicate file types when output goes to a terminal.

/proc is a virtual filesystem the kernel generates on the fly, exposing process and system information as files. Each running process has a directory /proc/PID with details like its command line, environment, and open file descriptors. Files like /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/meminfo describe the hardware. Tools like ps and top read from /proc behind the scenes.

/sys (sysfs) is a virtual filesystem exposing the kernel's view of devices, drivers, and hardware as a structured tree of files. You can read device attributes and sometimes tune kernel settings by writing to these files. For example, CPU and block-device settings live under /sys. It complements /proc, which historically mixed process and hardware data.

/dev holds device files that represent hardware and kernel devices as files you can read and write. /dev/sda is a disk, /dev/null discards anything written to it, /dev/zero produces endless zero bytes, and /dev/random supplies randomness. Modern Linux populates /dev automatically via udev as devices appear. Treating devices as files is a core Unix idea.

/dev/null is a special 'bit bucket' device: anything written to it is discarded, and reading from it returns end-of-file immediately. Redirect unwanted output there, like 'command 2>/dev/null' to silence errors or '> /dev/null 2>&1' to silence everything. It's the standard way to throw away output you don't care about. It's sometimes nicknamed the black hole.

Linux organizes files under a single root '/' following the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard. /bin and /usr/bin hold programs, /etc holds system configuration, /home holds user files, /var holds changing data like logs, /tmp holds temporary files, and /dev holds devices. This consistent layout means you can find things across distributions. Many modern distros now symlink /bin into /usr/bin.

/etc holds system-wide configuration files, almost all in plain text. Examples include /etc/passwd (user accounts), /etc/fstab (mounts), /etc/hosts (name-to-IP overrides), and per-service config under directories like /etc/ssh. Because it's plain text, you can edit, diff, and version-control it. The name historically meant 'et cetera', a catch-all for system files.

/var stores data that changes while the system runs: /var/log for logs, /var/spool for queued tasks like mail and print jobs, /var/cache for cached data, and /var/lib for service state. Because logs can grow without bound, /var filling up is a common cause of disk-full problems. Log rotation tools keep it in check.

/tmp is a world-writable scratch directory for temporary files; its sticky bit stops users from deleting each other's files. Contents are often cleared on reboot or after a set age, so never store anything important there. On many modern systems /tmp is a tmpfs living in RAM, making it fast but volatile. Programs use it for short-lived intermediate data.

tmpfs is a filesystem that lives in memory (RAM, with swap as backup) instead of on disk. It's fast and automatically empties on reboot, making it ideal for /tmp, /run, and other scratch space. Its size can grow up to a configured limit. Because it's volatile, never keep data you need to survive a restart in tmpfs.

Swap is disk (or partition or file) space the kernel uses as overflow when physical RAM fills up, moving idle memory pages out to make room. It prevents out-of-memory crashes but is far slower than RAM, so heavy swapping ('thrashing') hurts performance badly. 'free -h' and 'swapon --show' report swap usage. The 'swappiness' setting tunes how eagerly Linux swaps.

'free' shows total, used, and available memory plus swap. 'free -h' makes the numbers human-readable. The 'available' column is the most useful: it estimates memory programs can use, accounting for reclaimable cache. Linux deliberately uses free RAM as disk cache, so a low 'free' number with high cache is healthy, not a problem.

When Linux runs critically low on memory and swap, the kernel's OOM (out-of-memory) killer picks a process to terminate to free RAM and keep the system alive. It scores processes by memory use and an adjustable oom_score_adj value, usually killing a big memory hog. You'll find evidence in the kernel log ('dmesg' or journalctl). Apps can hint they're important to lower their kill priority.

'dmesg' prints the kernel's ring buffer of messages, including boot-time hardware detection, driver notices, and errors like OOM kills or disk faults. 'dmesg -T' adds human-readable timestamps and '-w' follows new messages live. It's the first place to look when hardware acts up or a USB device isn't recognized. The buffer is fixed size, so old messages eventually roll off.

A package manager installs, updates, and removes software along with its dependencies from trusted repositories. Debian and Ubuntu use apt with .deb packages; Fedora and RHEL use dnf with .rpm; Arch uses pacman. They track which files belong to which package and resolve dependency chains automatically. This is safer and tidier than downloading and compiling software by hand.

apt is the package manager on Debian, Ubuntu, and their derivatives. 'sudo apt update' refreshes the list of available packages, 'apt upgrade' installs updates, 'apt install name' adds software, and 'apt remove name' takes it away. It pulls .deb packages from configured repositories and resolves dependencies. 'apt search' helps you find package names.

dnf is the package manager for Fedora and RHEL-family distributions, the successor to yum. 'sudo dnf install name', 'dnf update', and 'dnf remove name' handle the basics, working with .rpm packages and resolving dependencies. 'dnf search' finds packages and 'dnf history' can undo transactions. It pulls from configured repositories.

'ldd' lists the shared libraries a program needs and where the dynamic linker would find them. It's useful for diagnosing 'cannot open shared object file' errors, which mean a required library is missing or not on the search path. The libraries themselves are resolved by the dynamic linker at runtime. Note: running ldd on an untrusted binary can be risky since it may execute it.

A shared library (.so file on Linux) holds code many programs reuse, loaded into memory once and shared, saving disk and RAM. Programs link against them dynamically, with the runtime linker (ld.so) resolving the references when the program starts. The alternative, static linking, bakes the code into the executable for portability at the cost of size. LD_LIBRARY_PATH can add extra search directories.

'ldconfig' rebuilds the cache that the dynamic linker uses to find shared libraries quickly. After installing a library into a new directory listed in /etc/ld.so.conf, run 'sudo ldconfig' so programs can locate it. Without updating the cache, you might hit 'cannot open shared object file' errors. It scans the standard library directories and writes /etc/ld.so.cache.

'watch' reruns a command at a fixed interval and shows the latest output full-screen, defaulting to every two seconds. 'watch -n 5 df -h' refreshes disk usage every five seconds, and '-d' highlights what changed since last time. It's handy for monitoring something that updates, without writing a loop. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

'tee' reads standard input and writes it to both the screen and one or more files at once, like a T-junction in plumbing. 'command | tee log.txt' shows output live while saving a copy. Add '-a' to append instead of overwrite. A common admin trick is 'echo value | sudo tee /sys/...' to write to a root-owned file from a pipeline.

'lsof' lists open files, and since Unix treats almost everything as a file, that includes regular files, sockets, and pipes. 'lsof -i :8080' shows what's using TCP port 8080, and 'lsof /path' shows who has a file open. It's invaluable for finding which process holds a file or port. You often need root to see other users' files.

'ss' (and the older 'netstat') reports network connections and listening sockets. 'ss -tlnp' lists TCP listening ports with the owning process and numeric addresses. It answers 'what is listening on this machine and which program owns it'. ss is faster than netstat because it reads kernel data more directly, and netstat is deprecated on many distros.

curl transfers data to and from servers over many protocols, most commonly HTTP. 'curl https://example.com' prints a page, '-o file' saves it, '-L' follows redirects, '-H' adds headers, and '-d' sends POST data. It's a scripting staple for hitting APIs and downloading files. '-I' fetches just the headers.

wget downloads files over HTTP, HTTPS, and FTP, and unlike curl it's geared toward fetching files non-interactively. 'wget URL' saves the file under its remote name, '-c' resumes a partial download, and '-r' can mirror an entire site. It's commonly used in scripts to grab installers and datasets. curl is more flexible for APIs; wget is simpler for plain downloads.

'ping' tests whether a host is reachable and measures round-trip time by sending ICMP echo requests. 'ping example.com' shows replies with their latency; press Ctrl+C for a summary including packet loss. No replies can mean the host is down, unreachable, or just blocking ICMP. It's usually the first step in diagnosing network trouble.

The 'ip' command is the modern tool for viewing and configuring Linux networking, replacing ifconfig and route. 'ip addr' shows interfaces and their addresses, 'ip route' shows the routing table, and 'ip link' manages interface state. It's part of the iproute2 package. The old net-tools commands still exist on some systems but are deprecated.

DNS turns hostnames like example.com into IP addresses. On Linux, /etc/resolv.conf lists the DNS servers to query, though systemd-resolved often manages it now. /etc/hosts can override specific names locally, and /etc/nsswitch.conf decides the lookup order. Tools like 'dig' and 'host' query DNS directly for troubleshooting.

'dig' queries DNS servers and shows detailed results. 'dig example.com' returns A records (IPv4 addresses); add a type like 'dig example.com MX' for mail records or 'dig +short example.com' for just the answer. You can target a specific server with '@8.8.8.8'. It's the go-to tool for diagnosing DNS problems precisely.

chroot runs a process with a different directory treated as its root '/', so it can't see files above that point. It's used for recovery (entering a broken install from a live system), building software in a clean tree, and lightweight isolation. chroot alone isn't a strong security boundary, since a privileged process can sometimes escape it. Containers build on stronger isolation mechanisms.

Namespaces isolate what a process can see of the system: there are separate namespaces for PIDs, network, mounts, users, hostnames (UTS), and IPC. A process in its own PID namespace sees a fresh PID 1 and can't see outside processes. Namespaces are a core building block of containers, giving each one its own apparent system. They're created with the clone() and unshare() calls.

Control groups (cgroups) limit and account for the resources a group of processes can use, such as CPU, memory, and I/O. systemd organizes services into cgroups, and containers use them to cap resource consumption. cgroups v2 unified the hierarchy into a single tree under /sys/fs/cgroup. Together with namespaces, cgroups make containers possible: namespaces isolate, cgroups limit.

A container packages an application with its dependencies and runs it as isolated processes on a shared host kernel, using namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resource limits. Unlike a virtual machine, it doesn't boot a separate OS kernel, so it starts fast and is lightweight. Docker and Podman are popular tools to build and run them. The isolation is process-level, not full hardware virtualization.

strace shows every system call a program makes and the result, which is great for seeing what files it opens, what it fails to find, and where it hangs. 'strace -f cmd' follows child processes and '-e trace=open' filters to specific calls. When a program mysteriously fails, strace often reveals the missing file or permission. It adds overhead, so use it for debugging, not production.

'history' shows the list of commands you've recently run, numbered. Press the up arrow or Ctrl+R to search interactively, and run an old command again with '!42' (by number) or '!!' for the last one. History is saved to a file like ~/.bash_history between sessions. Be mindful that secrets typed on the command line land in this file.

~/.bashrc is a script bash runs for each new interactive non-login shell, the place to set aliases, functions, prompt style, and shell options. Login shells read ~/.bash_profile (or ~/.profile) instead, which commonly sources .bashrc so both behave the same. Changes take effect in new shells or after 'source ~/.bashrc'. Keep heavy commands out of it to avoid slow shell startup.

'source file' (or its shorthand '.') runs a script in the current shell instead of a child process, so any variables, functions, or directory changes it makes persist. That's why you 'source ~/.bashrc' to apply config changes without opening a new terminal. Running the script normally would change only the child's environment, which then vanishes. Use source when you want the effects to stick.

'set -e' makes a bash script exit immediately if any command returns a nonzero status, so a failure doesn't silently cascade. It's a common safety setting at the top of scripts, often combined with 'set -u' (error on undefined variables) and 'set -o pipefail'. Be aware of its quirks: it ignores failures inside conditions and some compound commands. Many robust scripts use 'set -euo pipefail'.

By default a pipeline's exit status is just the last command's, so 'false | true' reports success. 'set -o pipefail' changes that: the pipeline fails if any command in it fails, returning the last nonzero status. It's essential when you care whether an early stage like a download or grep succeeded. It's usually paired with 'set -e' for safe scripts.

'trap' lets a shell script run a handler when it receives a signal or exits. 'trap "rm -f $tmpfile" EXIT' guarantees cleanup of a temp file no matter how the script ends. You can also trap signals like INT (Ctrl+C) to catch interrupts gracefully. It's the shell equivalent of a finally block.

The 'test' command, also written as '[ ... ]', evaluates a condition and returns success or failure for use in 'if' and loops. It checks files ('-f' exists as file, '-d' is directory), compares strings, and compares numbers ('-eq', '-lt'). In bash, '[[ ... ]]' is a more capable built-in version with safer handling of empty variables and pattern matching. Spaces around the brackets are required.

A bash 'if' runs a command and branches on its exit status, not a boolean. The form is 'if command; then ...; elif ...; else ...; fi'. Often the command is a test like 'if [ -f file ]; then'. Remember the closing 'fi' and the semicolon or newline before 'then'. Zero exit status means the 'then' branch runs.

A bash 'for' loop iterates over a list of words: 'for f in *.txt; do echo "$f"; done' processes each matching file. You can loop over command output, a brace range like {1..5}, or an array. Always quote "$f" inside to handle names with spaces. A C-style form 'for ((i=0;i<10;i++))' also exists in bash.

A bash 'while' loop repeats as long as a command succeeds. A common pattern reads a file line by line: 'while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file'. The 'IFS=' preserves leading and trailing spaces, and '-r' stops backslashes from being interpreted. This is the correct way to process lines, unlike looping over command output which mishandles whitespace.

Inside a script or function, arguments arrive as positional parameters: $1 is the first, $2 the second, and so on, with $0 holding the script's own name. '$#' is the count of arguments, '$@' expands to all of them as separate quoted words, and '$*' joins them into one string. Always use "$@" to forward arguments safely. 'shift' drops $1 and renumbers the rest.

IFS, the Internal Field Separator, is the set of characters bash uses to split unquoted expansions into words; by default it's space, tab, and newline. Changing it lets you split on other characters, like setting IFS=, to parse comma-separated data. Unquoted variable expansions undergo this word-splitting, which is why quoting "$var" is so important. Save and restore IFS if you change it temporarily.

Bash parameter expansion does more than print a variable's value. '${var:-default}' uses a fallback if var is unset, '${#var}' gives its length, '${var#prefix}' strips a leading prefix, '${var%suffix}' strips a trailing one, and '${var/old/new}' substitutes text. These let you manipulate strings without calling external tools like sed. The braces also clarify where a name ends, as in ${var}suffix.

Bash does integer math inside '$(( ... ))', so 'echo $((3 + 4 * 2))' prints 11. Variables can be used without the $ sign inside, like '$((count + 1))'. It handles the usual operators plus comparison and bitwise ops, but only integers — no decimals. For floating-point math, pipe to a tool like bc or awk.

'su' switches to another user account in the same terminal, prompting for that user's password. 'su -' (with the dash) starts a login shell, loading the target user's full environment, while plain 'su' keeps much of the current one. Historically people used 'su' to become root, but sudo is now preferred because it logs actions and uses your own password. 'su username' switches to a normal account.
