'whoami' prints your effective username, and 'id' shows your numeric user ID, group ID, and all the groups you belong to. These help confirm who a script is running as, especially after su or sudo. 'id -u' returns just the numeric UID, useful in scripts checking 'are we root' (UID 0). Groups determine a lot of your file access.

/etc/passwd lists user accounts, one per line, with colon-separated fields: username, an 'x' placeholder for the password, UID, GID, a comment, the home directory, and the login shell. Despite the name, real password hashes live in /etc/shadow, readable only by root, for security. Reading /etc/passwd tells you every account and its default shell. The fields haven't changed in decades.

/etc/shadow stores the actual hashed passwords and aging info for accounts, separated from /etc/passwd so only root can read it. Each line holds the username, the salted password hash, and fields for password expiry and minimum/maximum age. Storing hashes here instead of the world-readable passwd file is a key security improvement. The hash format is identified by a prefix like $6$ for SHA-512.

Linux groups let several users share access to files. Every user has a primary group and may belong to several supplementary groups, listed by the 'groups' command. File permissions have a group class, so adding a user to a group grants them that group's access. 'usermod -aG groupname user' adds a user to a group; the change takes effect on their next login.

'pstree' displays running processes as a tree, showing which process spawned which. It makes parent/child relationships obvious — for instance you can see every shell and program under a login session. 'pstree -p' adds PIDs. Because everything descends from PID 1, the whole system shows up as one big tree rooted at systemd.

'uptime' prints how long the system has been running, the current time, how many users are logged in, and the 1/5/15-minute load averages on one line. It's a quick health check: a freshly rebooted machine versus one up for months, plus whether it's currently busy. The load figures are the same ones top shows. For just the duration, 'uptime -p' gives a pretty form.

'date' prints the current date and time, and with a '+format' string you can shape the output, like 'date +%Y-%m-%d' for an ISO date useful in filenames. It also reads other time zones via the TZ variable. With root and a valid argument it can set the clock, though systems usually sync time automatically with NTP. It's a scripting staple for timestamps.

NTP (Network Time Protocol) keeps a computer's clock accurate by syncing with time servers over the network. On systemd systems 'timedatectl' shows and controls the clock, time zone, and whether NTP sync is on. Accurate time matters for logs, TLS certificates, and scheduled jobs. Many distros use systemd-timesyncd or chrony as the NTP client.

'locate' finds files by name almost instantly by searching a prebuilt database instead of scanning the disk like find. The database is refreshed periodically by 'updatedb', so brand-new files may not appear until it runs. It's much faster than find for name lookups but can be stale. On many systems the tool is provided as mlocate or plocate.

'stat' shows detailed metadata about a file: size, permissions in both symbolic and octal form, owner, inode number, and the three timestamps (access, modify, change). It reads the same inode information ls uses but in full. '--format' lets you print just the field you want for scripts. It's handy when 'ls -l' doesn't show enough.

'touch file' updates a file's access and modification times to now, and creates the file empty if it doesn't exist. It's commonly used to make placeholder files or to refresh timestamps so a build tool thinks something changed. '-t' or '-d' set a specific time, and '-c' avoids creating a missing file. Despite seeming trivial, it's a frequent scripting helper.

'mkdir' creates directories. '-p' makes a whole path at once, creating any missing parents and not erroring if it already exists, like 'mkdir -p a/b/c'. '-m' sets the permissions on creation. The '-p' flag is especially useful in scripts so you don't have to check for each level first.

'rm' deletes files, and with '-r' it removes directories and their contents recursively. There's no recycle bin — deleted files are gone. '-f' forces removal without prompts, and '-i' asks before each delete for safety. The infamous 'rm -rf /' attempts to wipe everything, which is why you must be extremely careful with recursive force deletes, especially as root.

'cp source dest' copies files. '-r' copies directories recursively, '-p' preserves permissions and timestamps, '-a' archives (preserve everything and copy recursively), and '-i' prompts before overwriting. By default cp follows symlinks and overwrites silently. Use '-u' to copy only when the source is newer.

'mv' moves or renames files and directories; there's no separate rename command in Unix. Within one filesystem it just relinks the entry, so it's instant; across filesystems it copies then deletes. '-i' prompts before overwriting and '-n' refuses to overwrite. Renaming is simply moving a file to a new name in the same directory.

'cat' prints file contents to the screen and, true to its name, concatenates multiple files when given several. 'cat -n' numbers lines and 'cat -A' reveals hidden characters like tabs. It's overused in pipelines: 'cat file | grep x' can usually be 'grep x file' instead. Still, it's the simplest way to dump a small file's contents.

'less' is a pager that lets you scroll through long output without loading it all at once. Navigate with arrows or PageUp/PageDown, search with '/pattern', press 'n' for the next match, 'G' to jump to the end, and 'q' to quit. It's the default pager for man pages and far more capable than 'more'. Its name is a pun: 'less is more'.

'man command' opens the manual page documenting a command, its options, and examples. Manuals are organized into numbered sections (1 for user commands, 5 for file formats, 8 for admin tools), so 'man 5 passwd' shows the file format while 'man 1 passwd' shows the command. Search within a page using '/' and quit with 'q'. 'apropos keyword' finds relevant pages.

'echo' prints its arguments followed by a newline. '-n' suppresses the trailing newline and '-e' enables escape sequences like \n and \t in bash. Behavior varies between shells and the external /bin/echo, so for portable escapes 'printf' is safer. echo is the simplest way to emit text or a variable's value.

'printf' formats and prints text using a format string with placeholders, much like C's printf. 'printf "%s is %d\n" name 42' substitutes the arguments in order. Unlike echo it doesn't add a newline automatically, so you write \n yourself, and it handles escapes consistently across shells. It's the reliable choice for precise or repeated formatting.

'read varname' reads a line from standard input into a variable, used for prompting or processing input line by line. '-p' shows a prompt, '-s' hides typed characters (good for passwords), and '-r' prevents backslash interpretation, which you almost always want. In loops, 'while IFS= read -r line' is the safe idiom for reading files. It reads one line per call by default.

'yes' prints a string (the word 'y' by default) over and over until stopped. It exists to feed automatic 'y' confirmations into commands that prompt, like 'yes | apt remove pkg', though most tools now offer a '-y' flag instead. Pass an argument to repeat that instead of 'y'. It surprisingly also serves as a quick CPU/throughput test.

'sleep N' pauses for N seconds before continuing, and GNU sleep also accepts suffixes like '5m' for minutes or '2h' for hours. Scripts use it to wait between retries or to space out actions. It does nothing but wait, consuming almost no CPU. Combine it in loops for simple polling or rate limiting.

'timeout DURATION command' runs a command but kills it if it exceeds the time limit, like 'timeout 30s curl ...'. By default it sends SIGTERM; add '-s KILL' or '-k' to force termination. It returns exit code 124 when the timeout fires. It's perfect for stopping commands that might hang in scripts and cron jobs.

'basename /a/b/file.txt' strips the directory and prints 'file.txt', and you can pass a suffix to strip too, like 'basename file.txt .txt'. 'dirname /a/b/file.txt' prints the directory part '/a/b'. Together they split a path into its pieces in scripts. Bash parameter expansion (${path##*/} and ${path%/*}) can do the same without spawning a process.

'realpath' resolves a path to its absolute, canonical form, following all symlinks and removing '.' and '..' segments. 'readlink -f' does much the same and also prints where a symlink points. They're useful in scripts that must know a file's true location regardless of how it was reached. realpath also has a '--relative-to' mode for relative paths.

'diff file1 file2' shows the differences between two text files line by line. '-u' produces the unified format with surrounding context that patch and git use, and '-r' recurses through directories comparing them. The output marks lines added, removed, or changed. It's the foundation of patches and version-control diffs.

'patch' applies the changes described in a diff file to source files, the classic way to share code fixes before Git. 'patch -p1 < changes.diff' applies a unified diff, with '-p1' stripping one leading directory from the paths. It can also reverse a patch with '-R'. It carefully tries to apply hunks even if line numbers shifted slightly.

'file name' inspects a file's contents to guess its type, rather than trusting the extension. It reports things like 'ASCII text', 'PNG image', or 'ELF 64-bit executable' by checking magic numbers near the start. This is handy when an extension is missing or misleading. It's a quick way to know what you're actually dealing with.

'xxd' and 'hexdump' display a file's raw bytes in hexadecimal alongside an ASCII rendering, letting you inspect binary data. 'xxd file' shows offset, hex bytes, and printable characters per line. 'xxd -r' even converts an edited hex dump back to binary. They're essential for debugging file formats, network captures, and corrupted data.

'base64' encodes binary data into safe printable ASCII text and decodes it back with '-d'. It's used to embed binary in text-only contexts like email, JSON, or config files. The trade-off is that encoded data grows about a third larger. 'base64 file' encodes; 'base64 -d file' restores the original.

Checksum tools like 'sha256sum' compute a fixed-length fingerprint of a file's contents, used to verify a download wasn't corrupted or tampered with. Run 'sha256sum file' and compare it to the value the publisher posted. MD5 and SHA-1 are now considered cryptographically broken, so prefer SHA-256. A '-c' mode checks files against a list of stored sums.

'dd' copies and converts data block by block, often used to write disk images to USB drives or clone partitions, like 'dd if=image.iso of=/dev/sdb bs=4M status=progress'. It's powerful but unforgiving: swapping 'if' (input) and 'of' (output) can wipe the wrong device, earning it the nickname 'disk destroyer'. Always double-check the target device. Add 'sync' and a sensible block size for reliability.

'mkfs' creates (formats) a filesystem on a partition or device, like 'mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1'. There are variants per filesystem type — mkfs.ext4, mkfs.xfs, mkfs.vfat — and the command erases existing data on that device. After formatting, you mount it to use it. Picking the wrong device here destroys data, so verify the target first.

ext4 is the long-standing default Linux filesystem, a journaling filesystem that records pending changes in a journal so it can recover quickly and consistently after a crash. It supports large files and volumes, extents for efficient storage, and delayed allocation for performance. It's reliable and well-tested. Newer options like XFS and Btrfs offer different trade-offs, but ext4 remains a safe default.

Btrfs and ZFS are advanced copy-on-write filesystems offering snapshots, checksums for data integrity, and built-in volume management. Snapshots let you capture a point-in-time view cheaply for backups or rollbacks. ZFS has a reputation for rock-solid integrity but historically lived outside the mainline kernel for licensing reasons; Btrfs ships in the kernel and is the default on some distros. Both detect and can repair silent data corruption.

LVM (Logical Volume Manager) adds a flexible layer between physical disks and filesystems. Physical volumes join into a volume group, from which you carve logical volumes that can be resized, snapshotted, or spread across disks. This lets you grow a filesystem without repartitioning. It's common on servers where storage needs change over time.

A partition table divides a disk into sections that can hold separate filesystems. The older MBR scheme is limited to four primary partitions and 2 TB disks, while modern GPT supports many partitions and huge disks. Tools like fdisk, gdisk, and parted edit partition tables. GPT pairs with UEFI firmware on current systems.

'fsck' checks a filesystem for errors and can repair inconsistencies, usually after an unclean shutdown. It must run on an unmounted filesystem, so the root one is typically checked at boot. Journaling filesystems like ext4 need full checks far less often because the journal handles most recovery. Running fsck on a mounted filesystem can corrupt it, so don't.

'blkid' lists block devices with their UUIDs, labels, and filesystem types. The UUID is a stable identifier that doesn't change if disks are reordered, which is why /etc/fstab references devices by UUID rather than /dev/sdX names. It's the quickest way to find a partition's UUID for a mount entry. Run it as root to see all devices.

'lsblk' shows block devices in a tree, listing disks and their partitions with sizes, types, and mount points. It's the clearest overview of your storage layout, like seeing that /dev/sda has partitions sda1 and sda2. '-f' adds filesystem type and UUID info. Unlike df, it shows devices whether or not they're mounted.

udev is the Linux subsystem that manages device nodes in /dev dynamically as hardware appears and disappears. When you plug in a USB drive, udev creates the device file and can run rules to set permissions, names, or trigger actions. Custom udev rules let you, say, give a specific device a stable name. It replaced the old static /dev with a dynamic one.

Kernel modules are pieces of kernel code, like device drivers, that can be loaded and unloaded at runtime instead of being built into the kernel. 'lsmod' lists loaded modules, 'modprobe name' loads one with its dependencies, and 'rmmod' removes one. This keeps the core kernel small while supporting lots of hardware on demand. Module config lives under /etc/modprobe.d.

'uname' prints system information. 'uname -r' shows the running kernel version, '-m' the machine architecture (like x86_64 or aarch64), and 'uname -a' dumps everything at once. It's the quick way to confirm which kernel you're on, which matters when installing drivers or matching kernel headers. Scripts use it to branch on architecture.

GRUB is the common Linux bootloader: after firmware hands off, GRUB presents a menu, loads the chosen kernel, and passes it boot parameters. Its config is generated (don't edit grub.cfg directly) from settings in /etc/default/grub plus scripts, regenerated with update-grub or grub-mkconfig. GRUB can boot multiple operating systems on one machine. It runs before the kernel and init.

A Linux boot goes: firmware (UEFI/BIOS) powers on and runs the bootloader, the bootloader (GRUB) loads the kernel and an initramfs, the kernel initializes hardware and mounts the root filesystem, then it starts PID 1 (systemd), which brings up services. Understanding these stages helps diagnose where a boot fails. The initramfs is a tiny temporary root used to load drivers needed to reach the real root.

The initramfs is a small temporary root filesystem the bootloader loads into memory alongside the kernel. It contains just enough drivers and tools to mount the real root filesystem — useful when the root lives on RAID, LVM, or an encrypted volume needing setup first. Once the real root is mounted, the system switches to it. It's rebuilt when kernels or storage drivers change.

Older SysV init used numbered runlevels (3 for multi-user text, 5 for graphical, 0 to halt, 6 to reboot) to describe system states. systemd replaced these with named targets like multi-user.target and graphical.target. 'systemctl get-default' shows the boot target and 'systemctl isolate' switches at runtime. Targets group the units that should be active in a given state.

On systemd systems, systemd-tmpfiles manages creation and cleanup of temporary files and directories based on rules in /etc/tmpfiles.d and /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d. It can wipe files in /tmp older than a configured age and ensure runtime directories exist with the right permissions at boot. This replaced older cron-based tmp cleanup. Each rule line describes a path, type, mode, owner, and age.

logrotate keeps log files from filling the disk by rotating them on a schedule: renaming the current log, optionally compressing old ones, and deleting those past a retention limit. Config lives in /etc/logrotate.conf and /etc/logrotate.d, with per-service rules. After rotating, it can signal a daemon to reopen its log file. It typically runs daily via cron or a systemd timer.

syslog is the traditional Linux logging system; rsyslog is a common modern implementation. Programs send messages tagged with a facility (like mail or auth) and a severity (from debug to emergency), and the logger routes them to files such as /var/log/syslog or to a remote server. systemd's journal often feeds or replaces it. Centralizing logs from many servers is a common use.

Standard Unix permissions cover only owner, group, and others, which can't express 'this one extra user gets write access'. Access Control Lists (ACLs) extend permissions to grant rights to specific users or groups. Use 'setfacl -m u:bob:rw file' to add a rule and 'getfacl file' to view them. A '+' after the permission string in 'ls -l' signals a file has ACLs.

Extended attributes let you attach extra name/value metadata to a file beyond the standard fields, stored in namespaces like 'user', 'security', and 'system'. SELinux labels and file capabilities live here. 'getfattr -d file' lists user attributes and 'setfattr' sets them. They're how features like immutability flags and security contexts ride along with files.

'chattr' sets special filesystem attributes on ext-family filesystems beyond normal permissions. The most famous is immutable: 'chattr +i file' makes a file unchangeable and undeletable even by root until you remove the flag with 'chattr -i'. 'lsattr' lists current attributes. The append-only attribute (+a) is handy for protecting log files from tampering.

SELinux is a mandatory access control system that adds a security layer beyond normal Unix permissions, enforcing policy based on labels attached to processes and files. Even root is constrained by policy. It runs in enforcing, permissive (logs but allows), or disabled modes, checked with 'getenforce'. It's default on Fedora and RHEL; AppArmor is the comparable system on Ubuntu and SUSE.

AppArmor is a mandatory access control system, an alternative to SELinux used by default on Ubuntu and SUSE. It confines individual programs using path-based profiles that list what files and capabilities each program may use. Profiles run in enforce mode (block violations) or complain mode (just log). 'aa-status' shows loaded profiles. It's generally considered simpler to manage than SELinux.

Linux capabilities split root's all-or-nothing power into fine-grained privileges, so a program can be granted just one ability instead of full root. For example CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE lets a process bind to ports below 1024 without being root. Set them on a binary with setcap and view them with getcap. This reduces risk compared to making programs setuid root.

'ulimit' shows and sets per-process resource limits in the shell, such as the maximum number of open files ('ulimit -n'), stack size, or core dump size. Each limit has a soft value users can raise up to a hard cap. Servers often raise the open-file limit so they can handle many connections. System-wide defaults live in /etc/security/limits.conf.

A core dump is a file capturing a process's memory at the moment it crashed, used to debug with a tool like gdb afterward. Whether cores are written depends on the 'ulimit -c' setting and where they go is set by /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern. On systemd systems, coredumpctl manages and inspects them. They're invaluable for diagnosing segfaults.

A segmentation fault happens when a program tries to access memory it isn't allowed to, like dereferencing a null or freed pointer. The kernel sends SIGSEGV, which by default terminates the process and may write a core dump. In C and C++ it's a classic sign of a pointer bug or buffer overrun. The shell often reports it as 'Segmentation fault (core dumped)'.

'pgrep name' prints the PIDs of processes whose names match a pattern, and 'pgrep -a' also shows their command lines. 'pidof program' similarly finds PIDs of a running program. These avoid the clumsy 'ps aux | grep' dance and pair nicely with kill, as in 'pkill name' to signal them directly. '-u user' limits to one user's processes.

In a shell script, 'wait' pauses until background jobs finish. With no arguments it waits for all of them; 'wait PID' waits for a specific one and returns its exit status. This lets a script launch several tasks in parallel with '&' and then collect their results before continuing. It's the basis of simple parallelism in shell scripts.

Wrapping commands in parentheses '( ... )' runs them in a subshell, a child copy of the current shell. Changes there — like 'cd', variable assignments, or 'set' options — don't affect the parent shell. This is handy when you want to change directory temporarily: '(cd /tmp && do_stuff)' returns you where you started. A subshell is a separate process.

Curly braces '{ commands; }' group commands to run in the current shell, without spawning a subshell as parentheses do. This is useful for redirecting several commands' output together, like '{ echo a; echo b; } > file'. Note the required spaces after '{' and the semicolon (or newline) before '}'. Because there's no subshell, variable changes inside persist.

Process substitution lets a command read another command's output as if it were a file, written '<(command)'. For example 'diff <(sort a) <(sort b)' compares two sorted lists without temp files. Bash connects them via a named pipe behind the scenes. The '>(command)' form works the other way, feeding output into a command. It's a bash/zsh feature, not POSIX sh.

The XDG Base Directory specification standardizes where programs store user files, reducing clutter in your home directory. Config goes in ~/.config (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME), data in ~/.local/share, cache in ~/.cache, and runtime files in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR. Many modern apps follow it instead of dumping dotfiles directly in $HOME. It keeps a home directory far tidier.

On Unix, any file or directory whose name starts with a dot is hidden from normal directory listings; that's the entire mechanism. Config files like ~/.bashrc and ~/.gitconfig use this so they don't clutter your view. Show them with 'ls -a'. People often keep their dotfiles in a Git repo to sync settings across machines.

Brace expansion generates strings before the command runs and, unlike globbing, doesn't depend on existing files. 'echo file{1,2,3}.txt' prints file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt, and ranges work too: '{1..5}' or '{a..e}'. It's great for creating many files or directories at once, like 'mkdir -p project/{src,test,docs}'. It happens earlier than wildcard expansion.

The shell expands a leading tilde to a home directory: '~' becomes your home, and '~user' becomes that user's home directory. So 'cd ~/projects' goes to projects under your home. It only expands at the start of a word and when unquoted. Inside double quotes '~' stays literal, which surprises people.

'env' prints the current environment variables, and it also runs a command with a modified environment, like 'env VAR=value command'. The popular shebang '#!/usr/bin/env python3' uses env to find python3 on PATH, making scripts portable across systems with different install paths. '-i' starts with an empty environment for reproducible runs. It's both a viewer and a launcher.

'chsh' changes a user's default login shell, the program started when they log in, recorded in the last field of their /etc/passwd entry. 'chsh -s /bin/zsh' switches to zsh, taking effect at the next login. Only shells listed in /etc/shells are allowed. This is how you move from bash to zsh or fish as your daily shell.

fish (friendly interactive shell) focuses on a great out-of-the-box experience: autosuggestions from history as you type, syntax highlighting, and helpful tab completion without configuration. Its scripting syntax is cleaner but intentionally not POSIX-compatible, so bash scripts won't run unchanged. Many people use fish interactively while keeping bash or sh for portable scripts. It's a popular modern alternative.

A frequent pattern is counting results of a search: 'grep -c pattern file' counts matching lines directly, while 'grep pattern file | wc -l' does the same through a pipe. Note 'grep -c' counts lines, not total matches, so a line with two matches still counts once. To count total occurrences use 'grep -o pattern file | wc -l'. Knowing the difference avoids subtle miscounts.

'comm' compares two sorted files and prints three columns: lines unique to the first file, lines unique to the second, and lines they share. Suppress columns with flags like '-12' to show only the common lines. Both inputs must be sorted for it to work correctly. It's a quick way to find what two lists have in common or differ on.

'join' merges two sorted files on a shared key field, like a database join. 'join file1 file2' matches lines whose first field is equal and combines them. You can pick the join field with '-1' and '-2' and choose the output format with '-o'. Both files must be sorted on the join key first, just like comm.

'paste' merges lines from multiple files side by side, separated by a tab. 'paste file1 file2' puts line one of each on the same output line. With '-d' you can choose a different delimiter, and 'paste -s' joins all lines of a single file into one row. It's the column-wise complement to cat's row-wise joining.

'tr' translates or deletes characters from standard input. 'tr a-z A-Z' uppercases text, 'tr -d "\n"' strips newlines, and 'tr -s " "' squeezes runs of spaces into one. It works on single characters, not words or patterns, so it's lighter than sed for simple substitutions. It only reads stdin, so feed it via a pipe or redirection.

'rev' reverses the characters of each line it reads, so 'echo hello | rev' prints 'olleh'. It's a small, fun utility occasionally useful for tricks like extracting the last field by reversing, cutting, and reversing back. It operates per line, not on the whole file's order. For reversing line order instead, use 'tac'.

'tac' prints a file's lines in reverse order, last line first — it's 'cat' spelled backward. It's handy for reading logs newest-first or undoing a sort. Unlike 'rev', which reverses characters within each line, 'tac' reverses the order of whole lines. You can also change the separator it splits on with '-s'.

'nl' numbers the lines of a file, more flexibly than 'cat -n'. By default it numbers only non-empty lines and lets you control the start, increment, and format of the numbers. Options choose whether to number all lines or only certain ones. It's a small tool for adding line numbers to output or source listings.

'fold' wraps long lines to a given width (80 by default, or set with '-w'), breaking at the column even mid-word unless '-s' tells it to break at spaces. 'fmt' is smarter for prose, reflowing paragraphs to a target width while respecting word boundaries. Both help format text for terminals or fixed-width output. They're the opposite of joining lines.

'expand' converts tabs to spaces and 'unexpand' converts leading spaces back to tabs. They help normalize indentation when files mix tabs and spaces, which can break makefiles or alignment. 'expand -t 4' uses a four-space tab stop. These small tools fix whitespace issues without a full editor.

'column -t' takes whitespace-separated input and aligns it into neat columns, great for making ragged output readable. You can set the input delimiter with '-s', for instance to pretty-print a colon-separated file. It's a quick way to turn messy command output into a tidy table. It only formats; it doesn't sort or compute.

'seq' prints a sequence of numbers: 'seq 5' gives 1 through 5, 'seq 2 2 10' steps by two, and '-w' pads with leading zeros for equal width. It's handy for loops, like 'for i in $(seq 1 10)', though bash brace expansion '{1..10}' often does the same. '-f' applies a printf-style format to each number.

'bc' is an arbitrary-precision calculator language, useful when the shell's integer-only arithmetic isn't enough. 'echo "3.5 * 2" | bc' gives 7.0, and 'bc -l' loads math functions and sets a decimal scale. It supports variables, loops, and functions for bigger calculations. 'dc' is its reverse-Polish-notation cousin.

jq is a command-line tool for slicing and transforming JSON, indispensable when working with APIs. 'curl api | jq ".items[].name"' extracts a field from each item, and filters can map, select, and reshape data. It pretty-prints JSON by default, so even 'jq .' makes minified responses readable. It's effectively sed/awk for JSON.

'nproc' prints the number of processing units available to the current process, accounting for CPU affinity and container limits. Build tools use it to parallelize, like 'make -j$(nproc)' to compile with one job per core. It can differ from the total physical cores if the process is restricted. It's the simple, portable way to ask 'how many CPUs can I use'.

'vmstat' and 'iostat' report live system performance. vmstat summarizes processes, memory, swap, I/O, and CPU at an interval, while iostat focuses on per-device disk throughput and utilization. They help pinpoint whether a slowdown is CPU, memory, or disk bound. They come from the sysstat package on many distros and are staples for performance triage.

'sar' from the sysstat package collects and reports system activity over time — CPU, memory, disk, and network — and can show historical data, not just the current moment. A background collector samples metrics periodically and stores them, so 'sar' can show what the system was doing an hour ago. This makes it valuable for diagnosing intermittent problems after the fact. It's like having a flight recorder for performance.

iotop is like top but for disk I/O, showing which processes are reading and writing the most. It's the tool to reach for when the disk is thrashing and load is high but CPU looks idle. It needs root because it reads per-process I/O accounting from the kernel. Sorting by I/O quickly reveals the culprit process.

nethogs groups network bandwidth usage by process, answering 'which program is hogging my connection right now'. Unlike most network monitors that show per-interface or per-connection totals, it attributes traffic to the responsible process. It needs root to inspect socket ownership. It's a quick way to catch a runaway download or chatty service.

tcpdump captures and displays network packets on an interface, letting you see real traffic for debugging. 'tcpdump -i eth0 port 80' shows web traffic, and '-w file.pcap' saves a capture to open later in Wireshark. Filters use the BPF syntax to narrow what's captured. It needs root because it puts the interface in promiscuous mode.

Linux filters network traffic in the kernel via netfilter. iptables was the long-standing front end for writing rules; nftables is its modern replacement with a cleaner syntax and the 'nft' command. Rules decide which packets to accept, drop, or forward based on addresses, ports, and state. Higher-level tools like ufw and firewalld generate these rules for you.

ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall) is Ubuntu's friendly front end over iptables/nftables for basic firewalling. 'sudo ufw allow 22' opens SSH, 'ufw enable' turns the firewall on, and 'ufw status' lists rules. It aims to make common cases simple without learning raw iptables syntax. Underneath it just manages kernel netfilter rules.

netcat ('nc') reads and writes data across network connections, earning it the nickname 'TCP/IP Swiss Army knife'. It can act as a quick server ('nc -l 1234') or client ('nc host 1234'), test whether a port is open, or pipe data between machines. It's invaluable for debugging connectivity and simple ad-hoc transfers. Beware that the plain version is unencrypted.

The ~/.ssh/config file stores per-host SSH settings so you don't retype them. A Host block can set the real hostname, user, port, identity file, and options, letting you type 'ssh myserver' instead of a long command. You can also define jump hosts and connection multiplexing here. It makes managing many servers far more pleasant.

ssh-agent holds your decrypted private keys in memory so you only type a key's passphrase once per session instead of every connection. Start it, then 'ssh-add' loads keys into it. Agent forwarding (with care) can let a remote host use your local keys to reach further hosts. It balances the security of passphrase-protected keys with convenience.

SSH can tunnel other traffic through its encrypted connection. Local forwarding ('ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 host') maps a local port to a remote service, useful to reach something behind a firewall. Remote forwarding ('-R') exposes a local service on the remote side, and dynamic forwarding ('-D') creates a SOCKS proxy. Tunnels let you securely access services without opening extra ports.

To make a destination an exact mirror of a source with rsync, add '--delete', which removes files at the destination that no longer exist in the source. Always test first with '-n' (dry run) and '-v' so you can see what would be deleted before it's real. Forgetting a trailing slash or the wrong direction with --delete can erase data. It's powerful but unforgiving, so double-check the paths.

A frequent surprise is that a command works in your terminal but fails under cron. The reason is cron runs jobs with a minimal environment and a short PATH, without your shell's aliases or variables. Fixes include using full paths to programs, setting PATH at the top of the crontab, and redirecting output to a log to see errors. Cron also emails output by default if mail is configured.

anacron runs periodic jobs that may have been missed while the machine was off, unlike cron which assumes the system runs continuously. It's ideal for laptops and desktops: a daily job will run after boot if it was due, rather than being skipped. It works in granularities of days, not minutes. Many systems use anacron to drive the daily/weekly/monthly job directories.

'at' schedules a command to run once at a future time, in contrast to cron's recurring jobs. 'at 3pm' then typing commands, or 'echo cmd | at now + 1 hour', queues a one-off task handled by the atd daemon. List pending jobs with 'atq' and cancel one with 'atrm'. It's perfect for 'do this thing later' without a permanent schedule entry.

'disown' removes a job from the shell's job table so it won't get SIGHUP when the shell exits, letting an already-running background job survive logout. It's the after-the-fact counterpart to starting something with nohup. 'disown -h' keeps the job listed but shields it from hangup. Useful when you forgot to use nohup before launching a long task.

'set -x' turns on shell tracing, printing each command (after expansion) with a '+' prefix as it runs, which is invaluable for debugging scripts. Turn it off again with 'set +x'. You can scope it to just part of a script. Combined with 'set -e', it shows exactly where a script went wrong before it exited.

Many robust bash scripts start with 'set -euo pipefail' as an unofficial 'strict mode': -e exits on error, -u errors on undefined variables, and -o pipefail catches failures anywhere in a pipe. Some also set IFS to just newline and tab to tame word-splitting. It catches mistakes early instead of letting a script blunder on after a failure. It's a widely recommended safety habit.

'exit' ends a script (or shell) immediately, optionally with a status code: 'exit 0' for success, 'exit 1' for a generic error. With no argument it returns the status of the last command. Choosing meaningful exit codes lets callers and automation react to how a script finished. By convention, codes above 128 indicate the script was killed by a signal.

A here-string feeds a single line of text to a command's standard input using '<<<', like 'grep foo <<< "$variable"'. It's a concise alternative to 'echo "$variable" | grep foo' that avoids spawning echo and a pipe. It's a bash and zsh feature, not in plain POSIX sh. Handy for passing a variable's contents into a command that reads stdin.

A 'case' statement matches a value against patterns, a clean alternative to long if/elif chains. The form is 'case $x in pattern) commands;; *) default;; esac', where patterns can use globbing like 'start*' and '|' to list alternatives. Each branch ends with ';;'. It's the standard way scripts parse a command argument like start/stop/restart.

'getopts' parses single-letter command-line options in a script in a standard way. In a 'while getopts "ab:" opt' loop, the spec 'ab:' means -a is a flag and -b takes an argument (the colon), with the value landing in $OPTARG. It handles bundling like -ab and stops at the first non-option. It's the portable built-in for option parsing, though it doesn't do long --options.

Bash supports indexed arrays: declare with 'arr=(a b c)', access an element with '${arr[1]}', all elements with '${arr[@]}', and the count with '${#arr[@]}'. Always quote "${arr[@]}" to keep elements with spaces intact. Bash 4+ also has associative arrays (key/value maps) via 'declare -A'. Arrays are a big reason to use bash over plain sh for real scripts.

An IP address is a number that identifies a device on a network, like a mailing address for computers. Routers use it to send data to the right place. IPv4 addresses look like 192.168.1.5 (four numbers separated by dots), while IPv6 addresses are much longer and use letters too.

IPv4 is the older internet addressing system that uses 32-bit addresses, giving about 4.3 billion possible addresses. That sounds like a lot, but the world ran out of fresh IPv4 addresses years ago. Addresses look like 203.0.113.7, with each of the four parts ranging from 0 to 255.

IPv6 is the newer addressing system that uses 128-bit addresses, giving roughly 340 undecillion possibilities (a 3 followed by 38 digits). That is enough to give every grain of sand its own address. They are written in hexadecimal groups like 2001:db8::1, and the double colon stands for a run of zeros.

DNS is the internet's phone book: it turns a human-friendly name like example.com into the numeric IP address computers need. When you type a website, your computer asks a DNS server for that address before it can connect. Without DNS you would have to memorize numbers for every site you visit.

HTTP is the language web browsers and servers use to talk to each other. The browser sends a request like 'GET me this page' and the server sends back a response with the page content. It is the foundation of the World Wide Web and was created by Tim Berners-Lee.

HTTPS is HTTP with encryption added by TLS, so data traveling between your browser and a website is scrambled and private. The 'S' stands for secure. Modern browsers show a padlock for HTTPS sites and warn you when a page is plain HTTP because eavesdroppers could read it.

TLS is the technology that encrypts data sent over the internet so snoops cannot read it and tampering can be detected. It is what puts the 'S' in HTTPS. TLS replaced the older, insecure SSL, though people still loosely call certificates 'SSL certificates'.

SSL was the original encryption protocol for the web, but every version of it is now considered broken and unsafe. It was replaced by TLS. People still say 'SSL certificate' out of habit, but what actually runs today is TLS.

TCP is a network protocol that delivers data reliably and in order, like a careful courier that confirms each package arrived. If a piece of data gets lost, TCP notices and sends it again. Web browsing, email, and file downloads all rely on TCP.

UDP is a fast, no-frills network protocol that fires off data without checking whether it arrived. It is like shouting messages and not waiting for a reply. That makes it great for live video, online games, and voice calls, where speed matters more than catching every lost packet.

A packet is a small chunk of data sent across a network. Big files are chopped into many packets, each labeled with where it came from and where it is going, then reassembled at the other end. Splitting data this way lets many computers share the same wires without waiting in one long line.

A port is a numbered doorway on a computer that lets different programs share one network connection. Web traffic usually uses port 443 for HTTPS and port 80 for HTTP. Ports range from 0 to 65535, and they let your machine run a website, a game, and email all at once without mixing up the data.

Port 80 is the default doorway for plain, unencrypted HTTP web traffic. When you type a website without 'https', the browser tries port 80. Most sites now redirect port 80 visitors over to the secure port 443 instead.

Port 443 is the default doorway for secure HTTPS web traffic. Almost all modern websites use it because the data is encrypted with TLS. When you see the padlock in your browser, your connection is flowing through port 443.

A URL is the full address of something on the web, like https://example.com/page?id=5. It has parts: the scheme (https), the domain (example.com), the path (/page), and sometimes a query (?id=5). URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator.
A domain name is the readable name of a website, like wikipedia.org. People rent domain names from registrars, usually paying each year. The system that maps these names to computer addresses is DNS.

A top-level domain is the last part of a website name, like .com, .org, or .uk. Country codes such as .jp (Japan) and .de (Germany) are also TLDs. There are now hundreds of them, including fun ones like .pizza and .ninja.

A subdomain is a prefix added to a domain to organize a site, like 'mail' in mail.google.com or 'shop' in shop.example.com. The owner of a domain can create as many subdomains as they like for free. Each can point to a different server or service.

GET is an HTTP method used to ask a server for information, like fetching a web page or an image. GET requests should not change anything on the server, just retrieve data. Any extra details usually ride along in the URL's query string.

POST is an HTTP method used to send data to a server, like submitting a form or uploading a comment. Unlike GET, the data travels in the request body rather than the URL. POST is meant for actions that create or change something.

PUT is an HTTP method that replaces a resource with the data you send, or creates it if it does not exist. It is idempotent, meaning sending the same PUT twice leaves the same result. APIs use PUT to update an entire record.

PATCH is an HTTP method used to make a partial update to a resource, changing only the fields you send instead of replacing the whole thing. For example, updating just a user's email without resending their whole profile. It is more efficient than PUT for small edits.

DELETE is an HTTP method that asks a server to remove a resource, like deleting a post or a file. Like PUT, it is idempotent: deleting something that is already gone still ends with it being gone. APIs use it to clean up data.

HEAD is an HTTP method that asks for a page's headers without the actual content. It is like asking 'how big is this and when did it change?' without downloading the whole thing. Tools use it to check if a file has been updated before downloading.

OPTIONS is an HTTP method that asks a server which methods and features it supports for a given address. Browsers send an automatic OPTIONS request, called a preflight, before certain cross-site requests to check permissions. The server replies with the rules it allows.

An HTTP status code is a three-digit number a server sends to describe how a request went. They are grouped: 2xx means success, 3xx means redirect, 4xx means you made a mistake, and 5xx means the server had a problem. The famous 404 means 'not found'.

Status code 200 means OK: the request worked and the server is sending back what you asked for. It is the most common code you will see when a web page loads normally. If everything is fine, browsers do not show it to you.

Status code 301 means a page has permanently moved to a new address, and the server tells your browser where. Browsers and search engines remember the new location for next time. Websites use 301 redirects when they reorganize or switch to HTTPS.

Status code 302 means a page is temporarily somewhere else, so follow the new address but keep checking the original. Unlike a 301, browsers do not assume the move is permanent. Sites use it for things like temporary maintenance pages.

Status code 304 means 'not modified': the page has not changed since you last downloaded it, so use your cached copy. This saves bandwidth because the server skips resending content you already have. It works together with caching headers like ETag.

Status code 400 means Bad Request: the server could not understand what you sent because it was malformed. It usually points to a mistake in the request, like broken JSON or missing required fields. The fix is on the sender's side, not the server's.

Status code 401 means Unauthorized: you need to log in or provide valid credentials to access this. Despite the name, it really means 'not authenticated.' The server is saying 'who are you?' rather than 'you're not allowed.'

Status code 403 means Forbidden: the server knows who you are but you are not allowed to see this. Unlike 401, logging in differently will not help because you simply lack permission. It is the digital equivalent of a 'staff only' door.

Status code 404 means Not Found: the server has no page at the address you asked for. It is the internet's most famous error, often shown with funny custom pages. A 404 usually means a broken link or a typo in the URL.

Status code 418 means 'I'm a teapot,' a joke code from an April Fools' standard about brewing coffee. Real servers should never use it for actual work, but some sites return it for fun. It is proof that internet engineers have a sense of humor.

Status code 429 means Too Many Requests: you are sending requests faster than the server allows. This is called rate limiting, and it protects servers from being overwhelmed. The polite fix is to slow down and try again after a short wait.

Status code 500 means Internal Server Error: something broke on the server's side and it could not finish your request. It is a catch-all for unexpected crashes or bugs in the server code. There is usually nothing the user can do except wait and retry.

Status code 502 means Bad Gateway: a server acting as a middleman got a broken reply from another server behind it. It often happens when a backend service is down or overloaded. Refreshing sometimes helps once the backend recovers.

Status code 503 means Service Unavailable: the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, often due to overload or maintenance. It is meant to be temporary, and servers can include a Retry-After header telling you when to come back. It is common during traffic spikes.

HTTP headers are extra lines of information sent with requests and responses, like labels on a package. They carry details such as the content type, the browser name, cookies, and caching rules. The actual page content travels separately in the body.

The Content-Type header tells the receiver what kind of data is in the message, like text/html for a web page or application/json for data. Browsers use it to decide how to handle the content. Getting it wrong can make a page show as raw code instead of rendering.

The User-Agent header is a string your browser sends that describes what software and device you are using. Servers can read it to send a mobile-friendly page or block old browsers. For historical reasons, almost every User-Agent string still contains the word 'Mozilla.'

A cookie is a small piece of data a website stores in your browser so it can remember you between visits. Cookies keep you logged in, remember your cart, and track preferences. The server sets them with a Set-Cookie header, and your browser sends them back on future requests.

The Set-Cookie header is how a server tells your browser to store a cookie. It can include flags like Secure (only send over HTTPS), HttpOnly (hide from JavaScript), and Expires (when to delete it). These flags help protect cookies from theft.

A cache is a temporary store of data kept close by so it can be reused quickly instead of fetched again. Browsers cache images and scripts so pages load faster on your next visit. Caching saves time and reduces network traffic, but stale caches can show old content.

A CDN is a network of servers spread around the world that store copies of a website's files close to users. When you load a site, the CDN serves images and scripts from a nearby server instead of a faraway one, making pages load faster. CDNs also help absorb traffic spikes and attacks.

A load balancer spreads incoming network traffic across several servers so no single one gets overwhelmed. It is like having multiple checkout lines and a manager directing customers to the shortest one. If one server fails, the balancer simply stops sending it traffic.

A proxy server is a middleman that forwards your network requests on your behalf. It can hide your real address, filter content, or cache pages to speed things up. Schools and companies often use proxies to control and monitor internet access.

A reverse proxy sits in front of web servers and handles incoming requests for them. It can balance load, add encryption, cache responses, and shield the real servers from direct contact. Popular reverse proxies include Nginx and HAProxy.

A firewall is a security guard for a network that decides which traffic is allowed in or out based on rules. It can block connections from suspicious addresses or to risky ports. Both personal computers and big networks use firewalls to keep attackers away.

NAT lets many devices on a home network share one public internet address. Your router rewrites the addresses on outgoing packets and remembers which device they came from so replies get back to the right one. NAT is a big reason the world survived running low on IPv4 addresses.

A router is a device that forwards data between networks, choosing the best path to its destination. Your home router connects your devices to the internet and shares one connection among them. The internet is essentially a giant web of routers passing packets along.

A network switch connects devices within a single local network and forwards data only to the device it is meant for. Unlike an old hub that shouted to everyone, a switch learns which device is on each port. This makes wired networks faster and more private.

A LAN is a network that covers a small area like a home, school, or office. Devices on a LAN can share files and printers and talk to each other quickly. Your home Wi-Fi and the computers plugged into it form a LAN.

A WAN is a network that spans a large area, connecting LANs across cities or countries. The internet is the biggest WAN of all. Companies with offices in different places use WANs to link them together.

A MAC address is a unique hardware identifier burned into a device's network card, written as six pairs of hex digits like 1A:2B:3C:4D:5E:6F. While IP addresses can change, MAC addresses are meant to stay fixed for the life of the device. Switches use them to deliver data on a local network.

A DNS lookup is the process of turning a website name into its IP address. Your computer asks a resolver, which may ask several servers up the chain until it finds the answer, then caches it for next time. All of this usually finishes in a fraction of a second.

A DNS resolver is the server that does the legwork of finding a domain's IP address for you. It queries root servers, top-level servers, and the domain's own servers, then returns the answer. Your internet provider runs one, but public ones like 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1 are popular too.

Root DNS servers sit at the top of the domain name system and point resolvers toward the right top-level domain servers. There are 13 root server identities worldwide, each backed by many mirror machines. They handle the very first step of finding any website's address.

An A record is a DNS entry that maps a domain name to an IPv4 address. When you visit a site, the A record is often what tells your browser which server to connect to. The AAAA record is its IPv6 cousin.

An AAAA record is a DNS entry that maps a domain name to an IPv6 address. It works just like an A record but for the newer, longer addresses. The four A's hint that IPv6 addresses are four times the size of IPv4 ones.

A CNAME record is a DNS entry that makes one domain name an alias for another. For example, www.example.com can be a CNAME pointing to example.com so they lead to the same place. It saves you from updating addresses in two spots when the target changes.

An MX record is a DNS entry that tells the internet which servers handle email for a domain. When someone sends mail to you@example.com, their server reads the MX record to find where to deliver it. Domains can list several MX records with priorities for backups.

A TXT record is a DNS entry that holds free-form text, often used for verification and email security. Services prove you own a domain by asking you to add a specific TXT record. Email rules like SPF and DKIM also live in TXT records.

A DNS record's TTL (Time To Live) says how long resolvers should cache the answer before asking again, measured in seconds. A short TTL means changes spread quickly but creates more lookups. A long TTL is efficient but slow to update when you move servers.

A DNS cache stores recently looked-up domain addresses so your computer does not have to ask again every time. This makes browsing faster. If a site moves and your cache is stale, clearing the DNS cache forces a fresh lookup.

DNS over HTTPS (DoH) encrypts your DNS lookups by sending them inside ordinary HTTPS traffic. This hides which sites you are looking up from anyone watching the network, including your internet provider. Many modern browsers can turn it on for extra privacy.

DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypts DNS lookups using TLS on a dedicated port, keeping them private from eavesdroppers. It does a similar job to DNS over HTTPS but is easier for network administrators to identify and manage. Both fight against snooping on which websites you visit.

A TLS handshake is the quick negotiation that sets up an encrypted connection before any real data flows. The browser and server agree on encryption methods, verify the server's certificate, and create shared secret keys. TLS 1.3 made this handshake faster, often needing just one round trip.

A TLS certificate is a digital ID card that proves a website really is who it claims to be. A trusted Certificate Authority signs it after checking the owner. Your browser checks the certificate during the handshake, and shows a warning if it is expired, fake, or for the wrong site.

A Certificate Authority is a trusted organization that issues digital certificates after verifying who owns a domain. Browsers ship with a list of CAs they trust, so a certificate signed by one is accepted automatically. If a CA misbehaves, browsers can remove it from the trusted list.

Let's Encrypt is a free, automated Certificate Authority that gives websites TLS certificates at no cost. It helped make HTTPS the default across the web. Its certificates last 90 days and are usually renewed automatically by software, so site owners rarely think about them.

A public key is half of a key pair used in encryption that can be shared with anyone. Data scrambled with a public key can only be unscrambled with the matching private key. This clever trick lets strangers send secret messages without ever sharing a password.

A private key is the secret half of a cryptographic key pair that its owner must never share. It can decrypt messages locked with the matching public key and create digital signatures. If a private key leaks, attackers can impersonate its owner, so guarding it is critical.

Encryption scrambles data using a key so that only someone with the right key can read it. It protects information both while stored and while traveling across networks. Modern web traffic is encrypted by TLS, which is why outsiders cannot read your HTTPS browsing.

Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to both lock and unlock data, making it fast. Its challenge is safely sharing that key with the other side. TLS solves this by using slower public-key crypto just to agree on a symmetric key, then switching to fast symmetric encryption for the rest.

Asymmetric encryption uses a pair of keys: a public one to lock data and a private one to unlock it. It lets people who have never met exchange secrets safely. It is slower than symmetric encryption, so it is often used only to set up a shared secret, not for bulk data.

A digital signature uses a private key to prove a message really came from you and was not changed. Anyone with your public key can verify it. TLS certificates and software updates are signed this way so you can trust their source.

Hashing turns data of any size into a fixed-length fingerprint using a one-way function. The same input always gives the same hash, but you cannot reverse a hash back into the original. Websites hash passwords so that even if the database leaks, the real passwords stay hidden.

SHA-256 is a popular hashing algorithm that turns any input into a 256-bit fingerprint, written as 64 hex characters. It is used in TLS certificates, software verification, and Bitcoin. Even a tiny change in the input produces a completely different hash.

An API is a set of rules that lets one program talk to another, like a menu of requests a service accepts. Weather apps, for example, call a weather company's API to fetch forecasts. APIs let developers reuse services without knowing how they work inside.

A REST API is a common style of web API that uses HTTP methods like GET and POST on addresses representing resources. Asking GET /users/5 might return user number five. REST is popular because it is simple, predictable, and works naturally with the web.

JSON is a lightweight text format for storing and sending data, made of names and values in curly braces. It is easy for both people and computers to read, which is why most web APIs use it. Despite the name, almost every programming language can read and write JSON.

A WebSocket is a two-way connection between a browser and a server that stays open so both sides can send messages anytime. Unlike regular HTTP, where the browser must ask first, WebSockets push updates instantly. Chat apps and live games use them for real-time communication.

HTTP/2 is a faster version of HTTP that can send many requests over a single connection at once, instead of one at a time. It also compresses headers and lets servers push files before you ask. These tricks make web pages load noticeably quicker than with HTTP/1.1.

HTTP/3 is the newest version of HTTP, built on a protocol called QUIC that runs over UDP instead of TCP. This avoids a slowdown where one lost packet stalls everything, called head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 connects faster and handles shaky mobile networks better.

Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data a network connection can carry in a given time, often measured in megabits per second. Think of it as the width of a pipe: wider pipes move more water at once. High bandwidth helps with downloads and streaming many things together.

Latency is the delay between sending a request and getting a response, measured in milliseconds. Low latency feels snappy, while high latency makes things feel laggy even on a fast connection. It is limited by distance, since data cannot travel faster than the speed of light through cables.

Ping is a tool that measures how long it takes a small message to reach a computer and come back. The result, in milliseconds, tells you the latency of the connection. Gamers watch their ping closely because a high one causes lag.

Throughput is the actual amount of data successfully moved over a network in a given time, which can be lower than the theoretical bandwidth. Congestion, errors, and overhead all eat into it. It is the real-world delivery rate, while bandwidth is the maximum possible.

DHCP automatically hands out IP addresses to devices when they join a network, so you do not have to set them by hand. When your phone connects to Wi-Fi, a DHCP server lends it an address for a while. This makes networks much easier to manage.

A default gateway is the device, usually your router, that your computer sends traffic to when it needs to reach the wider internet. It is the exit door from your local network. Without a gateway, your devices could only talk to each other, not the outside world.

A subnet is a slice of a larger network, created to keep groups of devices organized and to control traffic. A subnet mask defines which part of an IP address names the network and which names the device. Splitting a big network into subnets improves performance and security.

A subnet mask is a number like 255.255.255.0 that splits an IP address into a network part and a device part. It tells a computer which addresses are on its local network and which are far away. Modern notation writes it as a slash, like /24, counting the network bits.

CIDR is a way of writing a range of IP addresses using a slash and a number, like 192.168.1.0/24. The number says how many leading bits are fixed for the network, and the rest are free for devices. CIDR made IP address allocation far more flexible and efficient.

A socket is the endpoint of a network connection in software, identified by an IP address plus a port number. Programs open sockets to send and receive data, like plugging into a phone jack. A web server listens on a socket and accepts incoming connections through it.

The TCP three-way handshake is how two computers agree to start a reliable connection. One sends SYN, the other replies SYN-ACK, and the first answers ACK, like saying 'hello,' 'hello back,' and 'great, let's talk.' Only after this dance does real data start flowing.

Packet loss happens when data sent over a network never arrives, often due to congestion, weak signals, or faulty hardware. TCP detects loss and resends, but UDP just lets it go. In games and video calls, packet loss shows up as glitches, freezes, or dropped audio.

Jitter is the variation in delay between packets arriving over a network. Even with low average latency, uneven timing can ruin a video call or game. Devices use small buffers to smooth out jitter, trading a tiny bit of delay for steadier playback.

BGP is the protocol that big networks use to share routes and decide how to send traffic across the internet. It is like the internet's map-updating system, telling routers which way to reach distant networks. A bad BGP update can accidentally take large parts of the internet offline.

A DDoS attack floods a website or server with so much fake traffic that real users cannot get through. The flood comes from many hijacked computers at once, which is what 'distributed' means. Defenses include CDNs, filtering, and rate limiting to soak up or block the junk.

Rate limiting caps how many requests a user or program can make in a set time, protecting servers from overload and abuse. When you exceed the limit, the server replies with status code 429. APIs use it to keep service fair and stable for everyone.

CORS is a browser security rule that controls whether a web page can request data from a different website. By default, browsers block cross-site requests, and the other site must send special headers to allow them. CORS prevents a sneaky page from secretly using your logged-in sessions elsewhere.

The same-origin policy is a core browser security rule that lets a page interact only with content from the same site. Two pages share an origin if their scheme, domain, and port all match. This stops a malicious page from reading data on banking sites you are logged into.

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is an attack where a hacker sneaks malicious JavaScript into a web page so it runs in other visitors' browsers. It can steal cookies or hijack accounts. Websites prevent it by carefully escaping any user-supplied text before showing it.

Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tricks your browser into making a request to a site where you are logged in, without your knowledge. Because the browser automatically sends your cookies, the action looks legitimate. Sites defend with secret tokens that an attacker cannot guess.

SQL injection is an attack where a hacker types database commands into a website's input field to trick it into running them. It can leak or destroy data if the site builds queries carelessly. The defense is parameterized queries, which keep user input separate from the command.

A man-in-the-middle attack is when someone secretly sits between you and a server, reading or changing the data you exchange. Open Wi-Fi networks make this easier. HTTPS defends against it by encrypting traffic and verifying the server's certificate so an imposter is caught.

A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a remote server, hiding your traffic from your local network and changing your apparent location. People use VPNs for privacy, security on public Wi-Fi, and reaching content from other regions. Your data still exits at the VPN server, so you have to trust that provider.

FTP is an old protocol for moving files between computers over a network. It sends data and passwords without encryption, so it is now considered insecure. Safer replacements like SFTP (which runs over SSH) are recommended instead.

SFTP transfers files securely over an SSH connection, encrypting both the files and your login. Despite the similar name, it is not just FTP with security bolted on; it is a different protocol built into SSH. It is the modern way to move files to servers safely.

SMTP is the protocol email servers use to send messages to each other across the internet. When you hit send, your mail program hands the message to an SMTP server, which relays it toward the recipient. Receiving and reading mail uses different protocols like IMAP.

IMAP is a protocol for reading email while keeping it stored on the server. Because messages stay on the server, you see the same inbox on your phone, laptop, and tablet. It lets you organize mail into folders that sync everywhere.

POP3 is an older email protocol that downloads messages to one device and often removes them from the server. That makes it awkward for checking mail on multiple devices. Most people now prefer IMAP, which keeps mail synced across all their gadgets.

Telnet is an old protocol for connecting to a remote computer's command line over a network. It sends everything, including passwords, as plain text, so it is unsafe and mostly retired. SSH replaced it for secure remote access.

Wi-Fi is a family of standards for connecting devices to a network using radio waves instead of cables. A wireless router broadcasts a signal that nearby devices join. Newer versions like Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7 deliver faster speeds and handle crowded networks better.

Ethernet is the standard for wired computer networking, using cables to connect devices to switches and routers. It is usually faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi because it avoids radio interference. The familiar rectangular network cable with a clip is an Ethernet cable.

ICMP is a helper protocol that network devices use to send status and error messages, such as 'this destination is unreachable.' The ping and traceroute tools rely on ICMP to test connections. It carries no user data, just network housekeeping information.

Traceroute is a tool that maps the path your data takes across the internet, listing each router hop and how long each took. It helps diagnose where a connection slows down or breaks. On Windows the command is tracert, and on Mac and Linux it is traceroute.

ARP is the protocol that finds the hardware MAC address matching a known IP address on a local network. A device shouts 'who has this IP?' and the owner replies with its MAC. This lets data get delivered on the local network even though it was addressed by IP.

The OSI model is a way of describing networking in seven layers, from physical cables at the bottom to applications at the top. Each layer handles one job and talks to the layers above and below it. It is mainly a teaching tool that helps people reason about where problems occur.

The TCP/IP model describes how the internet actually works using four layers: link, internet, transport, and application. It is simpler and more practical than the seven-layer OSI model. The protocols TCP, IP, and HTTP each live at different layers of this stack.

A protocol is an agreed-upon set of rules for how computers exchange information. Like a shared language, it defines the format of messages and the order they go in. HTTP, TCP, and DNS are all examples of protocols that keep the internet working together.
A bit is the smallest unit of computer data, holding either a 0 or a 1. Network speeds are measured in bits per second, while file sizes are usually measured in bytes. Eight bits make one byte.

A byte is a group of 8 bits and is the basic unit for measuring data size. One byte can store a single character like the letter A. File sizes are given in bytes, kilobytes, and megabytes, while network speeds use bits, so a connection of 8 megabits per second downloads about 1 megabyte each second.

Base64 is a way of representing binary data, like images, using only printable text characters. Email and web systems use it to safely carry binary files through channels meant for text. It is encoding, not encryption, so it hides nothing and anyone can decode it.

A query string is the part of a URL after a question mark that carries extra data, like ?search=cats&page=2. Each piece is a name and value joined by an equals sign, separated by ampersands. Servers read these to customize the response, such as filtering search results.

The HTTP body is the main content of a request or response, carried after the headers. A response body holds the actual web page or data, while a request body might carry a form's contents or uploaded JSON. GET requests usually have an empty body.

A redirect is when a server tells your browser to go to a different address instead. It is signaled by a 3xx status code and a Location header pointing to the new spot. Sites use redirects to move pages, force HTTPS, or shorten links.

Keep-alive lets a browser reuse the same network connection for several requests instead of opening a new one each time. Setting up connections is slow, so reusing them speeds up page loads. HTTP/1.1 made keep-alive the default behavior.

A MIME type is a label that describes the kind of a file, like image/png or text/html. Servers send it in the Content-Type header so browsers know how to handle the data. The same labels are used in email attachments, which is where MIME originally came from.

An ETag is a short fingerprint a server attaches to a file so the browser can ask 'has this changed?' on the next visit. If the ETag still matches, the server replies 304 Not Modified and skips resending the file. This saves bandwidth and speeds up repeat visits.

The Cache-Control header tells browsers and proxies how long they may store a response and whether they may store it at all. Values like max-age=3600 mean 'reuse this for an hour,' while no-store means 'never save this.' It is the main lever for tuning web caching.

HTTP authentication is a built-in way for servers to ask for a username and password. Basic auth sends them encoded but not encrypted, so it is only safe over HTTPS. Modern sites usually prefer tokens or login forms over this old mechanism.

A bearer token is a secret string sent in the Authorization header to prove who you are to an API. Whoever holds (bears) the token gets access, so it must be kept secret and sent only over HTTPS. APIs hand out tokens after you log in.

A JWT is a compact token that carries claims about a user, like their ID, in a signed format. It has three dot-separated parts: header, payload, and signature. Servers can verify the signature to trust the token without storing session data, but the payload is only encoded, not secret.

OAuth is a standard that lets you grant an app limited access to your account on another service without sharing your password. The 'Log in with Google' button uses OAuth. You approve specific permissions, and the app gets a token instead of your actual credentials.

A session is how a website remembers you across multiple requests during a visit. The server stores your state and gives your browser a session ID, usually in a cookie, to identify you each time. When you log out or it expires, the session ends.

An operation is idempotent if doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once. In HTTP, GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent, while POST usually is not. Idempotency matters because it lets clients safely retry a request after a network glitch.

A webhook is a way for one service to notify another instantly when something happens, by sending an HTTP request to a URL you provide. Instead of you constantly asking 'anything new?', the service pushes the news to you. Payment and chat services use webhooks to report events as they occur.

Polling is when a program repeatedly asks a server 'is there anything new?' at regular intervals. It is simple but wasteful if updates are rare, since most checks return nothing. Webhooks and WebSockets are more efficient alternatives for real-time updates.

Long polling is a trick where the browser asks the server for updates, and the server holds the request open until news arrives or a timeout hits. It mimics real-time updates over ordinary HTTP. It was popular before WebSockets became widely available.

Server-Sent Events let a server push a one-way stream of updates to the browser over a single HTTP connection. Unlike WebSockets, the flow goes only from server to browser, which suits live news feeds and notifications. The browser's EventSource object makes them easy to use.

GraphQL is a query language for APIs that lets the client ask for exactly the data it needs in one request. Instead of many REST endpoints, there is usually one, and you describe the shape of the result. This avoids over-fetching and under-fetching data.

gRPC is a fast way for programs to call functions on other servers across a network, often used between microservices. It uses HTTP/2 and a compact binary format called Protocol Buffers instead of text. This makes it efficient but harder to read by hand than JSON.

XML is a text format for storing structured data using nested tags, like <book><title>...</title></book>. It was once the standard for web APIs and config files. JSON has largely replaced it for web use because JSON is shorter and simpler.

An HTTP method, also called a verb, states what action a request wants to take, like GET to read or POST to create. The method goes at the very start of a request. Choosing the right method makes APIs predictable and lets caches and proxies behave correctly.

The Content-Length header states how many bytes the body of an HTTP message contains. It lets the receiver know exactly when the message ends. When the size is unknown ahead of time, servers use chunked transfer encoding instead.

Chunked transfer encoding lets a server send a response in pieces when it does not know the total size in advance. Each chunk states its own length, and a zero-length chunk signals the end. This lets servers start sending data before they have finished generating all of it.

The Referer header (famously misspelled in the standard) tells a server which page linked you to the current request. Sites use it for analytics and to block hotlinking of their images. For privacy, browsers now often trim or hide this header.

The Accept header lets a browser tell the server which content types it would prefer, like JSON over XML. The server then picks the best match it can provide, a process called content negotiation. There are similar headers for preferred languages and encodings.

The Host header tells the server which website you want when many sites share one IP address. Because of it, a single server can host hundreds of domains and still route each request correctly. It became required in HTTP/1.1 for exactly this reason.

Virtual hosting lets one web server run many different websites on a single machine and IP address. The server reads the Host header to decide which site's content to serve. This is why cheap shared hosting can fit thousands of small sites on one computer.

DNS spoofing, or cache poisoning, is an attack that feeds a resolver a fake answer so a domain name points to an attacker's server. Victims think they are visiting the real site but land on a fake one. DNSSEC, which digitally signs DNS records, helps prevent it.

DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records so resolvers can verify the answers really came from the right source and were not tampered with. It guards against spoofing and cache poisoning. It does not encrypt your lookups, though; that is what DNS over HTTPS does.

Anycast lets many servers around the world share one IP address, and the network routes you to the nearest one. Big DNS providers and CDNs use it so users connect to a close, fast server automatically. It also spreads out attack traffic across many locations.

Unicast is normal one-to-one network communication, where a packet goes from a single sender to a single receiver. Most internet traffic, like loading a web page, is unicast. It contrasts with broadcast (to everyone) and multicast (to a group).

Multicast sends one stream of data to a group of interested receivers at the same time, without sending a separate copy to each. It saves bandwidth for things like live video to many viewers on a local network. The internet at large rarely supports it, so streaming sites use other tricks.

A broadcast sends a message to every device on a local network at once. Protocols like ARP and DHCP use broadcasts to find or announce things. Broadcasts stay within the local network because routers do not forward them, which prevents flooding the whole internet.
