Localhost is a name that always refers to your own computer, usually the IP address 127.0.0.1. Developers use it to test websites and servers running on their own machine before sharing them. Traffic to localhost never leaves the device.

127.0.0.1 is the loopback IP address that points right back to your own computer. Connecting to it lets software talk to other programs on the same machine. The whole 127.x.x.x range is reserved for this loopback purpose.

Private IP addresses, like those starting with 192.168 or 10, are reserved for use inside home and office networks and are never routed on the public internet. Many networks reuse the same private ranges because NAT translates them to a shared public address. This stretches the limited supply of public addresses.

A public IP address is globally unique and reachable from anywhere on the internet. Your home network usually has one public address that all your devices share through NAT. Servers need a stable public IP so visitors can always find them.

Packet sniffing is capturing and inspecting the data flowing over a network. Engineers use sniffers like Wireshark to debug problems, but attackers can use them to steal unencrypted data. Encryption with HTTPS and VPNs is the main defense against malicious sniffing.

Wireshark is a popular free tool that captures and displays network packets in detail. Network engineers use it to troubleshoot connections, learn protocols, and spot problems. It shows exactly what your computer sends and receives, layer by layer.

The MTU is the largest size, in bytes, that a single network packet can be on a given link, commonly 1500 bytes for Ethernet. Data bigger than the MTU gets split into multiple packets. A mismatched MTU along the path can cause mysterious slowdowns or stalls.

Fragmentation is when a packet too big for a link's MTU gets split into smaller pieces to fit, then reassembled at the destination. It works but adds overhead and can hurt performance. Modern systems often discover the safe size ahead of time to avoid fragmenting at all.

Congestion control is how TCP avoids overwhelming the network by adjusting how fast it sends data. It starts slow, speeds up while things go well, and backs off when it detects loss. This shared politeness keeps the whole internet from collapsing under heavy traffic.

A DNS zone is the part of the domain name system that one administrator controls, holding all the records for a domain. The records live in a zone file or database on authoritative name servers. Delegating a subdomain hands control of its own zone to someone else.

An authoritative DNS server holds the official records for a domain and gives the final answer about its addresses. Resolvers ask it when their cache runs out. Domain owners point their domain at authoritative servers, often run by their DNS provider.

WHOIS is a service that looks up who registered a domain name and when it expires. It used to show owners' contact details, but privacy rules now hide most personal information. People still use it to check availability and registration dates.

A registrar is a company authorized to sell domain names to the public, like GoDaddy or Namecheap. You rent a domain through them, usually paying yearly. They submit your registration to the registry that runs the top-level domain.

HTTP pipelining was an HTTP/1.1 feature that let a browser send several requests without waiting for each reply. In practice it caused problems because a slow first response blocked the rest, so browsers disabled it. HTTP/2's multiplexing solved the goal properly instead.

Multiplexing lets many requests and responses share a single connection at the same time, interleaved together. HTTP/2 introduced it to fix HTTP/1.1's limit of one request at a time per connection. The result is faster page loads with fewer connections.

Head-of-line blocking happens when one stuck item delays everything behind it. In TCP, a single lost packet can stall all the streams sharing that connection. HTTP/3 avoids this by running over QUIC, where each stream recovers from loss independently.

A network interface, or NIC, is the hardware that connects a computer to a network, whether by cable or Wi-Fi. Each one has a MAC address and can be assigned an IP. A single computer can have several, like a wired port and a wireless adapter.

Bandwidth throttling is deliberately slowing down certain network traffic. Internet providers sometimes throttle video streaming during busy hours, and servers may throttle heavy users. The broader practice of prioritizing or limiting traffic types is called traffic shaping.

The SameSite flag on a cookie controls whether it gets sent on requests coming from other websites. Setting it to Strict or Lax helps block CSRF attacks by not leaking the cookie to cross-site requests. Modern browsers default cookies to Lax for safety.

The Secure flag on a cookie tells the browser to send it only over encrypted HTTPS connections, never plain HTTP. This stops the cookie from leaking to eavesdroppers on an insecure link. Login cookies should always have this flag set.

The HttpOnly flag on a cookie hides it from JavaScript running in the page, so it can only be sent automatically by the browser. This protects session cookies from being stolen by cross-site scripting attacks. The cookie still rides along on requests as normal.

The Connection header controls what happens to the network connection after a request, such as keeping it open for reuse or closing it. In HTTP/1.1 it commonly carries 'keep-alive.' HTTP/2 manages connections differently and no longer uses this header.

The Origin header tells a server where a cross-site request came from, listing the scheme, domain, and port but not the path. Servers check it to decide whether to allow the request under CORS rules. It helps protect users from sneaky cross-site actions.

A preflight request is an automatic OPTIONS request a browser sends before certain cross-site calls to ask permission. The server replies with which methods and headers it allows. Only if the answer is favorable does the browser send the real request.

A WebSocket connection starts as a normal HTTP request that asks to 'upgrade' to the WebSocket protocol. If the server agrees, the same connection switches over and stays open for two-way messages. This clever reuse lets WebSockets pass through ordinary web infrastructure.

Round-robin DNS lists several IP addresses for one domain and hands them out in rotation, spreading visitors across multiple servers. It is a simple, cheap form of load balancing. Its downside is that it cannot tell when a server is down.

GeoDNS gives different answers to a DNS lookup based on where the request comes from, sending users to a nearby server. A visitor in Japan might get an Asian server while one in Brazil gets a South American one. CDNs use it to keep content close to users.

TLS termination is when a load balancer or reverse proxy handles the encryption and decryption, then passes plain traffic to the servers behind it. This offloads the heavy crypto work from the application servers. The proxy must be inside a trusted network for this to stay safe.

Server Name Indication lets a browser tell a server which website it wants during the TLS handshake, before encryption hides everything. This allows many HTTPS sites with different certificates to share one IP address. Without SNI, a server could not pick the right certificate.

An HTTP trailer is a header sent after the message body rather than before it, used with chunked encoding. It is handy for values you only know once you finish generating the content, like a checksum. Trailers are rarely used and not all clients support them.

Status code 100 Continue is a hint a server sends to say 'go ahead and send the rest of your request.' A client can ask first with an Expect header before uploading a large body, so the server can reject it early if needed. This avoids wasting bandwidth on a doomed upload.

WebSocket messages travel in small units called frames, each marked with whether it is text, binary, or a control signal like ping or close. Big messages can be split across several frames. This framing lets the protocol send and receive efficiently in both directions.

Port scanning is probing a computer to see which ports are open and what services are running. Administrators use it to check their own security, but attackers use it to find weak spots. The tool nmap is the best-known port scanner.

Nmap is a free tool that scans networks to discover devices, open ports, and the services running on them. Security professionals use it to audit and harden systems. Because it can also help attackers, you should only scan networks you own or have permission to test.

HTTP/1.1 was the workhorse version of HTTP for over two decades, adding persistent connections and the required Host header. Its main weakness is handling one request at a time per connection, which slows complex pages. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 fixed that with multiplexing.

DNS prefetching is when a browser looks up the IP addresses of links on a page before you click them. By doing this work early, the actual visit feels faster. Web developers can hint at which domains to prefetch using a special link tag.

Edge computing runs code on servers physically close to users, at the 'edge' of the network, instead of in a faraway central data center. This cuts latency and speeds up responses. CDNs increasingly let developers run small programs at the edge for personalized, fast pages.

A data center is a building full of computers, called servers, that store data and run online services. Big websites and clouds run from many data centers around the world. They need huge amounts of power and cooling to keep thousands of machines running.

Cloud computing means renting computers, storage, and services over the internet instead of owning the hardware yourself. Providers like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft run giant data centers you can use on demand. It lets a small team scale up to millions of users quickly.

Flushing the DNS cache clears the stored domain-to-address lookups on your computer, forcing fresh queries. It helps when a site has moved servers but you still reach the old one. On Windows you run ipconfig /flushdns, and Macs and Linux have their own commands.

The Upgrade header asks a server to switch the current connection to a different protocol, such as turning an HTTP connection into a WebSocket. If the server agrees, it replies with status 101 Switching Protocols. This is how WebSockets bootstrap over normal HTTP.

Status code 101 Switching Protocols means the server has agreed to change to a new protocol the client requested. It is most often seen when an HTTP connection upgrades to a WebSocket. After the 101, the connection no longer speaks plain HTTP.

The X-Forwarded-For header records the original visitor's IP address when a request passes through a proxy or load balancer. Without it, the server would only see the proxy's address. Servers use it for logging and geolocation, but it can be faked, so they trust it only from known proxies.

HSTS is a header that tells browsers to always use HTTPS for a site, even if a link says plain HTTP. Once set, the browser refuses insecure connections to that site for a set time. This protects against attackers trying to downgrade a connection to unencrypted HTTP.

A Content Security Policy is a header that tells the browser which sources of scripts, images, and styles a page may load. By blocking everything else, it limits the damage of cross-site scripting attacks. Developers tune the policy to allow only their trusted sources.

URL encoding replaces characters that are unsafe in a web address with a percent sign and a code, like turning a space into %20. This lets URLs carry spaces, symbols, and non-English text safely. Browsers and servers encode and decode it automatically.

An API endpoint is a specific URL where an API offers a particular function or piece of data, like /weather or /users/5. Each endpoint accepts certain HTTP methods and returns a response. Developers read an API's documentation to learn its endpoints.

An API key is a secret string that identifies and authorizes a program using an API. The service uses it to track usage, enforce limits, and bill if needed. Keys should be kept secret and never put in public code, since anyone with the key can use the service as you.

HTTP compression shrinks responses before sending them, so pages download faster. The server and browser agree on a method like gzip or Brotli using the Accept-Encoding and Content-Encoding headers. Text such as HTML and JavaScript can shrink dramatically, often by 70 percent or more.

Brotli is a modern compression method made by Google that often shrinks web text smaller than the older gzip. Browsers and servers negotiate it through HTTP headers. It is especially good at compressing the kinds of text used on web pages.

A bare domain like example.com (the apex) traditionally needs an A record pointing to an IP, because CNAMEs are not allowed there. Subdomains like www can use a CNAME to alias another name. Some DNS providers offer special 'ALIAS' or 'flattening' records to work around the apex limit.

A hop is each step a packet takes as it passes through one router on its way to the destination. The number of hops shows how many routers stand between you and a server. Each hop adds a little delay, which is why faraway sites tend to feel slower.

DNS supports many record types, each holding a different kind of information about a domain. Common ones are A and AAAA for addresses, MX for mail, CNAME for aliases, TXT for text, and NS for which servers are authoritative. Each answers a specific question about the domain.

An NS record names the authoritative servers responsible for a domain or subdomain. When you set up a domain, you point its NS records at your DNS provider's servers. Resolvers follow NS records to find where the real answers live.

The SOA record holds administrative details about a DNS zone, like the main name server, the admin's contact, and how often secondary servers should refresh. Every zone has exactly one SOA record at its top. It is the bookkeeping entry that keeps a zone running smoothly.

A PTR record does reverse DNS, mapping an IP address back to a domain name. Mail servers often check it to help confirm a sender is legitimate. It is the opposite direction of the usual name-to-address lookup.

An SPF record is a DNS TXT entry listing which servers are allowed to send email for a domain. Receiving servers check it to fight forged 'from' addresses and spam. It is one of three common email authentication methods, alongside DKIM and DMARC.

DKIM adds a digital signature to outgoing email, and the matching public key lives in the sender's DNS. Receiving servers verify the signature to confirm the message was not altered and really came from that domain. It works with SPF and DMARC to fight email forgery.

DMARC is an email policy, published in DNS, that tells receiving servers what to do when a message fails SPF or DKIM checks, such as reject it or mark it spam. It also sends reports back to the domain owner about abuse. Together these three guard against email spoofing.

Bandwidth and latency measure different things: bandwidth is how much data fits through at once, while latency is how long the first bit takes to arrive. A satellite link can have huge bandwidth yet high latency, feeling sluggish to click. For snappy web browsing, low latency often matters more than raw bandwidth.

Connection pooling keeps a set of network connections open and reuses them for many requests, instead of opening a fresh one each time. Because setting up connections is slow, pooling boosts performance for busy clients and servers. Databases and HTTP clients both commonly use pools.

REST uses many fixed endpoints and standard HTTP methods, while GraphQL uses one endpoint where the client describes exactly what data it wants. REST is simpler and caches easily; GraphQL avoids over-fetching but is more complex. Many modern apps mix both depending on the need.

A stateless protocol treats each request as independent, with the server keeping no memory of previous ones. HTTP is stateless, which is why cookies and tokens exist to recreate a sense of continuity. Statelessness makes servers easier to scale because any server can handle any request.

A stateful protocol keeps track of the conversation, remembering context between messages. TCP is stateful because it tracks which packets arrived and what comes next. Stateful systems can feel more natural but are harder to scale than stateless ones.

HTTP sends data as plain text anyone on the network could read, while HTTPS encrypts it with TLS so it stays private and tamper-proof. HTTPS also verifies you are talking to the real site, not an imposter. Today browsers treat plain HTTP as insecure and flag it with a warning.

A protocol stack is the set of networking protocols working in layers, each handling one job and relying on the one below. For the web, HTTP rides on TLS, which rides on TCP, which rides on IP. Stacking like this lets each layer be improved without rewriting the others.

In a recursive DNS query, your resolver does all the work and hands back the final answer. In an iterative query, each server replies with a referral pointing closer to the answer, and the asker follows the trail. Resolvers usually use iteration to talk to the chain of authoritative servers.

Cache busting forces browsers to fetch a fresh file instead of an old cached copy, usually by changing the file's name or adding a version number to the URL. When you update a script, a new name like app.v2.js sidesteps the cache. This is how sites push updates that take effect immediately.

Regular HTTP works in single request-and-response pairs where the browser must always ask first. A WebSocket keeps one connection open so the server can also push messages whenever it wants. That makes WebSockets ideal for chat, games, and live dashboards.

A web server is software that listens for HTTP requests and sends back web pages, images, or data. Popular ones include Nginx, Apache, and Caddy. The same word also describes the physical computer running that software.

Nginx (said 'engine-x') is a fast, widely used web server that also works as a reverse proxy and load balancer. It is known for handling huge numbers of connections efficiently. Many large websites put Nginx in front of their applications.

Apache is one of the oldest and most popular web servers, powering a large share of the internet for decades. It is highly configurable through modules and .htaccess files. Nginx has overtaken it in some areas, but Apache remains widely used.

Caddy is a modern web server famous for setting up HTTPS automatically, fetching and renewing TLS certificates with no manual steps. This makes secure sites simple for beginners. It uses a clean, short configuration file.

Ports from 0 to 1023 are called well-known ports and are reserved for standard services like HTTP on 80 and SSH on 22. Ports 1024 to 49151 are registered for specific apps, and the rest are free for temporary use. This numbering keeps services easy to find.

An ephemeral port is a temporary, high-numbered port your computer picks for the client side of a connection. When you load a website, your browser uses a random ephemeral port while the server stays on port 443. The port is released once the connection closes.

Network byte order is the agreed way to arrange the bytes of numbers sent over a network, specifically big-endian (most significant byte first). Computers store numbers in different orders internally, so they convert to this standard before sending. This ensures both sides interpret the numbers the same way.

The Expect header lets a client check with the server before sending a big request body, typically with the value '100-continue.' The server replies 100 Continue if it is willing to receive it, or an error to reject it early. This saves bandwidth on uploads that would be refused anyway.

A glue record is an extra DNS entry that gives the IP address of a name server when that server lives inside the very domain it serves. Without glue, a resolver would get stuck in a loop trying to look up the server's address. Glue records break that chicken-and-egg problem.

A network packet has two main parts: a header carrying control information like source and destination addresses, and a payload holding the actual data. As a packet moves down the protocol stack, each layer wraps it with its own header. Routers read these headers to decide where to forward it.

Encapsulation in networking means wrapping data with headers as it moves down the protocol layers, like putting a letter in nested envelopes. Your HTTP data gets a TCP header, then an IP header, then a link-layer frame. At the destination, each layer peels off its own header.

collections.Counter is a dict subclass for counting hashable items. Counter('banana') gives Counter({'a':3,'n':2,'b':1}), and .most_common(2) returns the two highest counts as (item, count) pairs. Missing keys return 0 instead of raising KeyError, so you can do counts[x] += 1 without checking first.

collections.defaultdict takes a factory function and calls it to create a default value the first time you access a missing key. defaultdict(list) lets you do d[key].append(x) without first creating the list. The factory is called with no arguments, so use int for 0, list for [], or set for an empty set.

collections.deque is a double-ended queue with O(1) appends and pops from both ends, unlike a list which is O(n) to pop from the front. Use append/appendleft and pop/popleft. Passing maxlen makes it a sliding window that automatically drops items from the opposite end when full.

collections.OrderedDict remembers insertion order and adds methods regular dicts lack, like move_to_end() and a popitem(last=False) that pops from the front. Since Python 3.7 plain dicts also preserve insertion order, so OrderedDict is now mainly useful for those extra methods and for order-sensitive equality comparisons.

collections.namedtuple builds a lightweight tuple subclass whose fields have names. Point = namedtuple('Point', 'x y') lets you write p.x instead of p[0], while staying a real tuple that is immutable and unpackable. The ._replace() method returns a new instance with some fields changed, and ._asdict() converts it to a dict.

collections.ChainMap groups several dicts into one view without copying them. Lookups search the maps in order and return the first hit, which is handy for layering defaults under overrides. Writes go to the first map only, and .new_child() pushes a fresh writable layer on top.

enumerate(iterable) yields (index, item) pairs so you can loop with a counter without managing one by hand. Pass a second argument to set the starting number, like enumerate(items, start=1). It is lazier and cleaner than 'for i in range(len(items))' and avoids off-by-one mistakes.

zip(a, b) pairs items from multiple iterables, stopping at the shortest one. It returns a lazy iterator, so wrap it in list() to see the pairs. The clever zip(*matrix) idiom transposes rows into columns, and dict(zip(keys, values)) builds a dict from two parallel sequences.

itertools.zip_longest pairs iterables but keeps going until the longest one is exhausted, filling missing values with fillvalue (default None). zip_longest('AB', '12345', fillvalue='-') keeps all five items. It is the opposite of plain zip, which stops at the shortest iterable.

itertools.chain(a, b, c) flattens several iterables into one continuous stream without building a big intermediate list. chain.from_iterable(list_of_lists) flattens one level of nesting and is the lazy way to merge many sequences. It works on any iterables, including generators and ranges.

itertools.count(start, step) is an infinite counter that yields start, start+step, and so on forever. It is useful with zip to attach numbers to an iterable or as the default in enumerate-like code. Because it never stops on its own, pair it with islice or a break to avoid an infinite loop.

itertools.cycle(iterable) repeats its items endlessly: cycle('ABC') yields A, B, C, A, B, C forever. It caches the items, so it works even if the source iterable is one-shot. Use it for round-robin assignment, alternating colors, or repeating patterns, always with a stop condition.

itertools.repeat(value, times) yields the same value over and over, either forever or a fixed number of times. A common use is repeat(0, 5) to feed a constant into map or zip. repeat with no count is sometimes faster than a range when you only need a fixed number of loop iterations.

itertools.islice(iterable, stop) or islice(iterable, start, stop, step) slices any iterator, including infinite ones, without supporting negative indices. It is the lazy equivalent of list[start:stop] and never builds the whole sequence. islice(count(), 10) safely takes the first ten numbers from an infinite counter.

itertools.product(a, b) yields every combination of one item from each iterable, like nested for loops. product(range(2), repeat=3) generates all 3-bit binary tuples. It is the tool for enumerating grids, coordinate spaces, or every setting combination without writing deeply nested loops.

itertools.permutations(iterable, r) yields all ordered arrangements of length r, treating positions as distinct. permutations('ABC', 2) gives AB, AC, BA, BC, CA, CB. With no r it uses the full length, so the count grows as a factorial and gets huge fast.

itertools.combinations(iterable, r) yields all unordered selections of r items, so AB and BA count as one. combinations('ABCD', 2) gives AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD. Use combinations_with_replacement when an item may be picked more than once.

itertools.groupby groups consecutive equal items, so you almost always sort by the same key first. It yields (key, group) pairs where group is a one-shot iterator you must consume before moving on. Unlike SQL GROUP BY it only groups runs that are next to each other, not all matching items everywhere.

itertools.accumulate(iterable) yields a running total: accumulate([1,2,3,4]) gives 1, 3, 6, 10. Pass a two-argument function as the func argument to do running max, product, or any fold, like accumulate(data, max) for a running maximum. An optional initial argument seeds the first value.

itertools.starmap(func, iterable) is like map but unpacks each item as arguments, so starmap(pow, [(2,3),(2,10)]) computes pow(2,3) and pow(2,10). Use it when your data is already a list of argument tuples. It is the natural partner of functions that take several positional arguments.

itertools.takewhile(predicate, iterable) yields items only until the predicate first returns False, then stops completely. takewhile(lambda x: x < 5, [1,2,6,1]) yields just 1 and 2. Its mirror image is dropwhile, which skips the leading run and yields everything after.

itertools.dropwhile(predicate, iterable) skips items while the predicate is True, then yields every remaining item even if some later ones would match. dropwhile(lambda x: x < 5, [1,2,6,1]) yields 6 and 1. It pairs with takewhile to split a sequence at its first turning point.

itertools.tee(iterable, n) splits one iterator into n independent ones that can be advanced separately. It buffers items that one branch has seen but another has not, so it can use a lot of memory if the branches drift far apart. Once you tee an iterator, do not use the original.

functools.reduce(func, iterable, initial) folds a sequence into one value by repeatedly applying a two-argument function. reduce(lambda a,b: a*b, [1,2,3,4]) computes 24. Python pushed it into functools because explicit loops or sum/math.prod are usually clearer, but it shines for custom accumulations.

functools.partial(func, *args, **kwargs) returns a new callable with some arguments pre-filled. partial(int, base=2) makes a binary parser you can hand to map. It is a clean alternative to a one-line lambda when you just want to lock in a few arguments of an existing function.

functools.lru_cache is a decorator that memoizes a function's results keyed by its arguments, dramatically speeding up repeated or recursive calls. Set maxsize to bound the cache or maxsize=None for unbounded. The arguments must be hashable, and you can inspect hits and misses with the wrapped function's cache_info().

functools.cache, added in Python 3.9, is a simpler unbounded memoizer equivalent to lru_cache(maxsize=None). It never evicts entries, so it is ideal for pure functions with a small, fixed set of inputs like fibonacci numbers. Because it grows forever, avoid it on functions called with endlessly varying arguments.

functools.wraps is a decorator used inside your own decorators to copy the original function's name, docstring, and metadata onto the wrapper. Without it, the decorated function reports the wrapper's name and loses its help text. Apply @wraps(func) to the inner wrapper function to fix this.

functools.cached_property turns a method into an attribute that is computed once on first access and then stored on the instance, so later reads are free. Unlike property it has no setter and caches per instance. Use it for expensive derived values that do not change after the object is built.

functools.singledispatch lets one function behave differently based on the type of its first argument, a form of overloading. Decorate the base function, then register type-specific versions with @func.register. It is a clean way to add type-based branching without a chain of isinstance checks.

functools.total_ordering is a class decorator that fills in the missing comparison operators from the ones you define. Provide __eq__ plus one of __lt__, __le__, __gt__, or __ge__ and it generates the rest. It saves boilerplate, though hand-written comparisons can be faster if performance matters.

functools.cmp_to_key converts an old-style comparison function that returns -1, 0, or 1 into a key function usable by sorted and list.sort. Python 3 removed the cmp argument, so this bridges code that genuinely needs pairwise comparison logic. For most sorts a plain key function is simpler and faster.

pathlib.Path is the modern object-oriented way to handle file paths, replacing most os.path string juggling. The / operator joins paths, like Path('logs') / 'today.txt', and methods like .exists(), .read_text(), .glob(), and .parent read clearly. Paths work across operating systems and convert to strings automatically when needed.

Path.read_text() reads an entire file into a string in one call and Path.write_text(data) writes one, both handling open and close for you. They take an optional encoding argument; default to encoding='utf-8' to avoid platform surprises. For binary data use read_bytes() and write_bytes() instead.

Path('.').glob('*.py') lazily yields matching files in a directory, and rglob('*.py') searches recursively through subfolders. They return Path objects, not strings, so you can chain more path methods. Use them instead of manually walking directories for simple pattern-based file finding.

Path('a/b/c').mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates a directory and any missing parents without raising if it already exists. Without parents=True it errors when intermediate folders are missing, and without exist_ok=True it errors if the target exists. This one line replaces a common try/except around os.makedirs.

os.path.join('folder', 'file.txt') builds a path using the correct separator for the current OS, so you avoid hardcoding slashes. If a later argument is absolute it discards everything before it. Modern code often prefers pathlib's / operator, but os.path.join is still everywhere in older codebases.

os.environ is a dict-like mapping of environment variables. Use os.environ.get('API_KEY') to read one safely without a KeyError, or os.getenv('PORT', '8000') to supply a default. Changes you make affect only the current process and its children, not the parent shell.

os.walk(top) yields (dirpath, dirnames, filenames) tuples as it descends a directory tree. You can prune the walk by mutating the dirnames list in place to skip folders you do not want to enter. For simpler recursive matching, Path.rglob is often more readable.

shutil offers high-level file operations: copy and copy2 duplicate a file (copy2 also preserves metadata), move relocates files or directories, and copytree clones a whole folder. rmtree deletes a directory and everything in it, so use it carefully. These wrap the low-level os calls with sensible behavior.

The tempfile module creates secure temporary files and directories. NamedTemporaryFile gives a file with a real name on disk, TemporaryDirectory makes a folder, and both clean themselves up as context managers. They place files in the system temp location and avoid race conditions that hand-rolled temp names suffer from.

json.dumps(obj) serializes a Python object to a JSON string, while json.dump writes directly to a file. Use indent=2 for pretty output, sort_keys=True for stable ordering, and ensure_ascii=False to keep non-ASCII characters readable. Pass a default function to handle types JSON does not know, like datetime.

json.loads(text) parses a JSON string into Python objects, and json.load reads from a file. JSON objects become dicts, arrays become lists, true/false become booleans, and null becomes None. Invalid JSON raises json.JSONDecodeError, which carries the line and column where parsing failed.

csv.reader wraps an open file and yields each row as a list of strings, correctly handling quoted fields and embedded commas. Always open the file with newline='' so the csv module controls line endings. For large files it streams row by row instead of loading everything into memory.

csv.DictReader reads each row into a dict keyed by the header row, so you access columns by name like row['price'] instead of row[2]. Its partner DictWriter writes dicts back out and needs a fieldnames list plus a writeheader() call. This makes column order changes far less likely to break your code.

datetime.now() returns the current local date and time as a naive datetime with no timezone attached. For timezone-aware UTC, prefer datetime.now(timezone.utc). Naive datetimes are a common bug source because comparing them with aware ones raises a TypeError.

strftime formats a datetime into a string using directives like %Y for four-digit year, %m for month, %d for day, %H:%M:%S for time. Its inverse, strptime, parses a string into a datetime given the same format. For machine-readable output, .isoformat() produces a standard ISO 8601 string.

datetime.timedelta represents a span of time and supports arithmetic, so datetime.now() + timedelta(days=7) gives next week. You can build one from days, hours, minutes, seconds, and more, and subtracting two datetimes yields a timedelta. Read .total_seconds() to get the whole duration as a float.

The zoneinfo module, added in Python 3.9, provides real IANA time zones from the system database. ZoneInfo('America/New_York') attaches a zone that handles daylight saving automatically. It replaced the need for the third-party pytz library in the standard library for most use cases.

re.match only succeeds if the pattern matches at the very start of the string, while re.search scans the whole string for the first match anywhere. A frequent bug is using match when you meant search and wondering why a mid-string pattern fails. re.fullmatch requires the pattern to cover the entire string.

re.findall(pattern, text) returns a list of all non-overlapping matches. With no groups it returns the matched strings, with one group it returns that group's captures, and with multiple groups it returns tuples. For match objects with positions, use re.finditer instead, which yields lazily.

re.sub(pattern, replacement, text) replaces all matches and returns a new string. The replacement can reference groups with \1 or \g<name>, or be a function that receives each match object and returns its replacement. Pass count to limit how many substitutions happen.

re.compile(pattern) builds a reusable regex object so you do not recompile the pattern on every call. Pass flags like re.IGNORECASE or re.MULTILINE here, or inline them as (?i) at the start of the pattern. Compiling helps readability and speed when a pattern is used many times in a loop.

Always write regular expressions as raw strings like r'\d+' so backslashes reach the regex engine instead of being interpreted as Python escapes. Without the r prefix, '\d' may trigger a warning and patterns with many backslashes become unreadable. Raw strings make regex code far less error-prone.

The with statement guarantees cleanup by calling a context manager's __enter__ on entry and __exit__ on exit, even if an exception is raised. The classic case is 'with open(path) as f:' which always closes the file. Many resources like locks, database connections, and temp files use this pattern.

The contextlib.contextmanager decorator turns a generator into a context manager. Code before the single yield runs on enter, the yielded value is what 'as' binds to, and code after yield runs on exit. Put that cleanup in a finally block so it runs even when the body raises.

contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError) is a context manager that silently ignores the listed exception types inside its block. It is a cleaner replacement for a try/except that just passes. Be careful to suppress only specific exceptions so you do not hide real bugs.

contextlib.ExitStack lets you enter a variable number of context managers and guarantees all of them are cleaned up in reverse order. It is perfect when you open an unknown number of files or want to register cleanup callbacks dynamically with callback(). This avoids deeply nested with statements.

A list comprehension builds a list from an iterable in one expression: [x*x for x in range(5)]. Add a filter with an if at the end, like [x for x in nums if x > 0], and use nested for clauses to flatten. They are usually clearer and a bit faster than an equivalent append loop.

A dict comprehension builds a dict directly: {k: v for k, v in pairs}. A common pattern inverts a dict with {v: k for k, v in d.items()} or filters one with a trailing if clause. It reads more clearly than building an empty dict and assigning keys in a loop.

A set comprehension uses braces and produces a set with duplicates removed: {word.lower() for word in words}. It is handy for collecting unique values while transforming them. Note that {} alone is an empty dict, not an empty set; use set() for that.

A generator expression looks like a comprehension but uses parentheses and produces items lazily one at a time, using little memory. sum(x*x for x in range(1000000)) never builds the full list. When a genexp is the only argument to a function, you can drop the extra parentheses.

A function containing yield is a generator: calling it returns an iterator and the body pauses at each yield, resuming where it left off on the next request. This lets you produce values lazily and even infinitely without building a list. State is preserved between resumes automatically.

yield from sub_iterable delegates to another generator or iterable, yielding all its values as if inline. It also forwards sent values and return results, making it the clean way to chain or compose generators. yield from flatten(sublist) recursively flattens nested structures with little code.

A generator's send(value) method resumes it and makes the paused yield expression evaluate to value, enabling two-way communication. The first call must be send(None) or next() to advance to the first yield. This powers coroutine-style patterns, though async/await has largely replaced manual use.

Starred assignment captures the leftover items into a list: first, *middle, last = [1,2,3,4,5] gives middle == [2,3,4]. Only one star target is allowed per assignment. This is cleaner than slicing when you want the ends and the middle separately.

In a function signature, *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. At a call site the same syntax unpacks: func(*my_list, **my_dict) spreads a list and dict into arguments. The names args and kwargs are convention, not required.

Putting a bare * in a function signature forces every parameter after it to be passed by keyword, like def connect(host, *, timeout=30). This prevents callers from passing options positionally and makes calls self-documenting. A bare / does the opposite, marking earlier parameters as positional-only.

A mutable default argument like def add(item, target=[]) is evaluated once when the function is defined, so the same list is shared across calls and accumulates surprises. The fix is to default to None and create a fresh list inside: target = target or []. This is one of Python's most famous gotchas.

str.join builds one string from an iterable of strings: ', '.join(['a','b','c']) gives 'a, b, c'. The separator is the string you call it on, which trips up beginners who expect list.join. Joining is far faster than repeated += concatenation in a loop because it allocates the result once.

str.split() with no arguments splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty pieces, which is what you usually want for tokenizing text. With an argument it splits on that exact separator, keeping empties. Pass maxsplit to limit splits, and use rsplit to count from the right.

str.strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace; lstrip and rstrip handle one side. Passing a string argument strips any of those characters, not the literal string, so 'xxhelloxx'.strip('x') gives 'hello'. To remove a known prefix or suffix exactly, use removeprefix and removesuffix instead.

str.removeprefix and str.removesuffix, added in Python 3.9, strip an exact leading or trailing string and return the rest, or the original if it does not match. 'test_run.py'.removesuffix('.py') gives 'test_run'. They fix the old bug of using strip(), which removes characters in any order, not a literal substring.

str.format inserts values into placeholders: '{} is {}'.format(name, age). You can use positional indexes like {0}, named fields like {name}, and format specs like {:.2f} for two decimals or {:,} for thousands separators. F-strings now cover most cases more concisely.

An f-string is a string literal prefixed with f where {expr} is evaluated inline: f'{name} scored {score:.1f}'. Since Python 3.8, the {value=} form prints both the expression text and its value, which is great for debugging. F-strings are the fastest and most readable way to format in modern Python.

Strings have predicate methods like isdigit, isalpha, isalnum, isspace, and isupper that return True only if every character qualifies and the string is non-empty. They are handy quick checks before parsing. Beware that isdigit accepts some exotic numeric Unicode characters, so use a try/except int() for strict integer validation.

enum.Enum creates a set of named constant members, so Color.RED is clearer and safer than a bare string or integer. Members have .name and .value, are singletons you can compare with 'is', and iterate in definition order. Enums prevent typos that plain string flags allow.

enum.IntEnum members are also real integers, so they compare and sort like numbers while keeping readable names. This is useful for HTTP status codes or priority levels that must interoperate with code expecting ints. Use plain Enum when you want to avoid accidental integer arithmetic on the members.

enum.auto() assigns the next automatic value to an enum member so you do not hand-number them. By default it produces 1, 2, 3, and you can override _generate_next_value_ to control the scheme. It keeps enums tidy when the actual values do not matter, only the names do.

The @dataclass decorator auto-generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from class-level annotated fields, cutting boilerplate. Use field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults to avoid the shared-default trap. Options like frozen=True make instances immutable and hashable, and order=True adds comparison methods.

In a dataclass, dataclasses.field customizes a single field. Use default_factory=list or dict for mutable defaults since a plain default would be shared across instances. Set field(repr=False) to hide it from the generated repr, or field(compare=False) to exclude it from equality checks.

dataclasses.asdict(instance) recursively converts a dataclass and any nested dataclasses into plain dicts, which is handy for JSON serialization. astuple does the same into nested tuples. Both make deep copies, so they are not free for large structures, but they save you writing conversion code by hand.

typing.Optional[int] means a value is either an int or None, and is exactly equal to Union[int, None]. Since Python 3.10 you can write int | None instead. It documents that None is an allowed value, which type checkers like mypy enforce, catching missing None checks.

A Union type means a value may be any of several types. The modern syntax is int | str | None, while older code uses typing.Union[int, str, None]. Type checkers then require you to narrow the type with isinstance before using type-specific operations, catching a class of bugs early.

You can annotate collections with their contents: list[int], dict[str, float], tuple[int, ...]. Since Python 3.9 the built-in types support this directly, so you rarely need typing.List or typing.Dict anymore. These annotations are checked by tools like mypy but ignored at runtime.

Type hints annotate variables, parameters, and return values, like def greet(name: str) -> str. Python does not enforce them at runtime, but tools like mypy and editors use them to catch bugs and offer better autocomplete. They serve as living documentation that cannot drift out of date silently.

typing.Any is an escape hatch that tells the type checker to allow any operation on a value, effectively turning off checking for it. It differs from object, which only allows operations valid on every type. Overusing Any defeats the purpose of type hints, so reach for it sparingly.

typing.Callable annotates function-valued parameters. Callable[[int, str], bool] means a function taking an int and a str and returning a bool, and Callable[..., None] allows any arguments. It documents the expected signature of callbacks so type checkers can verify how you call them.

typing.Literal restricts a value to specific constants, like Literal['r', 'w', 'a'] for a file mode. The type checker then flags any other string at call sites. It is a lightweight way to express a small fixed set of allowed values without defining a full Enum.

typing.TypedDict describes the expected keys and value types of a dictionary used like a record. It lets type checkers verify dict-shaped data, such as parsed JSON, without converting it into a class. Mark keys as not required with total=False or NotRequired for optional fields.

typing.Protocol enables structural typing, also called duck typing for type checkers: any object with the right methods satisfies the Protocol without inheriting from it. Define the expected methods, and a parameter typed as that Protocol accepts any matching object. It captures 'has these methods' rather than 'is this class'.

Inheriting from abc.ABC and decorating methods with @abstractmethod makes a class that cannot be instantiated until all abstract methods are implemented in a subclass. This enforces an interface contract at instantiation time. It is the explicit alternative to structural typing with Protocols.

sorted(iterable, key=func) sorts by the result of calling func on each item, not the item itself, like sorted(words, key=len). Add reverse=True to sort descending. The sort is stable, so items with equal keys keep their original order, which lets you sort by multiple criteria in stages.

To sort by several criteria, return a tuple from the key function: key=lambda p: (p.last, p.first) sorts by last name then first. For mixed ascending and descending on numbers, negate a value like key=lambda x: (-x.score, x.name). Because Python's sort is stable, you can also sort in passes from least to most significant.

operator.itemgetter(1) returns a function that grabs index 1 from each item, and itemgetter(0, 2) grabs a tuple of those positions. It is a faster, clearer key function for sorting lists of tuples or dicts than an equivalent lambda. Its sibling attrgetter does the same for object attributes.

operator.attrgetter('name') builds a function that fetches an object's name attribute, ideal as a sort or map key. attrgetter('user.name') even follows dotted paths into nested attributes. It pairs with methodcaller, which calls a named method on each item, to avoid writing repetitive lambdas.

min and max accept the same key argument as sorted, so max(people, key=lambda p: p.age) returns the oldest person, not just their age. They also take a default argument that is returned when the iterable is empty, avoiding a ValueError. Pass several positional values to compare them directly.

The bisect module does binary search on a sorted list. bisect.bisect_left finds the insertion index for a value, and bisect.insort inserts while keeping the list sorted, both in O(log n) for the search. It is the efficient way to maintain a sorted list or to map a number to a bucket boundary.

The heapq module turns a plain list into a binary min-heap. heappush and heappop keep the smallest item at index 0 with O(log n) operations, making it perfect for priority queues. nlargest and nsmallest efficiently grab the top or bottom k items, and for a max-heap you push negated values.

The array module stores numbers compactly in a typed array, using far less memory than a list of Python ints or floats. You pick a typecode like 'i' for signed int or 'd' for double. It is useful for large homogeneous numeric data when you do not want the full NumPy dependency.

Sets support fast membership tests and algebra: a | b is union, a & b is intersection, a - b is difference, and a ^ b is symmetric difference. Use a <= b to test subset. Converting two lists to sets and intersecting is the quick way to find common elements.

frozenset is an immutable set, so it is hashable and can be a dictionary key or an element of another set. Build one with frozenset(iterable). Use it when you need a fixed set of items as a key, such as caching results by the set of arguments regardless of order.

dict.get(key, default) returns the value for a key or the default instead of raising KeyError when the key is missing. dict.setdefault(key, default) goes further by inserting the default if absent and returning it, which is handy for building lists per key. For counting, Counter or defaultdict is usually cleaner.

dict.setdefault(key, default) returns the existing value if the key is present, otherwise it inserts default and returns that. It lets you group items in one line: d.setdefault(k, []).append(v). A defaultdict often reads more clearly when every access should create a default.

Since Python 3.9 the | operator merges dicts into a new one and |= updates in place: defaults | overrides keeps the right-hand values on key clashes. Before 3.9 you used {**a, **b} unpacking. Both create shallow copies, so nested mutable values are shared.

dict.keys(), .values(), and .items() return live view objects that reflect later changes to the dict and support set-like operations on keys. Iterating items() is the idiomatic way to loop over key-value pairs. Avoid adding or removing keys while iterating a view, which raises a RuntimeError.

To invert a dict you can write {v: k for k, v in d.items()}, but remember that duplicate values collapse since keys must be unique. If multiple keys share a value and you need to keep them all, build a defaultdict(list) and append. Inversion only round-trips cleanly when values are unique and hashable.

The walrus operator := assigns a value as part of a larger expression, added in Python 3.8. It shines in while loops, like while (line := f.readline()):, and in comprehensions to avoid computing something twice. Use it sparingly, since overuse can hurt readability.

Python's conditional expression is value_if_true if condition else value_if_false, like status = 'ok' if code == 200 else 'error'. It is an expression, so it can appear inside a comprehension or a function argument where a statement cannot. Avoid nesting them deeply, which quickly becomes unreadable.

The match statement, added in Python 3.10, does structural pattern matching. case clauses can match literals, destructure tuples and lists, bind names, match dataclass or dict shapes, and add an if guard. A bare case _ is the wildcard catch-all. It is far more powerful than a chain of if/elif.

EAFP, 'easier to ask forgiveness than permission', is the Pythonic style of trying an operation and catching the exception, rather than LBYL, 'look before you leap', which checks conditions first. try/except avoids race conditions, like a file being deleted between a check and a read. Both have their place, but EAFP is idiomatic in Python.

A try block can have except clauses for errors, an else clause that runs only if no exception occurred, and a finally clause that always runs for cleanup. Putting code in else instead of the try body narrows what the except actually guards. finally runs even if you return or re-raise inside the try.

raise NewError('context') from original_error explicitly chains exceptions, so the traceback shows the new error was caused by the original. Without 'from', Python still shows the implicit chain when an exception happens during handling. Use 'from None' to deliberately suppress the original cause.

Define custom exceptions by subclassing Exception, like class ConfigError(Exception): pass, to give callers precise types to catch. Group related errors under a common base class so users can catch the whole family. Avoid inheriting from BaseException, which is reserved for things like KeyboardInterrupt that should not be casually caught.

Python 3.11 added ExceptionGroup to bundle multiple exceptions raised together, common in concurrent code. The new except* syntax catches and handles a specific type from within the group while leaving others to propagate. This solves the old problem of only being able to surface one error from many parallel tasks.

assert condition, message raises AssertionError if the condition is false, used for sanity checks during development. Crucially, assertions are stripped when Python runs with the -O optimization flag, so never use them for validating untrusted input or enforcing security. Reserve them for invariants you believe are always true.

The logging module is the standard way to emit diagnostic messages, far better than scattering print calls. It has levels DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL, and you control which appear with a single configuration call. Use logging.getLogger(__name__) per module so output is organized and filterable.

Logging levels rank severity: DEBUG for detailed tracing, INFO for normal events, WARNING for unexpected but recoverable situations, ERROR for failures, and CRITICAL for the worst. Setting the logger's level to WARNING, for example, suppresses DEBUG and INFO. Choosing the right level keeps logs useful instead of noisy.

Pass log arguments separately, like logger.info('user %s did %s', user, action), instead of pre-formatting with an f-string. The logging module only builds the message string if that level is actually enabled, saving work for suppressed debug logs. It also lets log aggregators group messages by their template.

The argparse module parses command-line arguments into a tidy namespace. You add_argument for each option, declaring its type, default, and help text, then call parse_args. It auto-generates a --help message and usage errors, making it the standard choice for building real command-line tools.

sys.argv is the list of command-line arguments, where sys.argv[0] is the script name and the rest are the user's arguments as strings. It is fine for trivial scripts, but for anything with options or flags, argparse handles parsing, defaults, and help for you. Remember the arguments are always strings until you convert them.

sys.exit(code) ends the program, where 0 means success and any nonzero value signals an error to the calling shell. You can also pass a string, which is printed to stderr before exiting with code 1. It raises SystemExit, so a broad except can accidentally swallow it; catch specific exceptions instead.

The 'if __name__ == "__main__":' guard runs code only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported as a module. This lets a file act both as a reusable library and as a runnable script. It also protects against problems with multiprocessing on some platforms, which re-imports the main module.

The pickle module serializes almost any Python object to bytes and back, preserving complex structures. The big caveat is security: unpickling data can execute arbitrary code, so never unpickle anything from an untrusted source. For data shared across languages or stored long-term, prefer JSON or another safe format.

The shelve module gives you a dict-like object backed by a file on disk, so keys persist between runs. Values are pickled automatically, which means the same untrusted-data caution applies and only string keys are allowed. It is a quick way to add simple persistence without a real database.

The sqlite3 module is a full SQL database built into Python's standard library, storing everything in a single file or in memory. Use parameterized queries with ? placeholders to avoid SQL injection, never string formatting. It is perfect for local apps, prototypes, and tests that need real SQL without a server.

With sqlite3, pass values as a tuple in the second argument: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?', (uid,)). This lets the database safely handle quoting and blocks SQL injection. Never build queries by formatting strings, and remember a single-value tuple needs the trailing comma, like (uid,).

The hashlib module computes cryptographic hashes like SHA-256. Feed it bytes, not str, so encode text first: hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest(). Hashes verify integrity and are one-way. For storing passwords use a slow, salted algorithm such as the dedicated hashlib.scrypt or a library like bcrypt, never a plain fast hash.

The secrets module generates cryptographically strong random values for security purposes, unlike the random module which is predictable. secrets.token_hex() makes a random token, token_urlsafe() makes a URL-safe one, and choice() picks securely. Use it for passwords, API tokens, and reset codes.

The uuid module makes universally unique identifiers. uuid4() generates a random 128-bit ID with effectively no collision risk, ideal for database keys or filenames. uuid1() encodes the machine and time, which can leak information, so uuid4 is the usual safe default. Convert to a string with str(my_uuid).

The base64 module encodes binary data as ASCII text so it can travel through text-only channels like JSON or email. base64.b64encode takes bytes and returns bytes, with urlsafe_b64encode swapping the + and / characters for - and _. Base64 is encoding, not encryption; it provides no secrecy at all.

Format specs after a colon control number display: {:.2f} fixes two decimals, {:,} adds thousands separators, {:>10} right-aligns in ten columns, {:05d} zero-pads, and {:.1%} shows a fraction as a percent. They work in f-strings and str.format alike. Combine them, like {:>10,.2f}, for aligned currency.

The decimal module gives exact base-10 arithmetic, fixing the floating-point surprise where 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. It is the right choice for money and anything needing precise rounding. Always build Decimals from strings, like Decimal('0.1'), since a float argument carries the binary imprecision in.

The fractions module's Fraction type stores exact rational numbers, so Fraction(1, 3) + Fraction(1, 3) + Fraction(1, 3) equals exactly 1, not 0.999. It automatically reduces to lowest terms and supports normal arithmetic. Use it when you need exact ratios rather than approximate floating-point results.

The math module provides floating-point math: sqrt, sin, cos, log, exp, the constants pi and tau, and helpers like factorial, gcd, and isclose. math.isclose(a, b) is the correct way to compare floats for near-equality instead of ==. math.inf and math.nan represent infinity and not-a-number.

math.isclose(a, b) safely checks whether two floats are nearly equal, which is how you should compare floating-point results instead of ==. It uses both a relative tolerance (rel_tol) and an absolute one (abs_tol); set abs_tol when comparing values near zero. This avoids bugs from tiny rounding errors that == cannot tolerate.

The statistics module covers everyday stats without NumPy: mean, median, mode, stdev, variance, and quantiles. fmean is a faster float-only mean, and harmonic_mean and geometric_mean handle special averages. It works on any iterable of numbers and is plenty for small data analysis in scripts.

The random module generates pseudo-random numbers for simulations and games, not security. random.random() gives a float in [0,1), randint(a,b) an integer inclusive of both ends, choice picks one item, sample picks several without repeats, and shuffle reorders a list in place. For security, use the secrets module instead.

random.seed(value) makes the random sequence reproducible, so the same seed yields the same numbers every run, which is invaluable for testing and debugging simulations. Without a seed, Python seeds from the system time and OS entropy. Note seeding the global generator affects every later random call in the program.

string.Template offers simple $-based substitution, like Template('Hi $name').substitute(name='Sam'). It is less powerful than f-strings but safer for user-supplied templates because it cannot execute arbitrary code or access attributes. safe_substitute leaves unknown placeholders untouched instead of raising.

The textwrap module reflows and reformats plain text. wrap returns a list of lines fit to a width, fill returns them joined, dedent removes common leading whitespace (great for triple-quoted strings in code), and shorten truncates with an ellipsis. It is handy for terminal output and cleaning up indented literals.

The unicodedata module inspects and normalizes Unicode. normalize('NFC', text) combines characters into a canonical form so visually identical strings compare equal, which matters because an accented letter can be encoded multiple ways. It also exposes a character's name and category, useful for stripping accents or classifying text.

str.encode() turns text into bytes using an encoding (default UTF-8), and bytes.decode() turns bytes back into text. Files, sockets, and hashes work in bytes, so you cross this boundary constantly. A UnicodeDecodeError usually means you guessed the wrong encoding; UTF-8 is the safe modern default.

In Python 3, str holds Unicode text and bytes holds raw 8-bit data, and they never mix implicitly. You cannot concatenate them or compare them as equal. Network and file I/O often deal in bytes, so encode text before sending and decode bytes after receiving, choosing UTF-8 unless you know otherwise.

bytearray is the mutable cousin of bytes, so you can change individual byte values in place and extend it without making new objects. This makes it efficient for building up binary buffers or modifying data byte by byte. Slicing and indexing return integers for single bytes and bytearrays for ranges.

The struct module converts between Python values and C-style packed bytes using a format string, like struct.pack('>I', 1024) for a big-endian 4-byte unsigned int. It is essential for reading binary file formats and network protocols. The first character sets byte order and alignment: > big-endian, < little-endian, ! network order.

int.to_bytes(length, 'big') turns an integer into a fixed-length byte sequence, and int.from_bytes(data, 'big') reverses it. You specify the length and byte order. These are the clean, dependency-free way to serialize integers for binary protocols when struct's format strings feel like overkill.

The bin, hex, and oct functions return string representations with 0b, 0x, and 0o prefixes. To parse, pass a base to int, like int('ff', 16) or int('0b101', 0) where base 0 reads the prefix. Underscores are allowed in numeric literals for readability, such as 1_000_000 or 0xFF_FF.

divmod(a, b) returns the quotient and remainder as a tuple in one call: divmod(17, 5) gives (3, 2). It is handy for converting totals into units, like divmod(total_seconds, 60) to get minutes and remaining seconds. It avoids computing // and % separately and reads more clearly.

Python's round uses banker's rounding, rounding halves to the nearest even number, so round(0.5) is 0 and round(1.5) is 2. This reduces cumulative bias in large datasets but surprises people expecting always-up rounding. For money or strict control, use the decimal module with an explicit rounding mode.

The built-in pow(base, exp, mod) computes (base ** exp) % mod efficiently, even for huge exponents, without ever building the giant intermediate number. This modular exponentiation is the backbone of cryptography like RSA. Plain base ** exp % mod would first compute the full enormous power, which is far slower.

all(iterable) returns True if every item is truthy, and any(iterable) returns True if at least one is. They short-circuit, stopping as soon as the answer is known, and accept a generator so you can write any(x > 100 for x in data). Note all of an empty iterable is True and any of an empty one is False.

filter(func, iterable) lazily yields items where func returns truthy; filter(None, items) drops all falsy values. It returns an iterator, so wrap it in list to materialize. A comprehension like [x for x in items if cond] is usually considered more readable and equally fast.

map(func, iterable) lazily applies func to each item and can take several iterables to feed multiple arguments at once. It returns an iterator, so consume it with list, sum, or a loop. For simple transformations many Pythonistas prefer a generator expression, but map shines when func is an existing named function.

In a boolean context, empty containers, 0, 0.0, empty strings, and None are falsy, while everything else is truthy. This lets you write 'if items:' instead of 'if len(items) > 0:'. Be careful that 0 and empty are falsy, so 'if value:' wrongly skips a legitimate zero; compare to None explicitly when zero is valid.

== compares values for equality, while 'is' compares object identity, asking whether two names point to the very same object. Use 'is' only for singletons like None, True, and False: write 'if x is None'. Using 'is' on numbers or strings works sometimes due to caching but is unreliable and a real bug source.

Python lets you chain comparisons naturally: 0 <= x < 100 means 0 <= x and x < 100, evaluating x only once. This reads like math and is clearer than writing the two comparisons with an explicit and. You can chain more than two, like a < b < c < d.

Slicing extracts a subsequence with [start:stop:step], where start is inclusive and stop is exclusive. seq[::-1] reverses, seq[::2] takes every other item, and negative indices count from the end. Slicing a list returns a shallow copy, so seq[:] is a quick way to copy the top level.

Negative indices count from the end: seq[-1] is the last item and seq[-2] the second to last. This avoids the verbose seq[len(seq)-1]. In slices, seq[:-1] drops the last item and seq[-3:] takes the last three, which is handy for trimming.

Assignment never copies; both names point to the same list. For a shallow copy use list(x), x[:], or x.copy(), which duplicates the outer list but shares the inner objects. For a fully independent clone of nested structures, use copy.deepcopy. Forgetting this leads to surprise mutations through aliases.

copy.deepcopy recursively copies an object and everything it contains, so the result shares nothing with the original. It correctly handles cycles by tracking already-copied objects. It is slower and more memory-hungry than a shallow copy, so reach for it only when nested mutable data must be fully independent.

Lists are mutable and meant for ordered collections you change, while tuples are immutable and often used for fixed records or as dict keys. Because tuples cannot change, they are hashable (if their contents are) and slightly lighter. A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (x,).

list.append(x) adds a single item, even if x is itself a list, so appending [1,2] nests a list inside. list.extend(iterable) adds each element of the iterable individually. Confusing the two is a frequent bug; use extend or += to concatenate and append to add one element.

list.insert(i, x) places x before index i, list.remove(x) deletes the first occurrence by value (raising ValueError if absent), and list.pop(i) removes and returns the item at i, defaulting to the last. Inserting or popping near the front is O(n) because later items shift; use a deque for heavy front operations.

reversed(seq) returns a lazy iterator that yields items back to front without copying the sequence, so it is memory-friendly for large lists. seq[::-1] also reverses but builds a full new list. For an in-place reverse of a list, list.reverse() mutates it and returns None.

list.sort() reorders a list in place and returns None, while sorted(iterable) leaves the input alone and returns a new sorted list. A classic bug is writing items = items.sort() and getting None. Use sorted when you need to keep the original or when sorting any iterable, not just a list.

Strings are immutable, so methods like upper, replace, and strip return new strings rather than changing the original. This means s.replace('a','b') has no effect unless you reassign s. Building a string by repeated concatenation in a loop is slow; collect parts in a list and ''.join them instead.

str.replace(old, new) returns a new string with every occurrence of old swapped for new, and a third count argument limits how many. Because strings are immutable it does not change the original, so you must reassign the result. To replace by pattern rather than a literal, use re.sub.

str.startswith and str.endswith test prefixes and suffixes and return a bool. A handy trick is passing a tuple of options, like name.endswith(('.jpg', '.png', '.gif')), which is True if any match. They are clearer and faster than slicing the string and comparing.

str.find(sub) returns the index of the first occurrence or -1 if not found, while str.index raises ValueError when absent. Use find when missing is normal, index when absence is a real error. To just test presence, the 'in' operator like 'cat' in text is simpler than either.

str.count(sub) returns how many non-overlapping times a substring appears, and accepts optional start and end bounds to search a slice. 'banana'.count('a') is 3. For counting characters across a string, collections.Counter is more general and gives you all counts at once.

str.title() capitalizes the first letter of each word but mishandles apostrophes, turning "don't" into "Don'T". For case-insensitive comparison, str.casefold() is stronger than lower() because it also folds special characters like the German ß. Use casefold, not lower, when comparing text from many languages.

Multiplying a string by an integer repeats it: '-' * 20 makes a 20-dash line and 'ab' * 3 gives 'ababab'. The same works for lists, but beware that [0] * 3 of an immutable element is fine while [[]] * 3 creates three references to the same inner list. Use a comprehension for independent inner lists.

You can combine tools: for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(list1, list2)) gives an index plus paired items, with parentheses to unpack the zip tuple. This beats manual index bookkeeping. When you only need parallel items and no counter, drop the enumerate and just zip.

A for or while loop can have an else clause that runs only if the loop finished without hitting a break. It is perfect for search loops: break when found, and the else handles the not-found case. The name is confusing; read it as 'no break' rather than 'otherwise'.

The nonlocal keyword lets an inner function rebind a variable in the nearest enclosing function rather than creating a new local one. Without it, assigning to that name inside the inner function would shadow the outer one. It is what makes closures that update an enclosed counter work.

The global keyword declares that assignments inside a function should target the module-level variable instead of creating a local. You only need it when you assign, not when you merely read a global. Heavy use of global often signals that data should be passed as arguments or held in an object instead.

A closure is a nested function that remembers variables from the function that created it, even after that outer function has returned. This lets you build customized functions, like a multiplier factory that captures its factor. Each call to the factory captures its own copy of the enclosing variables.

A classic gotcha: functions defined in a loop that reference the loop variable all see its final value, because closures capture the variable, not its value at definition time. Fix it by binding the value as a default argument, like lambda x, i=i: x + i. This snapshots i at each iteration.

A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a replacement, applied with @ syntax above a definition. It wraps the original to add behavior like timing, logging, or caching without editing the function body. Pair it with functools.wraps so the wrapped function keeps its name and docstring.

A decorator that takes arguments needs three nested layers: an outer function taking the arguments, a middle one taking the function, and an inner wrapper. @repeat(3) calls repeat(3) first, which returns the actual decorator. The extra layer is what lets you configure the decorator at the point of use.

Decorators can also wrap classes, receiving the class and returning a (possibly modified) class. The built-in @dataclass works this way, and you can write your own to register classes or inject methods. For per-instance behavior, descriptors or metaclasses are usually a better fit than a class decorator.

The @property decorator turns a method into a read-only attribute, so obj.area calls the method with no parentheses. Add a matching @area.setter to allow assignment with validation. This lets you start with a plain attribute and later add logic without changing how callers access it.

@staticmethod defines a method that takes neither self nor cls, just a function grouped under the class for organization. @classmethod receives the class as cls and is the idiomatic way to write alternative constructors, like a from_string factory that returns cls(...). cls respects subclassing, so factories return the right subtype.

Defining __slots__ as a tuple of attribute names stops Python from giving each instance a __dict__, saving memory and slightly speeding attribute access. The trade-off is you cannot add attributes not listed in __slots__. It is worth it when you create huge numbers of small, fixed-shape objects.

__repr__ should return an unambiguous, ideally eval-able representation aimed at developers, shown in the REPL and by repr(). __str__ returns a friendly, readable form for end users, shown by print() and str(). If you define only one, define __repr__, since __str__ falls back to it when missing.

Define __eq__ to control equality, but if you do and want the object usable in sets or as a dict key, you must also define __hash__ consistently, since defining __eq__ alone makes the class unhashable. Objects that compare equal must hash equal. For immutable value objects, base both on the same fields.

An object is iterable if it has __iter__ returning an iterator, and an iterator has __next__ that returns the next value or raises StopIteration when done. Implementing these lets your class work in for loops and comprehensions. Often the simplest implementation is a __iter__ method that is itself a generator using yield.

__getitem__(self, key) makes obj[key] work, __setitem__ makes assignment work, and __delitem__ handles del. Implementing __getitem__ alone also makes an object iterable through the old protocol if it accepts integer indices starting at 0. These let your class behave like a list or dict.

Defining __call__ makes instances callable like functions, so obj() runs that method. This is useful for objects that carry configuration but act like a function, such as a multiplier or a stateful counter. It is the mechanism behind class-based decorators and many function-like helpers.

Implementing __enter__ and __exit__ makes a class usable in a with statement. __enter__ sets up and returns the value bound by 'as', while __exit__ tears down and receives any exception details. Returning True from __exit__ suppresses an exception, so usually return None to let it propagate.

The method resolution order is the linearized sequence Python searches for attributes across base classes, computed by the C3 algorithm and visible as Class.__mro__. super() follows this order rather than naming a parent directly, which makes cooperative multiple inheritance work. Calling super() consistently in every class keeps the chain intact.

super() returns a proxy that dispatches method calls to the next class in the MRO, letting subclasses extend rather than replace parent behavior. In Python 3 you call it with no arguments inside a method. Use it especially in __init__ to ensure parent initialization runs, and consistently across a hierarchy for multiple inheritance.

isinstance(obj, cls) checks whether an object is an instance of a class or its subclasses, and issubclass checks a class relationship. Pass a tuple of classes to test several at once, like isinstance(x, (int, float)). Prefer isinstance over comparing type(obj) == cls, which fails for subclasses.

getattr(obj, 'name', default) reads an attribute by string name and returns the default if it is missing, setattr(obj, 'name', value) writes one, and hasattr tests presence. They enable dynamic, data-driven attribute access where the name is computed at runtime. Use them when a name comes from a string rather than being known in code.

vars(obj) returns the object's __dict__ of instance attributes, and dir(obj) lists all accessible names including inherited methods. dir() with no argument lists names in the current scope. They are introspection tools for exploring objects interactively or for debugging, not usually for production logic.

The two-argument form iter(callable, sentinel) repeatedly calls the callable and yields results until one equals the sentinel. A classic use is iter(lambda: f.read(1024), b'') to read a file in chunks until EOF. It turns a call-until-done pattern into a clean iterator.

next(iterator) advances an iterator and returns its next value, raising StopIteration when exhausted. Pass a second argument as a default to return instead of raising, like next(gen, None). Combined with a generator expression, next(x for x in items if cond) finds the first matching item lazily without scanning the rest.

StopIteration is the signal an iterator raises when it has no more items, which for loops catch automatically to end.
