Since Python 3.7, letting StopIteration leak out of a generator turns into a RuntimeError instead of silently ending the generator, preventing a confusing class of bugs. Use return inside a generator to stop it cleanly.

A generator produces values one at a time and holds only its current state, so it can process a billion items or an infinite stream in constant memory. A list holds everything at once. Trade-offs: you can iterate a generator only once and cannot index it or take its len.

itertools functions like product, permutations, and combinations return lazy iterators, so they never build the full, often astronomically large, result in memory. You consume them one item at a time in a loop. Wrapping one in list() to count or store it can blow up memory, so prefer summing or filtering lazily.

json cannot serialize a datetime by default. Pass a default function to json.dumps that converts unknown objects, like default=str or one that calls .isoformat(). On the way back, json gives you the string, and you parse it with datetime.fromisoformat. There is no automatic round-trip for custom types.

To serialize custom objects, pass default=func to json.dumps; it is called for any value json cannot handle and should return something serializable. For more control, subclass json.JSONEncoder and override its default method, then pass cls=YourEncoder. Common targets are datetimes, sets (convert to lists), and Decimals.

The configparser module reads and writes INI-style configuration files with sections in brackets and key = value lines. Values come back as strings, so use getint, getfloat, and getboolean for typed reads. It is built in and great for simple human-editable settings, though TOML is now Python's preferred config format.

tomllib, added in Python 3.11, parses TOML configuration files, the format used by pyproject.toml. It is read-only and you must open the file in binary mode, like tomllib.load(open('config.toml', 'rb')). For writing TOML you still need a third-party library, but reading is now standard library.

For adding numbers, the built-in sum is clearer and faster than functools.reduce with operator.add, and math.prod (Python 3.8+) multiplies a sequence. Reach for reduce only when the operation is genuinely custom. sum also takes a start value, useful as sum(items, start=0) or to concatenate lists, though join is better for strings.

math.prod(iterable), added in Python 3.8, multiplies all the numbers in an iterable, the multiplication counterpart to sum. math.prod([1,2,3,4]) is 24. It takes an optional start value and is clearer than a reduce or a manual loop for computing products like factorials or array sizes.

range is a lazy, memory-light sequence, not a list, so range(1_000_000_000) costs almost nothing until you iterate it. It supports indexing, slicing, len, and the 'in' test, and that membership test is O(1) for arithmetic ranges. Wrap it in list() only when you actually need a concrete list.

Format specs control alignment with <, >, and ^ for left, right, and center, optionally preceded by a fill character. f'{name:*^20}' centers name in 20 columns padded with asterisks. Combine with a width to build tidy tables in terminal output without manual spacing.

Since Python 3.8, f-strings support a self-documenting form: f'{value=}' prints both the expression text and its value, like 'value=42'. Add a format spec after it, like f'{ratio=:.2f}'. This is a fast, readable replacement for typing the variable name twice in print debugging.

sys.path is the list of directories Python searches when importing modules, built from the script's directory, the PYTHONPATH environment variable, and installation defaults. Appending to it lets you import from custom locations, though packaging your code properly is cleaner. Import order matters because the first match on the path wins.

The importlib module imports modules programmatically when the name is only known at runtime, via importlib.import_module('package.name'). importlib.reload re-imports an already loaded module, useful in interactive sessions after editing code. It is the supported alternative to the discouraged __import__ builtin for dynamic imports.

A directory becomes a regular package when it contains an __init__.py file, which runs when the package is first imported and can expose a curated public API. Since Python 3.3, namespace packages can omit it, but a normal package still uses it to control imports and define __all__. Keep heavy work out of it to avoid slow imports.

Inside a package, a leading dot makes an import relative: from . import sibling imports from the same package and from ..pkg import x goes up one level. Relative imports only work when the file is run as part of a package, not as a top-level script, which is a common source of ImportError confusion.

Defining __all__ as a list of names in a module controls what 'from module import *' brings in, and signals the module's intended public API. It does not stop explicit imports of other names. Curating __all__ keeps wildcard imports clean and documents which symbols are meant for outside use.

A circular import happens when two modules import each other, and it can fail because one is only half-initialized when the other tries to use it. Fixes include moving the import inside a function so it runs later, importing the module rather than a name from it, or restructuring to break the cycle. It often signals tangled module boundaries.

The weakref module creates references that do not keep an object alive, so it can still be garbage-collected. WeakValueDictionary holds values weakly, useful for caches that should not pin objects in memory. When the target is collected, the weak reference becomes None or vanishes from the weak collection, preventing memory leaks from lingering caches.

CPython frees most objects immediately via reference counting: when the last reference goes away, the object is destroyed. A separate cyclic garbage collector in the gc module periodically cleans up reference cycles that counting alone cannot reclaim. You rarely manage memory by hand, but understanding this explains why __del__ timing can be tricky.

The contextvars module provides context-local variables that work correctly with async tasks and threads, unlike thread-locals which break across awaits. A ContextVar holds a value scoped to the current execution context, and each task gets its own copy. It is how libraries propagate request data through async code cleanly.

Passing frozen=True to @dataclass makes instances immutable: assigning to a field raises FrozenInstanceError, and the class gets a __hash__ so instances work as dict keys and set members. This is ideal for value objects that should never change after creation. Use object.__setattr__ in __post_init__ if you must set a field during construction.

A dataclass can define __post_init__, which runs right after the generated __init__ finishes, for validation or computing derived fields. Fields declared with field(init=False) are skipped by __init__ and typically set here. It is where you put logic that the auto-generated constructor cannot express on its own.

typing.NamedTuple lets you define a named tuple with a class body and type annotations, like a Point class with x: int and y: int. It reads more clearly than collections.namedtuple and adds type hints, while still producing a real, immutable tuple. You can also give fields default values and add methods.

Pathlib's object methods replace most os.path functions: Path.exists() for os.path.exists, p.parent for os.path.dirname, p.name for basename, p.stem and p.suffix for splitext parts, and the / operator for join. New code should prefer pathlib for readability, while os.path remains common in older code and a few low-level cases.

The glob module matches filenames with shell-style wildcards: glob.glob('*.txt') in the current directory, '**/*.py' with recursive=True for a deep search. The related fnmatch module matches a single name against a pattern without touching the filesystem. Pathlib's glob and rglob methods cover the same ground in object form.

subprocess.run runs an external command and waits for it to finish, returning a CompletedProcess with returncode, stdout, and stderr. Pass the command as a list of arguments, add capture_output=True and text=True to get strings, and check=True to raise on failure. Avoid shell=True with untrusted input, which invites injection.

Calling subprocess with shell=True runs your command through the shell, so unsanitized input can inject extra commands. The safe approach is to pass the command as a list of separate arguments and leave shell=False (the default), which never invokes a shell. Only use shell=True for trusted, fixed commands that genuinely need shell features.

Because of the Global Interpreter Lock, threads in CPython cannot run Python bytecode in true parallel, so threading helps I/O-bound work where threads wait on the network or disk. For CPU-bound work that must use many cores, use multiprocessing, which runs separate processes each with their own interpreter and GIL. Python 3.13's experimental free-threaded build aims to relax this.

The Global Interpreter Lock is a mutex that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time in CPython, simplifying memory management but limiting CPU-bound parallelism. I/O releases the GIL, so threads still help with network and disk waits. Python 3.13 ships an experimental build that can disable the GIL for real multi-core threading.

concurrent.futures offers a high-level interface for parallelism. ThreadPoolExecutor suits I/O-bound tasks and ProcessPoolExecutor suits CPU-bound ones, and both share the same API. executor.map applies a function across inputs, while submit returns a Future you can check or wait on. Using it as a context manager cleanly shuts down the pool.

asyncio runs concurrent I/O on a single thread using async def coroutines and await. await yields control while waiting, letting other coroutines run, which scales to thousands of network connections cheaply. asyncio.run starts the event loop, and asyncio.gather runs several coroutines concurrently and collects their results.

An async def function is a coroutine that does nothing until awaited or scheduled on the event loop. Inside it, await pauses on another awaitable and frees the loop to run other tasks. You can only await inside an async function, and mixing blocking calls into async code stalls the whole loop, defeating the purpose.

asyncio.gather(*coros) schedules several coroutines to run concurrently and returns their results in order once all finish. Pass return_exceptions=True to collect errors instead of failing fast on the first one. It is the simplest way to fan out many independent async I/O operations, like fetching several URLs at once.

asyncio.create_task schedules a coroutine to run concurrently in the background and returns a Task you can await later. Unlike calling a coroutine directly, it starts running on the event loop right away. Keep a reference to the task, since the loop only holds a weak reference and an untracked task can be garbage-collected mid-run.

The queue module provides thread-safe FIFO, LIFO, and priority queues for passing work between threads safely. queue.Queue handles all the locking, so producers put and consumers get without races. A common pattern uses a sentinel value or task_done/join to signal and wait for completion. For async code use asyncio.Queue instead.

threading.Lock guards a shared resource so only one thread accesses it at a time, preventing data races. Use it as a context manager, 'with lock:', to guarantee release even if the body raises. Keep critical sections small, acquire multiple locks in a consistent order to avoid deadlock, and prefer queues for passing data.

time.perf_counter() returns a high-resolution monotonic timer ideal for measuring elapsed time, since it never goes backward and ignores system clock changes. Subtract a start reading from an end reading to get seconds as a float. Use time.time() only for wall-clock timestamps, not for measuring durations.

The timeit module measures how long small code snippets take by running them many times, smoothing out noise. From the command line, python -m timeit '"-".join(str(n) for n in range(100))' benchmarks an expression. In code, timeit.timeit runs a statement repeatedly and returns the total time, giving fairer comparisons than a single perf_counter reading.

time.sleep(seconds) pauses the current thread for the given number of seconds, accepting a float for sub-second delays. It blocks only that thread, so other threads keep running. In async code use 'await asyncio.sleep(seconds)' instead, since time.sleep would freeze the entire event loop.

The calendar module works with dates at the month and year level: calendar.monthrange gives the weekday of the first day and the number of days in a month, isleap tests leap years, and it can render text or HTML calendars. It complements datetime, which handles specific points in time.

The fileinput module loops over lines from multiple files, or from standard input if no files are given, like a typical Unix filter. fileinput.input() with inplace=True even lets you edit files in place by printing the replacement for each line. It is a quick way to build grep- or sed-style command-line tools.
